Each discipline could feature on the Oscar podium The monochrome look with occasional glimpses of duotone and even muted full colour is really quite beautiful.

There's one scene in particular when Thomas Hutter (the surveyor sent in search of the Dracula, Count Orlok - a weak link with his daft Transylvanian voice played by Bill Skargård) walks through a forest and rests at a crossroads. The black and white design embraces the forest and the gently snowing sky to silhouette our hero in a scene that is as much a work of art as you will see in any cinema this year - it ranks alongside the umbrella scene in Conclave for breathtaking visual artistry.

But the great news stops there. Aside from two very good Exorcist-lite possession scenes Lily-Rose Depp shows she has not inherited her father's acting skills, failing to muster real tears when required. She's passable, but no more. Nicholas Hoult huffs and puffs his way through his role suggesting he too is being asked a little too much by Eggers. There's a particularly am-dram moment when he is helped home to is house with a bit of limping that's straight out of your local church hall.

Aaron Taylor Johnson and Emma Corrin make a rather better fist of it as the married friends of the stricken Hardings who take them into their care (not that that ends well). And Willem Dafoe is pretty good value as the pantomime Prof. Albin Eberhart von Franz.

There's no real acting glory on show here and that rather lumbers a production that veers between high camp comedy (unintentionally) and reasonably intense jeopardy, but it's all a bit too long and the story too well known to really grab you by the cohonas.

The script's a bit cod in places and it works (I think as Stoker intended) more as a love story than a horror, so in that respect I suppose it succeeds more than it fails, but overall it's a bit of a disappointment. Its current score of 7.8 on IMBD mystifies me. It's certainly not that good.

reviews.author: jkanecoleman
reviews.body:
The story of Nosferatu isn't going to be original, especially if you are familiar with the lore/Bram Stoker's Dracula. What is original is the vision this film is retold in. It's a throw back to when films created atmosphere and you don't know what is going to happen.

The acting is top knotch and cinematography and score are peerless. Those looking for a fast food horror film will be disappointed, but if you want something with gothic substance and shadowy bleakness, this retelling is for you. Possibly my favorite version of a Wallachian Warlord turned Vampire.

The middle does drag a slight bit, which is why I gave it an 8, but it's a wonderful film made for those that crave more from their movies.

reviews.author: danyel_008
reviews.body: The movie started well for me but I slowly lost interest little by little when minutes passed, the story is slow paced and unnecessary long, the tone is very dark and they keep it until the movie finishes which is good. The visuals are stunning and the atmosphere from that time is very well put in the movie, it makes you feel like you are there. The horror scenes are good but sometimes cringe and too long. The cast is stacked with legends and talents. As you can see there are a lot of advantages and disadvantages but in essence the movie is decent but can be boring for some people. I'm not sure if I recommend it or not, like I said in the title, mixed feelings. For some people can be good and for others can be cringe and boring.

reviews.author: codykself
reviews.body: Honestly, reading through the reviews I was shocked to see how so many found this movie "boring" to "walking out", as the atmosphere and buildup of this film is one of the best in modern horror to date. So many times the true nature of the horror genre is bled out through useless jump scares, an over abundance of gore for shock value, or with "supernatural" elements that are just laughable. Cut to 2024 Nosferatu and you'll understand what a horror movie should be. The eerie suspense, the constant feeling of dread, and the overwhelming sense of Orlock stalking from the shadows- all of this is just the sprinkles on top of the Great-Movie-Sunday. The cinematography was beautiful, the set was astonishing considering the budget used, and the fantastic use of negative space and subtle hints in the backgrounds of scenes make for a constant feeling of someone stalking from the shadows beyond. This movie is not only a fantastic example of what makes a horror film great, but specifically finds the scariest and most horrifying aspects of the Vampire genre and combines them with a world class example of utilizing "the unknown" to bring forth dread and terror. Wonderful. I can't wait to see more from Eggers after this incredible adaptation- I truly believe this will be viewed as one of the Dracula greats.

reviews.author: Beyondtherain
reviews.body: I thought this film would be much more intense and way scarier...it was just decent...The jump scares all failed and the Nosferatu makeup failed, I was waiting for Nosferatu to show up but realized the tall dude with the mustache was him...he looked like Stone cold steve austin or Freddie Mercury ...Jump scares are cheap scares but even in this film they were VERY CHEAP and didn't work, I loved the visuals and settings, but the Nosferatu himself didn't work for me. He was not scary. The Last Voyage of the Demeter was a bit better but no one probably cares lol. Also the original Nosferatu design is so much scarier...was hoping we would get that kind of makeup along with a twist...we didn't get much at all...will never rewatch this film again sadly. Decent for a 1st time watch...Loved the Lighthouse, liked the VVITCH...sadly this one let me down.

reviews.author: mskturi
reviews.body:
The story of Dracula/Nosferatu has been told enough times in the past with better acting, script, scares, scenery, atmosphere, and most importantly-- backstory!

Despite the hype generated around this film, it was a disappointing, cliched train wreck imo. The much anticipated gothic setting, costume, lighting, and makeup were the only aspects to appreciate here. It also scored high on the revolting-meter, if that's your taste in merit.

There was nothing new in terms of re-telling the Bram Stoker story. In addition, it didn't follow logic-- for example: how can you bring someone from Transylvania to Germany via boat? I don't believe there's a sea separating the two.

The acting was melodramatic: exaggerated convulsing, crying, screaming, and moaning throughout the film. Yes we know, it's about carnal pleasures and nothing else.

Lily Depp has a boring, flat, permanently droopy-lidded on-screen presence without variation of mood. Her husband (Hoult) doesn't seem to care much about anything except saving himself and getting a quick one. Nosferatu has a hilariously over-the-top booming wheezing fake-accented voice and is not scary~ neither in his scurvy nakedness nor his bear-skin cloak. He has no character outside of being an irritable, tyrannical hermit with a Lorax mustache making raspy gurgling sounds. His creeping shadow-clawed hand and Latin whispering brought neither foreboding nor anticipation to scenes--having seen this visual repeated in previous films. The story and characters were predictable and one-dimensional-- I was hoping someone would crack a joke to turn it into a parody.

There's no big reveal about why the two main characters, who appear to have zero chemistry, fell in love in the first place, or an offer to tell the story from another interesting angle. Could Eggers not have found a good screenwriter instead of trying to do everything himself?

I found Nosferatu to be an unconvincing and shallow rendition of an iconic love story.

The only merit that kept me from falling asleep during the 2 hours was the deafening sound effects of convulsing, screaming, wailing, blood-glugging, hooves pounding, wood creaking, stone crumbling, chains rattling, rats squealing, coffins and doors clanking open and shut, just to make sure I've got the full sensory vampire/gothic experience rammed into my brain.

reviews.author: ivfangs
reviews.body: I read the first few wave of reviews and although I had high hopes, some negative reviews really curbed my expectations. Now a few hours after seeing and digesting the film I got to say this movie was really well done. The negatives others had about the movie didn't resonate with me at all. I felt like this movie is a real gem that should be enjoyed in the theater. The cinematography is the precipice and the actors did an incredible job. You feel the emotions and strife in every scene. The movie score is fantastic as well. As a vampire movie lover, Nosferatu 2024 has made its mark as a must see. Very well done!

reviews.author: elicopperman
reviews.body:
As of this Christmas day, horror filmmaker Robert Eggers has released his own retelling of the iconic Dracula knockoff, Nosferatu. Marking the second theatrically released remake of F. W. Murnau's gothic horror classic, the film has marked a return to form for Eggers in bringing the source material into the 21st century. It appears his efforts have paid off as the film has garnered critical acclaim for its passionate recreation of the gothic nightmare, especially following its world premiere in Berlin earlier this month. So looking at the film on its own merit, how well does it come off in a modern lense?

Much like the original film, Eggers' feature follows a real estate salesman named Thomas Hutter, who is tasked with securing residence for wealthy Transylvanian Count Orlok, only to discover that the vampiric count is infatuated with his wife Ellen. In regards to how the story is told, a lot of emphasis is put on Orlok's desire towards Ellen and destroying anyone and anything in his path. Many of the terrifying sequences are carried through strikingly dark shot composition and spine tingling music, allowing the mere presence of Orlok, the black plague he unleashes in Germany, and those who fear him to seep into one's soul. Cinematographer Jarin Blaschke depicts a respectful homage towards 19th-century Romanticism, allowing the thrills to unfold amidst the erotic tension and body horror on display. In fact, the erotic elements feel more terrifying than the film's intended terror shown, which does make sense given how truly demonic Orlok's lust towards his prey is. Through these notable production qualities, the tale of Nosferatu has never felt this artistically frightening before.

With a strongly crafted feature comes a solid cast, and Bill Skarsgard nearly steals the show portraying Orlok in all his creepy alore. Seeing him interact with Nicholas Hoult as Thomas and Lily-Rose Depp as Ellen individually lends to some truly gut wrenching tension as he consumes their souls, allowing a lot of genuine fear to set in as the aforementioned characters lose their grip on reality. While Friedrich Harding has too obvious of a payoff, Aaron Taylor-Johnson elicates the right amount of blinded skepticism through stoic yet ruffled stubbornness. Emma Corrin portrays arguably the film's most sympathetic character in Friedrich's wife Anna, and any scene where she's by her children or Ellen could make one shed a tear in concern. Also, you can never go wrong with Willem Dafoe in any role he's in, as he brings the role of Prof. Albin Eberhart Von Franz to life with subtle devotion and intrinsic knowledge beyond the realm of organic science. One can't deny how talented Robert Eggers is to the point of instilling such devoted trust in his cast for this kind of movie.

Brilliantly crafted and acted as it is gothically haunting, Robert Eggers' remake of Nosferatu is a spellbinding horror that pays its deepest respect towards the original German expressionist film and offers a repulsively beautiful look into the titular character. Now that the film has been unleashed for the world to see, I cannot recommend it enough for horror fans, Nosferatu enthusiasts and the general public alike. Time will surely tell what Eggers' next project will entail, but if this passion project of his has proven anything, it's that his divine admiration towards cinematic horror will be unlike anything else out there.

reviews.author: wednesdayskorner
reviews.body:
No spoilers in saying Nosferatu is an appropriately dark, gothic, gorgeously grotesque, vampyre horror film.

I would recommend not being in a theater with a lot of distracting food service. I saw the 35 mm at Alamo Drafthouse and would have preferred not seeing people walking back and forth like they do there.

The Northman, The Lighthouse, The Witch are all primers for the Eggers technique.

I was fascinated by the prosthetics. The large, looming physicality of the count is felt in the sound and visual effects.

Minimally lit using candles, lanterns and natural light. The camera lingers for all the special moments and sometimes I wanted more time to observe.

The actor who plays Knock (the "Renfield" to Orlok) is Simon McBurney. This is a character he probably waited his whole life to play.

Can't mistake Lily-Rose Depp. She looks like both of her parents.

🐀

reviews.author: Vince_D
reviews.body:
I've somehow never seen a Robert Eggers film before, so I wasn't sure what to expect. As soon as the film started, I was drawn to how the pacing, camerawork, and production design reminded me of a kind of classic filmmaking that feels all but lost today. Every frame here feels like it belongs on the wall of a gallery -- beautifully composed, alive with detail. This is the kind of film that immerses you in its world with such care and precision that you almost forget you're watching a film at all. Interestingly, it felt like more than just a remake of F. W. Murnau's original Nosferatu (1922) -- which it paid homage to without the expressionism -- but also to Coppola's Bram Stoker's Dracula (1992), and even the atmosphere of the old Hammer Horror films.

What I really loved about this film was the masterful use of the camerawork to support the story. A perfect example is the scene where Hutter leaves for Orlok's castle. As Hutter walks away, the camera slowly pulls back from Ellen as she stands center frame with a look of despair. It's a subtle moment, but the way the camera pulls back conveys her sense of abandonment and isolation.

Then there's the "Borgo Pass" sequence, which might be one of the most captivating and brilliantly paced stretches of film I've seen in years. From Hutter's departure from the Gypsy village to his trek through desolate mountains, and finally to his arrival at Count Orlok's castle, the cinematography is extraordinary.

As for the performances; Lily-Rose Depp's anguish and melancholy, and the way she is treated as hysterical due to the societal norms of the era, is as effective as anyone could be, dispelling any notions of nepotism-casting I walked into the film with. Her character's treatment as "hysterical" due to the era's societal norms adds layers to her performance. Similarly, Nicholas Hoult brings a believable vulnerability to Hutter. Also, Bill Skarsgård and Willem Dafoe are great as Orlok and Von Franz, respectively, each embodying their characters with menace and gravitas.

It has been argued that in the original novel, Stoker was addressing themes of disease and xenophobia -- issues that remain disturbingly relevant today. Stoker's vampire served as a metaphor for the spread of contagion and the fear of the "other," reflecting the anxieties of a Victorian society grappling with outbreaks of disease and the growing influx of immigrants. Whether or not it was Eggers' intention in Nosferatu, these fears are resurrected with chilling resonance. The film evokes the unease of outside threats invading a community, whether through Orlok's supernatural influence as a metaphor for dangerous outsiders or the stark imagery of vampirism as a disease spreading like a plague. In a world still reeling from global pandemics and grappling with tensions over immigration and cultural displacement -- regardless of which side of the aisle one leans toward -- these themes feel as urgent as ever, reminding us how fear of the unknown continues to shape our collective psyche.

That said, the film is not without flaws. I found the ending somewhat confusing. Without giving away spoilers, Ellen's motivation was clear and understandable, but Orlok's final decisions felt ambiguous and out of character. Also, as captivated as I was, the film could have easily trimmed 20 minutes off the runtime; a complaint I have of most modern films.

Nosferatu isn't just a remake, nor is it merely a reimagining. In an era dominated by Superhero films and shaky cam-found footage fodder, Nosferatu is a reminder of what cinema can be when filmmakers care deeply about every frame, every sound, and every emotion.

reviews.author: dajm-85166
reviews.body: I had high hopes as I'm a fan of The Witch and The Lighthouse, but this movie was such a letdown. A few (very few) jump-scares aside, this movie did not provide a sense of fear, tension or dread. The use of dark lighting was overused and frustrating. The repeated scenes of characters' screaming fits of hysteria - ineffective and increasingly annoying. Worst of all, Orlok himself was simply not scary. As a child, I remember seeing clips from the original Nosferatu and finding it terrifying... in particular, Orlok's face, and the searing, iconic mage of his shadow walking up the stairs. But Eggers dropped the ball on this one. Skarsgard was made up big and ugly, yes, but fingernails aside, his certainly will not go down as one of the more frightening iterations of Dracula.

reviews.author: windowseat-29175
reviews.body:
I don't usually go for horror movies, but this one really surprised me.

Nosferatu was haunting and completely captivating-I couldn't look away (well, except for a few intense scenes, you know what I mean...).

It had this creeping sense of doom that kept me on edge the whole time, and the eerie atmosphere was just perfect. Sometimes I felt like I'm in a someone's bad dream.

The performances were absolutely amazing, and the whole vibe felt like a dark fairy tale made just for grown-ups.

It's chilling, beautiful, and unforgettable-a modern horror that's both visually stunning and deeply unsettling. Definitely one of the few horrors I'd indeed recommend!

reviews.author: danielgroza
reviews.body:
Equal parts repulsive and inviting, Robert Eggers' "Nosferatu" is worthy of bearing the name of its progenitor, F. W. Murnau's 1922 legend of the same title. But like all self-respecting filmmakers, Eggers also does more than just remake the classic movie with the modern, more accessible movie technology of the 21st Century. He also wants to leave his own teeth marks in it, so to speak.

More particular, his imprint is in the story's unlikely sexuality which he is not afraid to explore in all its taboo glory. There is, of course, a cryptic darkness, sense of dread and unbearable horror that doesn't ease down until the very end, but the occult lore its title character belongs to bears an unhealthy sense of morbid curiosity; the deadly danger surrounding him is an aphrodisiac; his degraded corpse-like towering figure--hinting at necrophiliac fantasies--target the darkest, most sadistic of perversions and guilty pleasures of our subconscious. This impossible antithesis is the engine of this movie, and is perfectly visualized in the very final shot--both beautiful and a blasphemy.

The entire thing is dark, slow and like its characters, some scenes are cleverly edited such that we also find it difficult to say what we are seeing is a dream or reality. Shades of black dominate its visuals, with the 19th Century German town of Wisborg looking both real and like a movie set, especially during an infamous shot referencing the original, in which the shadow of Orlok's hand flies over it as he spreads death to its inhabitants. And what a horrific being Orlok is. Portrayed by Bill Skarsgård, who is no stranger to characters belonging to the realm of cosmic evil, he perfectly nails the voice, as we hear Orlok way before we can truly see him. His approach to his voice--slow, thick, and loud, accentuating the R-sounds--gives Orlok an ancient aura, like he truly has spent Centuries serving darkness in solitude.

On the opposite side of the spectrum, we have Lily-Rose Depp's Ellen Hutter, an emotionally vulnerable maiden whose purity and helplessness paint her as the beauty to Skarsgård's beast. Depp's performance is twisted and tormented throughout, from anxiously begging her naive husband Thomas (Nicholas Hoult) not to go to Orlok's castle in the Carpathians to her constant torment at night, driven both by fear and sexual desire. Constantly, the movie is aggressively bombarding us with a loud score, as if trying to wake us up, but our nightmare is to powerful for us to do so. Add to that Orlok's constant tormented grunt and you have an incessant display of horror, one meant to fully consume its audience.

Let's be honest: 1922's "Nosferatu" was not scary, the technology was simply not there to do it so, but it was haunting, with Max Shreck's Orlok living rent-free in our minds. Now, over 100 years later, Eggers has more than the resources he needs to make this truly horrifying. And combined with arcane lore that makes us feel cursed just by looking at it, "Nosferatu" is like a damned box, one we open at our own risk, and once we do, we just can't shake that dreadful feeling that what we witnessed is haunting us long after the credits roll.

reviews.author: falling-sideways
reviews.body:
Went into this super excited. From the first time you saw Orlok's moustache, all I could think of was Jim Carrey's doctor Robotnik, and I haven't even seen any of the Sonic movies. I was having a good time up to that point.

I saw this with 3 other people and I came out of it with the most favourable opinion. Visually, it leaned hard on Sleepy Hollow and the Corpse Bride. There were scenes where Ellen looked almost identical to Victoria. Story telling-wise it fell short of both. The timeline was tricky to follow. (How do you get 3 custom coffins in 2 hours in the 1830's?)and characters not aging etc. Parts felt edgy for the sake of being edgy. I dunno. It had some visual striking moments and some moments with good performances but overall, disappointing.

reviews.author: EdgarST
reviews.body:
The «Nosferatu» of 2024 really missed its opportunity with everything technology offers now. My initial resistance (and probably that of most of those who saw the 1922 versions by F. W. Murnau and the 1979 versions by Werner Herzog) was not understanding why they needed to adapt Bram Stoker's novel «Dracula again» following the 1922 aesthetic and option, and using the same title. A young friend told me that classics should be "updated for the new generations to see," to which I replied that, according to his logic, a new Mona Lisa should be painted or a David re-sculpted every now and then. The friend argued that it was not the case, since those are works of art.

So what are the films of Murnau and Herzog? That is where I saw part of the problem: young people everywhere in the world have grown up under the imposition of the term "entertainment" to the detriment of understanding what is art. People do not see cinema as a possible artistic expression, and when they are confronted with film works with artistic intentions, such those made by Antonioni, Buñuel, Altman, Kurosawa or Pasolini, they call it "pretentious." Postmodernists like Wes Anderson managed to harmonize commercial ends with art, but not all filmmakers are so gifted.

Robert Eggers, the screenwriter-director of this new «Nosferatu» (there are others, such as the 2023 film directed by David Lee Fisher), is not a filmmaker who stands out artistically, as he has shown with «The VVitch» and «The Lighthouse,» melodramas distinguished by affected aesthetic and stereotyped dramaturgy. Here he does not go beyond that, but instead of reconciling the present with the ideas and options of the masters who preceded him, as Herzog did (he broke the subterfuges of Murnau, who did not have the rights to film Stoker's novel, and opted for an ending similar to Polanski's "Dance of the Vampires"), he speaks to us again of a "Count Orlok", when everybody who is familiar with Stoker's knows that this bloodthirsty entity is none other than Dracula.

Eggers was inspired by Herzog's images, casting Lily-Rose Depp (although she is not as beautiful as the Herzogian pale and tragic heroine as played by Isabelle Adjani), imitated images from William Friedkin's «The Exorcist,» introduced nudity and gratuitous (and ugly) sex, as well as an occult subplot (by Willem Dafoe, as a libertine imitation of the novel's no-nonsense Dr. Van Helsing), created dialogues worthy of a soap opera (derivative of a 19th century novel), to the syrupy strains of Robin Carolan's score; carried his movie at a very slow pace, and extended the projection to 132 endless minutes, contrary to how Murnau and Herzog understood it, based on a simple, direct and horror plot.

Perhaps the most regrettable thing is that this film does not inspire much horror (at least not the audience that saw it in the theater with me, who found it inspiring soft giggles). Perhaps Lily-Rose Depp will be nominated for the Oscar for Best Tremor Actor of the Year, or Jarin Blaschke for the photography, but here the unreal prevails over the real images. Maybe you like the blood of Eggers' "gore" option (in the other versions, blood is very discreet)... But for me this work gave very little. Go and see it if you want. The film has its defenders.

reviews.author: troy-daniel-bush
reviews.body:
I've waited a long time for it, I watched the trailers and featurettes more than once, and I told myself it was gonna be the best movie I would see in 2024. And let me just say that it's not often a movie meets and surpasses the hype you create for yourself.

This movie might be a masterpiece. I'm not too sure yet. I don't see much wrong with it.

Every single performance is outstanding!

Eggers once again nails the time period that he tackles in terms of costumes, environments, and dialogue.

Speaking of the dialogue, it was compelling throughout!

The lengths Bill Skarsgård went to to portray this iconic character are truly admirable!

Nicholas Hoult needs to be in more movies!

Lily Rose Depp is absolutely insane!

You don't recognize Bill Skarsgård in any way whatsoever! His acting and makeup is that good!

The story is simple but intriguing. And it's elevated by the immaculate presentation, and the exploration of the respective themes.

The cinematography is gorgeous!

The musical score is haunting and powerful!

On a first watch, the pacing and editing feels off, but on a second watch you get a much better feel for them. At least that was the case for me.

The jumpscares in the movie are awesome!

You care about the characters facing Orlok! And the vampire himself is vile, disgusting, and intimidating. Take that, Stephanie!

For me it's one of those movies that gets better the more you think about it and the more times you watch it.

This is my second favorite movie from Eggers; behind The Lighthouse.

reviews.author: don-32621
reviews.body:
I loved the VVitch, but was less mesmerized and frightened by the Lighthouse. Nosferatu lands decidedly towards the former with just a tad bit of the dark humor rife in the latter. Eggers' maintains a reverence for the original simple story while taking full advantage of modern day visual and sound tools.

Willem Dafoe chews up the scenery in the most delightful and appropriate manner while Lily-Rose Depp delivers a convincing performance as the child bride whose soul has been hijacked by the mysterious, dark demon.

An unrecognizable Bill Skaarsgard is terrifying as the sinister and brutal Count Orlock with costuming and effects begging for Oscar consideration.

PRO TIP: for the full effect pre-view your trip to the theater with a screening of the original film.

reviews.author: jonas_sj1
reviews.body: It's amazing when a movie positively surprises you even though you already expected it to be good. Nosferatu is pretty much everything i hope it would be, and a bit better! It's the most narratively conventional movie that Eggers has done so far, wich was totally expected since it's basically a remake, but he adds a modern spin and edge to it that makes this version just as interesting and compelling as the original one. The movie is so good that not even the loud and stupid group of teenage girls sitting in the row behind me could ruin the experience. Add to that the fat and rude guy in the chair next to me... Not even those things ruined the mood that the movie put me in. It's not a perfect film, it starts to drag a bit after Thomas leaves Orlock's castle, and some of the supporting characters needed more development, but apart from that, Nosferatu is an effective ghotic horror that features some great performances, striking imagery, and a dark atmosphere that lingers with you long after you've watched it.

reviews.author: m-drennanjones
reviews.body:
I would have liked the movie better had Lilly Rose Depp not been the lead female. She has a dead eyed look to her and it seemed that is how she appeared for the whole of the movie. She is almost emotionless. Is she acting or is that just her face? I can't tell anymore. I would have liked to see her and Emma swap roles.

The plot and filmography was enjoyable. The male actors were good in their roles. Willem DaFoe was magnificent. Once again Bill Skaarsgard is able to transform into something unrecognizable and nail it, which I did not expect. There wasn't a lot of depth to some characters. I'd have like more of a back story to Ellen and Thomas.

reviews.author: JTReviewsPlus
reviews.body:
Nosferatu is a story that is heavily inspired by folklore that for some, might be a lot to take in all at once. However make no mistake, Robert Eggers masterfully crafts an engaging movie that's both immersive and suspenseful.

If you're familiar with Brahm Stoker's Dracula, you know what Nosferatu is about as it's a German adaptation of the story with a few changes here and there.

Bill Skarsgaard portrays a menacing Count Orlok AKA Nosferatu as he is legitimately unrecognizable. His accent is heavy, his voice is deep, and the makeup team captured that supernatural appearance that's gross to look at.

It's impressive how believable everyone was in this movie because the script perfectly captures the 1800s era. There were words and phrases I'd never heard of before and the fact everyone spoke it fluently and believably is a testament to the talent on-screen. Lily-Rose Depp stood out to me in particular since so much was required of her performance-wise. Willem Dafoe's third team-up with Eggers is another phenomenal one as he provides intrigue and a surprising amount of humor to the tale.

Nosferatu is a slower-paced story that captures the era it's set in to amazing effect. It's beautifully disturbing more than it is scary in the traditional sense. There's nuance to Nosferatu that may encourage deeper thinking afterward or another viewing entirely but the fantastic performances, engaging characters, and gothic setting make for a memorable retelling of the 1920's classic nonetheless.

reviews.author: Dabec70
reviews.body: How is this movie rated M, while One Piece is rated MA15+, is beyond me. I went with my 14yo daughter who had her eyes closed throughout the movie. An older teenage girl sitting next to us did the same. The movie is an uneasy, stomach upsetting, art form. Robert Eggers has coined himself with this and his previous couple of movies as probably the most original horror movie director of the current time. Stakes are high for his next movie. This is the best made Dracula movie I have seen, and I have seen them most, although the ending was a bit flat. Great acting from everyone. The picture, effects, colour and execution are excellent.

reviews.author: geddyneilalex28
reviews.body:
I mean if you have read the book, or seen the first one, you kinda know what you are in for. This is not sparkle vampires playing baseball in the rain.

The visuals are amazing, and the acting is good as well. The story is the story. If you don't like gothic romance, don't watch it.

All in all, a decent movie, but one I'm already starting to forget less than an hour later. I don't see this movie being a classic, cult, or otherwise, however, if you have a couple of hours to kill, it is a decent way to spend it.

Take it for what it is, and you will be fine. With this one, expectations are going to be key.

reviews.author: cauley-21289
reviews.body: People who gave this anything lower than an 8 don't understand the kind of art Eggers is making with his films. The more I think about it. The more I want to rate it higher. It's one of the best movies of the year and it snuck in at the finish line. Top 3 easy of 2024. I truly believe that no one could play this part of Count Orlok like Skarsgaard. His commitment to the prosthetics and the voice and hearing about his daily process to do the voice and all the other cast was great. It's a masterfully concocted tale of a truly classic movie in Murnau's Nosferatu (1922). I could go on and on about how good it it but only one way to understand where I'm coming from. See it, you won't be disappointed.

reviews.author: simeonpenev
reviews.body:
Nosferatu. Well. I have many things to say but I want to express my feelings about how well Robert Eggers followed the original story. I have watched "The Witch" which I liked but this is on another level. Not only the fact that he kept the story but he refined everything. The cinematography was perfect, there were a few scenes that made me feel amazed, the lighting, the atmosphere, if you like art you will certainly enjoy this chef-d'oeuvre.

I will also mention the games of the actors, they performed very well, Bill Skarsgard did as always an amazing performance, I believe the future of horror lies with him. Bon lecture!

reviews.author: PotassiumMan
reviews.body:
Robert Eggers has concocted a superior version of the iconic vampire story that rivals its predecessors. His remake is one that embraces Gothic horror and an eerie sense of dread. The quieter a scene is, the more fear you will experience. The film is an homage to the classic, with more reliance on shadows than gore. We see very little of Count Orlok in the beginning. He remains in the dark as a menacing presence, brought forth with great conviction by Skarsgard, who perfectly captures his percolating voice.

Lily-Rose Depp is ideal as the object of Nosferatu's desire. She is crippled by his power yet wise to his ways. While the count haunts her dreams constantly (and others later on), she warns those close to her about the impending threat. Out of everyone in the film, she knows the count the most intimately and can predict his behavior. Nicholas Hoult is her husband who works hard to care for her but also travels to the vampire's castle with the intent of completing the sale of a home, little knowing that the count intends to claim his wife as his possession. Wilem Dafoe is no stranger to this material and is exceptional here as a discredited, but insightful physician who recognizes the world of vampires as real and evil and insists on society being equipped to defeat them. Simon McBurney is well-deployed as Hoult's employer who also turns out to be the count's slavish, but enthusiastic servant who works quietly to enable Nosferatu in any way possible.

While this film could have benefited from some editing, it never loses its power and is gripping from start to finish, with a powerful and poignant conclusion. With lush cinematography and a foreboding soundtrack, it makes its mark as one of the best Gothic horror films in recent memory. Highly recommended.

reviews.author: iwatchfilmz
reviews.body:
Bill Skarsgard is quickly becoming one of the greatest character actors of this generation. His name will be up there with Gary Oldman. That man was unrecognizable, in voice and appearance, and he brought something to this role that I'm not sure anyone else could. Mesmerizing is the best word I can use to describe his performance.

Lily Rose-Depp made choices that could've easily become comical or hokey, but she played this role with so much maturity that I could not take my eyes off of her.

The mood of this film was spot-on.

Every single actor/actress was fantastic. Nobody slipped in their performance and with a movie like this, one person COULD throw off the mood and ruin the whole thing. But that did not happen here, so kudos for the casting choices.

Robert Eggers is a genius. Full stop. There were a couple jump scare moments but they were done efficiently and intentionally and they fit perfectly, which, judging by other modern horror movies, is difficult to do. Eggers wasn't trying to scare people just for the sake of scaring people which elevated this film from good to incredible.

Horror movies aren't given the credit they deserve from the major film awards, but this one showed why that is a mistake.

This was a blatantly creepy film, but above that, it was a cinematic masterpiece that just happened to be horror and I loved every minute of it.

reviews.author: pinballwizard-83712
reviews.body: Robert Eggers's astonishing visual stunning Gothic horror masterwork is a reimagining of the classic 102 year old German silent film by F. W. Murnau of the same name. Taking place in Germany in 1838 it concerns a young timid estate agent named Thomas Hutter, impressively played with a solid conviction by Nicholas Hoult, who travels to a castle in the Carpathian Mountains in Transylvania to have some papers for the purchase of an old mansion signed by the mysterious Count Orlok, played brilliantly by an unrecognizable Bill Skarsgard in spellbinding transformative turn that is truly terrifying, and his unnerving vocal performance must also be mentioned for it is absolutely chilling. Hutter will soon learn the Count Orlok is not just an ancient vampire monster but an embodiment of pure evil. While staying at the Orlok castle he begins to have a series of horrible nightmares, it seems that Count Orlok is obsessed with Hutter's beautiful new wife Ellen, magnificently played by Lily-Rose Depp in an emotionally powerful performance of great physicality, he plans to take her away from him at all costs. Ellen has some kind of psychic connection with Count Orlok and she begins to act more erratically as he gets closer, which leads her physician Dr. Wihelm Sievers, marvelously played by Ralph Ineson, to send for an expert of the occult Professor Albin Eberhart von Franc, remarkably played by Willem Dafoe who adds some macabre humor to his magnetic performance, he suspects at once that this is the evil work of a 'Nosferatu." Flawless direction by Egger, who also wrote the intelligent screenplay. Jarin Blaschke's extraordinary dream-like cinematography captures the dark menace of German expressionist cinema, Robin Carolan's haunting original score is highly effective, and the meticulous period recreation and production design by Craig Lathrop is amazing. Superb supporting performances by Aaron Taylor-Johnson, Emma Corin, Simon McBurney, Adela Hesova, and Stacy Thunes. I am love this artistic achievement which is a blend of horror and eroticism and a total triumphant. Highly recommended.

reviews.author: RightOnDaddio
reviews.body:
I was excited for this film. I was waiting for this film. I paused completing my Top Ten Best Films of 2024 List here on IMBD, until I saw this film. But here I am out of the theater, in the cold rain here in late December, a little disappointed and a little mystified.

What happened?

I love the 1922 and 1979 versions of the title character's films.

Love them.

Honestly, I think I love the '79 Werner Herzog version the most.

(wince) Don't hate.

But I also love the work of Robert Eggers thus far.

The Lighthouse is his finest film, one of this century's greatest cinema efforts.

The Northman is his worst, but it's still not so bad. Just his worst.

This is close to his worst, but it's not.

It definitely pales to the two previous versions of Nosferatu that I cited from the last century.

This movie looks great.

But definitely not as gorgeous as the Werner Herzog film.

And it's too long.

And if I'm completely honest, there are many scenes with too much comedic potential, apparently, as people were actually audibly snickering in parts inside the theater.

And the ending. That ending. The final scene, had some people in stitches.

I almost started laughing because I could also see why they might find humor in that part.

But I also can see what the filmmaker was going for there.

Not his worst film.

Not the best version of Nosferatu.

Sadly, no longer eligible for my end of the year Best list.

But I'm still an admirer of the director's work and still look forward to his future projects.

reviews.author: PerryAtTheMovies
reviews.body:
8.0/10 (Highly Recommend)

Every year on my birthday I go see a movie in theatres because it's a failsafe way for me to actually enjoy myself. This year's movie was no exception. While I really had no clue on what to expect from "Nosferatu" I wasn't left wanting.

I feel it has a good story. The setting is introduce well though slightly confusing. The climax and ending are pleasing though kind of expected. The cinematography is fantastic. I enjoyed the way moments were captured and it pulls you in for the scares even though they were anticipated.

The acting is good and may or may not make you feel at unease for certain moments. The swing of emotions is definitely unsettling at times. Bill Skarsgard was good but off for me. I couldn't unsee him as Pennywise, but the character he plays is definitely not a character I would want to come across in real life.

Overall, this movie is a great 21st century film that feels like an early movies horror like 1920s/30s-1950s-ish. It definitely worth seeing in theatres. It's gruesome, and horrifying even though certain moments are to be expected. The era is captured quite well, and the darkness of the tale is unsettling. I definitely feel this movie has multiple watches in it, but over the course of a year instead of months or days. The only true downside was some of the speaking parts. I couldn't understand what was being said. All in all it was a great birthday movie and I'm glad I saw it.

That's it for now. Thanks for taking time to read my review. Happy watching and enjoy the show!

reviews.author: erollence
reviews.body:
First, I'm glad I saw this in the theater. I like to financially support films like this. That said, I won't be buying the Blu-ray.

There is a misconception among many modern day directors/cinematographers: DARK = SCARY. It's been false time and again. The worn-out idea is not true.

It was so dark I couldn't tell the difference between the day and night scenes. Seriously! That's an important factor in a vampire movie! Should I make a run for it? If it's daytime; sure! If it's nighttime; nope! What about NOW? Is it day or night?! Uh, I can't tell!

I'm sure others are raving about the makeup. Most shots of the vampire are very dimly lit long shots. There was one close up of just his eyes, and I can only image the light source was a single candle about 100 feet away. So utterly dark I couldn't even tell if he had eyebrows! I really did want to SEE the vampire. Are his fangs close together like in the classic silent movie? Uh, maybe? Never saw 'em.

Dark cinematography aside, there was really just one scene that was truly creepy/scary. I found "Last Voyage of the Demeter" to be better for delivering thrills and chills. Don't be surprised if all the gushing (pun intended) 10 star reviews don't live up to expectations.

reviews.author: ancutalumei
reviews.body:
Cinematography was on point with a gothic vibe, but the plot was boring and couldn't keep me focused on wanting to find out it's storyline.

Really expected more from this movie and tbh the 1922 one was so much better than this inspite of it's time.

Although I was excited for this movie and for the plot overall it didn't live up to my expectations or atleast from what my friends told me that it was a great horror movie, well it wasn't.

Being a horror fanatic I did see many horror movies and many horror genres, some made me thrilled some made me scared, some made me excited and some like this one just made me question why didn't I just clean the house in the time i spent in front of the tv.

Do better!

reviews.author: garethwooduk
reviews.body:
If you remember Bram Stocker's Dracula from 1992 then you'll love this equally scary intense atmospheric gothic love story set in the same time period of the late 19th Century.

To be honest, plot is a bit of a rehash of the 1992 horror, but this time taking place in a Victorian like City in Germany.

Instead of being set in Whitby, this time our main antagonist 'Count Orlock' sets up home in Germany in a dilapidated haunted rundown mannor.

I was really impressed by the intensene horror through out the movie with some really gritty disturbing scenes with an epic cast and hats of to Bill Skarsgård playing the count so ferociously and full of vigor, I've never felt so petrified for the next scene, great film!

reviews.author: lnarruda
reviews.body:
Though the story follows the basic outline of Stoker's novel, the character of Orlok is depicted as a much more grotesque and sinister figure compared to the suave and charismatic Dracula. The film's slow pacing and deliberate, almost hypnotic progression builds a grear atmosphere.

In Nosferatu, Depp's performance is expected to strike a delicate balance between innocence and terror, as her character is both a victim and a catalyst for the narrative's unfolding. Given the expressionistic and atmospheric style that Eggers is known for, her acting will likely emphasize subtlety, using body language, facial expressions, and emotional nuance to convey her character's internal horror.

The cast as a whole holds up and we have a really nice result.

Really suberb film.

reviews.author: nitishraj-30999
reviews.body:
This movie is just outstanding on cinematography. The acting of Lily Rose depp and Bill Istvan Günther Skarsgård on point .. Amazing art ..they were too good .. the costumes were too good backing 1800s.

It's more a gothic genre than a scary one ..there is more goreness..Emma corrin did well with her supporting role ... The Suspense was little bit lacking but it's entertaining..The story was strong when it start and after halftime it's drag little bit with the dreams call .. Sound effects were soo good to create the gothic call .. Nudity was moderate ( or you can say less than moderate )Amazing in Dolby Recommend to must watch it ..

reviews.author: Alexander_Blanchett
reviews.body: Good new take on an very old story. Dark, grim and very atmospheric just how you would expect from Robert Eggers. Not the biggest fan of vampire movies simply because that's not my kind Lg mythology but this is different and I mostly enjoyed it. Great performances all around. Most outstanding was Lily-Rose Depp who convinced me the first time as an actress. At first you have the impression she overacts but in the second half she really shows what she has In her ( no pun intended ). Actually very much awards worthy. Bill Skarsgard was again very scary and it's even more scary to see how convincing he is doing that. Another winning performance and another cult character he can add to his portfolio. Willem Dafoe was very memorable and had some of the most iconic scenes in the film. Nicholas Hoult and Emma Corrin were both fine but the weakest links compared to the rest of the cast. Technically it was fantastic with some of the best production design and make up work of the year and a very haunting cinematography and editing. Definitely a film that will go down as one of the most gothic horror films of the last years and easily comparable to the former entries of that character .

reviews.author: filmephile
reviews.body:
The film is a feast for the eyes. The cinematography, particularly when it comes to the use of lighting and shadows, is really great. The score is also haunting and adds a sense of dread. The atmosphere is opaque and creepy.

Where this film falls apart is in its execution and the story's tenuity. If someone were to watch this film with no knowledge of the original film by Murnau nor the original book by Stoker, they'd be very confused as to what was going on in this film. There isn't much interiority nor backstory. The film is very much style over substance.

Some of the performances are solid, while some of the performances are mediocre. Rose-Depp is generally impressive here, albeit there are a few moments wherein she twists and contorts her body that are unintentionally strangely funny. Hoult is just alright and sometimes feels ineffectual. Taylor-Johnson's performance is irritating, whiney and frankly acts like an annoying man-child, though that's more the script's fault than the his. Corrin doesn't have much to do, but is good in her few scenes of acting as a shoulder to lean on for Ellen. Dafoe is pretty solid, though he can feel campy at times. McBurney, who was unknown to me prior to this film, is a real revelation; although he has a smaller role, he steals every scene he's in and is truly unsettling. And finally, Skarsgård as the eponymous character does a good job disappearing into this role. He's quite literally visually and vocally unrecognizable. The moustache he wears at times is distracting and jarring, albeit that wasn't his fault.

There isn't very much that's new here if you've seen the original, but the film is worth checking out for its suffocating Gothic atmosphere, some solid performances, and its beautiful cinematography.

reviews.author: Rachelle8765
reviews.body:
Well maybe i was one of the few people that did not watch the original Nosferatu and i really did not know how it was going to end so i was thrilled and fascinated and simply fell in love with this movie. I watched the original the day after and it was so nice to see the homage in the remake to the original, very very well done.

The rich background that was written for count Orlok and Ellen made the whole movie. It was somehow romantic and disgusting and amazing.

The acting, the makeup, the costumes the cinematography , everything just perfection!

I am definitely watching this again sometime soon.

reviews.author: pranavchopra-66755
reviews.body: I have seen many reviews disregarding this movie, I left feeling the exact opposite. The performances were grand, the story grim, and the cinematography perfect. It was a GREAT MOVIE. Depp was stellar in her portrayal. She was terrifyingly good. All actors did an incredible job. If you don't have an attention span, maybe this movie isn't for you but I didn't think it was long, or drug on. I viewed it as a great play, with many different acts. Turing from horror to supernatural to even some action. All I can say is don't let any of the reviews make your judgements for you, go see it yourself and you'll be pleased.

reviews.author: elidonbreshta
reviews.body:
Although this is a very well made film (nice job for that budget indeed) this doesn't live up to the expectations and hype, i've seen people and critics praising it a lot but in reality this is just a weak copy of Coppola's Dracula (in technical terms). It feels rushed in execution and to be honest The Last Voyage of the Demeter was a much better movie than this (even if that movie was mediocre) but at least it showed a proper depiction of the departure/voyage/arrival and the creature itself nonetheless. I really wanted to love this and indeed i enjoyed it and i loved the costumes and photography, but apart from that it's just a story we've seen multiple times. Since this was a dream project for Robert i actually expected much more from him....but no. Nicholas Hoult is very good in this and so is Bill's performance, people were praising Lily's acting but in reality all she does throughout the entire movie is just cry a little bit and make some cringe movements, and that's it. Dafoe plays the "crazy doc" part, not much to say about him, Aaron was also good, Emma was totally wasted. I don't know, i just expected more from this but i left the theater thinking "Damn, this could've been much better".

This definitely belongs to my 2024 best films list nonetheless but i kinda feel disappointed!

reviews.author: noxferatu
reviews.body:
I went into this movie with blank expectations - I thought to myself: this could be my new Roman Empire or totally mediocre. If I'm being honest with myself then this isn't new or original but it was disgusting and spooky and gloomy and especially Lily Rose Depp was amazing in her performance. I loved the use of makeup and old school gore in this, Eggers was able to capture the eerie atmosphere of the 1922 Nosferatu and bring it to life with modern equipment. Probably my favourite part is Nosferatu himself, the care that went into the costume design and SFX Makeup is incredible. Everything about the costuming of this movie is absolutely delightful, the fit and silhouette of the dresses and suits shows how much thought was put into the setting. Even if the storyline lacks some depth and isn't very original in the genre of vampire horror, Eggers Nosferatu is still a must see for me, because it is just so beautiful to look at.

Perfect movie for vampire enthusiasts who are fed up with sexy and beautiful creatures of the night and need a dose of living corpse for a change. Also perfect for fellow (period) costume design connoisseurs that still can't get over the catastrophe that was Little Women. Is it the feminist masterpiece many of us hoped for? No, but it doesn't need to be. It's just a nicely arranged piece of classical horror.

reviews.author: scarymonster33
reviews.body:
I don't ever feel compelled enough to write a review but Nosferatu is the odd occasion where I'll make an exception. I went to see in with low expectations as I always do with films these days but I was positively surprised - it was extraordinary, compelling and mesmerizing. We went to see it 1 January when it opened here in the UK. The cinema was unexpectedly packed for a matinee. I have never ever heard it so quiet. Nobody coughing, talking, eating noisy food, fidgeting in their seats - nothing - just stunned silence. This movie is truly captivating and transports you into another world. I have to add I have always been a huge fan of Murnau's 1922 original silent movie masterpiece, the only movie in fact to ever give me nightmares. Schreck's titular character was truly terrifying to me. So perhaps I was slightly biased going into this movie, however my expectations were low nevertheless, as as far as remakes go this movie - and Hollywood remakes in general - don't have a good track record.

I was pleased to see that the German setting and different time period of the original were adhered to (rather than going back to the turn of the century standard template of the original Bram Stoker novel and having it all anglicised), Setting it in the earlier part of 19th century Germany was true genius and greatly aids the gothic and poetic feel of the movie. For example, due to the action taking place before there were trains, main character Hutter has to travel to Transylvania on horseback, even going on foot for the last part of the journey. Which automatically makes it more haunting and dangerous than a simple train journey, and we get to soak in the strange and beautiful scenery more. This was very clearly a labour of love by someone who did their research, understood the original and also had a background in German romanticism of the era during which it is set. The film effortlessly captures the sad, romantic and forlorn beauty of a Caspar David Friedrich painting, a Goethe poem or a Schubert song cycle (Winterreise springs to mind). The cinematography is the best I have ever seen in a horror movie, perhaps in any movie period. You could freeze frame every shot, print it out and hang it on your wall it's a work of art. I cannot use any term to describe it other than breathtaking.

In terms of the story and plot it keeps pretty close to the original with a few changes and additions each of which enriched and enhanced rather than took away. Brilliant performances by all in particular Hoult, Skarsgard and Dafoe. Overall though I must say the male performances were better than the females. Therein lies my only criticism of the movie. Throughout, Depp lacked expression in her eyes. However it has to be said, her character is in some kind of trance/ under Orlock's spell for large parts of it so this may have been the thinking behind the "dead" eyes. Skarsgard is spellbinding and terrifying as the revolting titular character, refreshingly and brilliantly hidden in the shadows for a lot of the movie. A true monster, the kind you were hiding under the bed from as a child. There are no glamorous, sophisticated, tragically misunderstood heartthrob vampires in this movie! No - he's just evil.

To enjoy the movie as much as I have, I think it does help to have a bit of context and background on the whole thing - so do watch the original 1922 silent movie and even the Herzog (1979) remake. Even though easily the weakest of the three Nosferatu films - it's still worth it for Klaus Kinski's usual unhinged and creepy yet mesmerizing brilliance alone. Also, Shadow of the Vampire (2000), which was about the making of the 1922 original, is a recommendation - very quirky, off the wall and unexpectedly humorous at times! It stars John Malkovich as Murnau and - coincidentally - also Dafoe who puts in a stunning performance as Schreck. Anyway, forget all the other Dracula movies like the over-the-top camp Hammer horrors or the bombastic Coppola epic - this isn't anything like those films. This is something entirely different. But for those of you that love the original and all things gothic horror - this is a real treat! And if you are planning on ever seeing please go now and watch it on the big screen - it won't be the same on the small screen.

reviews.author: eddie_baggins
reviews.body:
Refusing to rest on his laurels or at the same time be beaten down by the rather disappointing financial performance of his biggest swing yet that was his 2022 Viking infused fever dream The Northman, director Robert Eggers has emerged once more to tackle a reimagining of one of horror's most revered cinematic properties Nosferatu, providing us with one of the genres most atmospheric and memorable offerings of the modern era, while at the same time further establishing his name as one of Hollywood's most interesting filmmakers.

First appearing on the scene with his brilliant British offering The Witch in 2015, Eggers has quickly established himself as a unique voice in the industry and while not everyone of his films might hit the same for each viewer there's little doubting that we are witnessing the career of an all time writer/director who at the age of 41 at the time of writing has a lot of prime years ahead of him should he so desire.

Pleasantly over performing from a box office standpoint with well over $130 million in takings globally so far off a relatively small $50 million dollar production budget, this bleak and unashamedly odd gothic horror is drenched in ominous dread, stunning artistry and haunting imagery as Eggers takes us on a wild ride through a vampire infused Europe where Lily-Rose Depp and Nicholas Hoult's newly married couple Ellen and Thomas Hutter come face to face with Bill Skarsgård's skin-crawling Count Orlock who appears hellbent on making Ellen his own no matter the cost.

A well-worn tale thanks to Nosferatu's core story taking much from the famed and iconic Dracula, there's certainly nothing revolutionary or ground-breaking about Nosferatu's narrative and some viewers may find its delivery slightly too off-putting but with a core collection of fantastic performances, stunning production design and visual spectacle (Thomas's arrival at Orlock's remote castle is worth the price of admission alone) and Egger's resolute direction ensure something that is so familiar also feels so new and vibrant.

Overcoming the disappointment of her short-lived and maligned TV series The Idol and taking a giant leap from bit parts in so-so features, Nosferatu is also notable for a career making performance from Lily-Rose Depp who gives it her all as a character that's not always entirely likeable or someone you'll agree with but who is a commanding presence nonetheless thanks to Depp's commitment.

Tasked with a range of emotions and character beats Depp proves to be a worthy leading lady and even though she's overshadowed by a scenery-chewing Willem Dafoe as oddball occult researcher Prof. Albin Eberhart von Franz and an awards worthy Skarsgård (making further claims for the best man in the business when you need someone in a horror under the guide of hideous make-up) as the instantly iconic villain that is Count Orlock, there's no doubting that Eggers has unlocked a talent within Depp that should allow her to match her fathers prime years in Hollywood.

Flawed in parts but undeniably brilliant in so many facets, Nosferatu is one of the most impressive horror films to come out of Hollywood in some time and gives us all further reason to regard Eggers as one of the most unique and boundary pushing filmmakers working right now.

Final Say -

Fears of what could happen to a revered piece of horror history are nothing but fleeting memories now this new version of Nosferatu has made its way into the public domain. A stunning achievement in artistry and craftsmanship and an engaging and unnerving tale of love and the human condition in its own right, Robert Egger's latest trip to the darkside is a blast from start to finish.

4 pigeons out of 5

Jordan and Eddie (The Movie Guys)

reviews.author: alvanhoye
reviews.body: The film is beautiful and immersive. Pacing is a bit of an issue, but I think most of Eggars films start slow for world building and move quickly toward the end. Fundamentally, the film isn't about logic, it's about old magic. Not everything is understood and there's a lot of things left unsaid because it doesn't matter why they happen, what matters is how it make you feel. Whether you like the film or not will depend on how you feel about this kind of story telling. Modern stories rely on explaining the why. Eggars functions like many old stories and folk tales where the why isn't always important. Evil exists and its motivations aren't always clear.

reviews.author: bleu30
reviews.body:
Endings make or break a movie and this is a classic example where the ending makes this a forgettable movie.

We're in a 19th century German village and Nosferatu is east in Bohemia. A woman named Ellen (played by Lily-Rose Depp) calls out "Come to me, come to me" and this awakens Nosferatu from his long sleep. Ellen's husband, Thomas (played by Nicholas Hoult) is hoping to start a new job, in real estate. His boss tells him, there is a client in Bohemia who is too weak to make the trip and that if he makes this journey to complete the contract and bring him to the village, he will be hired by the company. He accepts.

He makes it there, albeit after some interesting and unwanted, detours. At the destination, which is really a castle, Thomas "meets" Nosferatu or to Thomas just a client. Thomas is very suspicious and scared, but does sign a contract. Thomas asks to leave, but Nosferatu does not let him and traps him in the castle.

Nosferatu then unleashes a plague upon the German town and also starts to possess some individuals in that town to do his bidding. All of this is very well down and interesting.

However, in the last one-third of the money, the movie lacks creativity and surprise. The ending is not satisfying and is way too simple. I have a hard time imagining someone writing this movie and doing such a good job on just about every part but then not thinking of any decent way to close the movie up.

I do want to point out that there are also some somewhat creepy parts. I'm mainly referring to demon on human sex scenes. So it is a bit of a weird movie. But I do not think that hurts it.

Overall, I just can't give it a 7 because the most important part of a movie is the ending. And I cannot give it a 5 because of the many different parts that the movie does a good job with: the acting, the writing (with the exception already mentioned), the scenery, and the appearance of Nosferatu.

reviews.author: katiecooperx
reviews.body:
Lily Rose Depp offers an unforgettable performance and went to places I didn't know she was capable of. I felt moved by her devotion to the character. Skarsgard completely transforms with every villainous character he takes on, and he truly outdid himself as Count Orlok.

So many beautiful and creative shots, I tried to take in the stunning wardrobe and appreciate the dark and eerie set design while just in awe. The atmosphere and world created by Eggers was enough to keep me locked in for the entirety of the movie and when it ended I would have happily watched it from the beginning all over again.

Everything I look for in a horror movie. No notes, simply Eggers best film yet.

reviews.author: gbrietigam
reviews.body:
I admittedly went into Nosferatu not knowing much about the vampire, and I hadn't seen the previous two movies. If you have an existing knowledge of the lore, I think you might enjoy the extensive world building in this film much more than I did, so bear that in mind.

The film began interestingly enough. I was hooked in the first half, as the male protagonist (Thomas Hutter) traveled to meet Count Orlock. I really enjoyed the tense and scary tension between the two of them as they were meeting. The cinematography, sets, and costumes were stunning and added to the immersion in the creepy world.

In the second half, though, I felt the film just lost its shape, and the script began aimlessly throwing a lot of random and short pieces of superfluous fluff that added a lot of needless complexity to the story, while at the same time not really adding much, and distracting from a clear plot. There are a lot of blink and you miss it tidbits of facts and information that never end up being important to the resolution of the story that just drag the whole story along and slow it down. There might be a main character or two that as you're watching you're trying to remember who they are and how they were introduced.

The run time of 132 minutes is way too long. It could safely be trimmed to 90 minutes, and several characters completely cut, and I think you'd have a much better film.

The cinematography and production design were strong points. Acting was solid. The first quarter to half of the story was engaging, before trailing off. For those reasons, I still give this film a 6/10. I'd recommend to anybody interested in vampire lore. If not, I'd skip.

reviews.author: felixcole-51974
reviews.body:
Perhaps it was because I have seen the silent film a few times, including just the other day in preparation to see this in the theater.

I thought it was excellent. Broody, dark, well directed, filmed and cast. I didn't see a bad performance here. Simon Mcburney was perfect as Herr Knock.

This version sticks very close to the silent film. If I had any nit to pick, they didn't need such graphic special effects! They could have relied in the imaginations of the audience. All the places the silent film lacked, due to how early it was made, this delivers.

I don't know what the reviews with lower ratings were expecting. Maybe they like everything explained in detail so they don't need to pay attention or think?

Maybe they should watch or rewatch the original?

It's a triumph for all involved.

reviews.author: Sleepin_Dragon
reviews.body:
It's the first time I've been more excited about New Year's day, than Christmas day, the release of Nosferatu. A strange day to release a vampire horror, but it gave us something to look forward to, to begin 2025 with.

Visually, spectacular, one of the most breathtakingly beautiful films I have seen for ages, the sets, costumes, locations etc are all incredible, talk about a feast for the senses.

I did enjoy it, but if I'm truly honest, I was hoping for a little more, I liked the gore and the gothic tone, I really liked the scares, what frustrated me most, the storyline, I feel awful being critical, but it just felt a little padded out, some scenes felt too long and slow, making the film drag at times.

The acting was terrific, and I have to heap praise on the performance of Lily Rose Depp, she deserves an award for this.

I'd definitely recommend seeing it.

7/10.

reviews.author: xufrfbm
reviews.body: The story was merely an afterthought in this film. The director forgot the story. There's no character development. You don't care what happens to the characters. It's just all cinematography which is good, but that's not enough. Coppola's Dracula blows this away. There's some good acting by the female lead but you don't care if she lives or dies. I'm surprised at the industry acclaim with such an awful script. Dracula is one of the best books of all time. They should have focused first on a good script before focusing on the atmospherics. In short this is the director's self indulgent crap that for some reason the industry is afraid to ask what about the story?

reviews.author: simpleveracity
reviews.body:
If you aren't a fan of dramatic acting or historical pieces, then you will not like this movie. It's as simple as that. It's okay if you don't prefer these or other forms of traditional theatre, but you also shouldn't force yourself to enjoy them. Please don't watch this to save yourself from boredom.

If you are a fan of storylines, regardless of how they are depicted whether it be in a theatrical or contemporary sense, then you will likely appreciate the amount of effort put into making this an immersive and engaging film. You might enjoy the special effects and horror, and maybe the relationships between the characters. However, you would probably feel like this could have been better if it were more direct in its approach on the themes or dialogue. In other words, your lack of immersion will probably stop you from enjoying this movie.

If you are a fan of theatre, classic horror, a prolific reader, and/or an interest in cinematography, then you will love this film as much as I did. This is a masterpiece, and it will be a timeless example of modern horror. There is no modern rendition of this story that has captured the level of detail, characterization, and setting that this film has. This is the most accurate and impactful adaptation of both Dracula and Nosferatu. This is the type of media that defines the images around words such as vampire, and it will forever be one of the highest quality depictions of what that term used to be known for: evil incarnate.

reviews.author: parksiet
reviews.body:
I feel like every time I see a new Robert Eggers movie, I come out of it saying: "Now, this is Robert Eggers' masterpiece!" And Nosferatu is no exception - Robert Eggers continues his impressive streak of crafting highly detailed and transportive period films with Nosferatu, one of the most seductively macabre films ever made. Extremely atmospheric and immersive, it is a pure gothic nightmare of a film, its astonishing imagery and seductive tone will linger with you. Robert Eggers delivers the year's most bone-chilling and unsettling movie, with genuinely impeccable craftsmanship that oozes creativity on every technical front. There is not a second wasted by Eggers in this movie: he plunges you head first you into 1800s Germany with tremendous use of sound, some of the smartest use of colour I can remember, and maybe the best camera work I've seen all year. There are visual moments in this movie that made my jaw drop. In typical Eggers fashion, he is utterly deliberate with each frame used in this movie. Eggers just goes there. He makes bold artistic choices and takes chances. And I loved all of them. This film is crafted with such careful precision and it's beautiful to watch.

I also loved all of the performances. Lily-Rose Depp gives every ounce of her body and soul to this eye-popping performance of tormented possession, Nicholas Hoult and Aaron Taylor-Johnson were also really impressive, while Bill Skarsgård fully transforms like nothing you've ever seen before. He continues to impress me with the way he submerges himself into these dark, villainous characters and manages to make them so unique and distinct. The overall portrayal of Count Orlok is so utterly compelling every moment he's on screen that his presence lingers even when he's not. Bill Skarsgård's dark, alluring performance, the grotesque makeup, atmospheric sound design, Jarin Blaschke's spellbinding cinematography, and Robin Carolan's haunting score all come together to reimagine a gothic classic, culminating in a breathtaking final shot that sent chills through my body as I left the theatre.

However, the true star of the film is the blocking. Nosferatu accomplishes what very few films nowadays don't even dare to attempt. Coherent blocking, framing, and proper editing (which allow for every other aspect of the film to blossom with efficiency into an entertaining experience). Set design gets to shine, phenomenal performances get to ACTUALLY exist with weight to them, movement gets to matter across the axis, and audiences get to experience a breath of fresh air because they really don't make them like this anymore. If you had told me this was a film made in the 60s-80s (a golden era of film technique), I would have believed you. No movies look like this today, it was wonderful to see!

Nosferatu is another masterwork in tension and period detail from Robert Eggers. There is a seductive quality to this film that pulls you in and doesn't let go until the final gut punch of a frame, as its atmosphere and cinematography are hypnotic. Nosferatu is a beautiful, terrifying, sweaty nightmare that you never quite want to wake up from. If you are looking for a truly immersive horror experience, this is it. Nosferatu is one of the best movies of the year, and Eggers' best film yet. I am so, so in love with it!

(How the hell is this movie not getting any awards attention???)

reviews.author: ryandannar
reviews.body:
Watched the new Robert Eggers "Nosferatu" on New Years Day. I loved it, but I also want to say that I'd worked hard to keep my expectations low. Based on the trailers, I had feared that Eggers would deliver a conventionally-beautiful "gothic period piece" full of lovely visuals but lacking in heart. I feared a handsome but shallow film, essentially.

On the other hand, I was really HOPING that Eggers would deliver a version of the story which might answer my biggest complaints about the two previous versions. I'd recently watched both earlier versions -- the 1922 F. W. Murnau original, and the 1979 Werner Herzog version. And hey, both films are worthwhile, and have myriad strengths by which to recommend them. But I felt like there was a major weakness common to both these earlier versions of the story, and it was simply this: Both films are extremely episodic, they have no regard for pacing, and the characters in both films frequently lack meaningful motivations for their actions.

It's not so surprising that the characters in the original silent film were paper-thin and sometimes acted in ways which were unbelievable. That was kind of how most movies were back then; the lack of sound fairly limited what could be established, character-wise, because all dialogue had to be displayed as title-cards. And so, a lot of the characters in the F. W. Murnau original behave in strange and rather inexplicable ways, leaving us to either decide that they're complete nincompoops, or to invent our own rationale for their behavior.

Herzog's film had fewer excuses on that front, given advances in filmmaking grammar and technology -- and yet it still made many of the same mistakes. Herzog humanizes Nosferatu, turning him into an actual character with very relatable human fears, and that's certainly an interesting innovation. It's also nice how Herzog pivots entirely to Lucy's perspective for the last act of the film; he gives her much more meaningful screen-time, and succeeds in making her sacrifice at the end of the film feel more powerful as a result.

But Herzog's film drags glacially. And until that final act, his film still has trouble finding believable motivations for its characters, and the plot still seems built upon some inexplicable notions. For instance, isn't it weirdly convenient and kinda silly that the ol' Count is looking to move-house, and then falls into deep fated love with the wife of his real-estate agent, based only on a tiny and blurry picture kept in a locket? Perhaps some people see in this "the randomness of evil." I see in it a poorly-established character motivation.

We also have the matter, in both earlier films, of Ellen's/Lucy's visions/fits/sleepwalking episodes. Ellen/Lucy is the wife of the real-estate agent -- the woman whom the vampire falls into lust with. The Murnau and Herzog films both suggest that Ellen/Lucy had a history of such episodes, before the vampire casts his spell over her. This history never proves important, other than to set her up as a character with a certain "psychic sensitivity." It's more of a plot-device -- in the sense that, once the vampire's spell is cast, it is as if the vampire is harnessing this weakness/sensitivity to commune with her.

To finally get back to the present: I was really kind of shocked and delighted by just how thoroughly the new Robert Eggers film remedies all of my problems with the previous versions. It's like the dude read my mind and delivered exactly what I wanted, only better.

First off: Eggers BEGINS his film with a sequence which centers the entire story around Ellen/Lucy's experience. It certainly bucks convention for her to be the protagonist from the outset -- but there's a really good reason for that, and it's basically because she's the most interesting character; she has the most meaningful conflict.

That would have been true in any version of this film -- but here, that opening scene establishes a new context for her visions, and it makes her history relevant in ways that it never was in the Murnau or Herzog versions. It also, rather brilliantly, establishes a much more relevant and compelling REASON for WHY the vampire seeks to move to her town in the first place. And it does all of this without losing the scary implication that evil can act at random, selecting helpless targets who least deserve it.

That opening scene, and the context it establishes, is the first of several brilliant tweaks that Eggers brings to the material. Overall, it seems that from a storytelling perspective, his efforts have mostly been in the service of doing exactly what I had hoped he would do -- he brings a clarity of motivation to all of the characters, and a greater sense of visceral inevitability to the plot, all without abandoning the broad strokes and the most famous "beats" of the original two films.
