So to explicitly compare the three, I'd say this: While the first two versions of Nosferatu had lots of great ideas, and many spooky visuals, they were both marred by a rather episodic quality, some questionable pacing, and a lot of poorly-established character motivations. The new Eggers film delivers a version of the story which plays as a compelling and immersive drama, with characters whose motivations actually make sense, and a sense of pacing which draws us viscerally from one scene to the next. His film held me like a vice from first shot to last.

Eggers also gives us a visual sensibility, and a sound-design, which are far more crisply stylized than either of the previous versions. Sometimes when a film gets too stylized, it can lose something, can start to feel hermetically-sealed. But I think the approach here really works. I mean, it worked for me. Not only did I find this film FAR creepier than either previous version of this tale -- but I also thought that many of Eggers's audiovisual-design choices were quite meaningful.

For instance, in one of the beats that each version of the film hits, the young real-estate agent is met on a mountain-road by a mysterious carriage sent by the Count. The carriage itself is, I think, meant to be sinister. The thought, I gather, is something about a man delivering himself naively into the embrace of evil. His entrance into the carriage is the fateful step, that step he cannot take back.

In the original version, Murnau did what he could to make the carriage, and Tom/John's ride within it, seem otherworldly. But you know, it was the early days of film, and the techniques he used have not withstood the test of time. To modern eyes, or at least to my eyes, that scene in the original plays as unintentionally comical.

Herzog includes the carriage, but doesn't really do much with it. A carriage arrives, in the darkness, yes. But the carriage is baroquely ornate, not exactly "foreboding" -- and the driver seems friendly, and the music sounds hopeful, and the whole scene just doesn't play as tense or foreboding in the slightest. The beat is there, but it's not very effective except to say, "And then John took a carriage to the castle."

Eggers sets the scene at a moonlit crossroads in a dense alpine forest. First of all: The "crossroads" is a perfect idea. Where is the devil met? At a crossroads, of course -- where one is invited down the wrong path. And how does the devil arrive? Well, in this Eggers telling: Silently. The carriage glides supernaturally down the road, almost without sound. The door to the carriage opens by some unseen hand. Tom Hutter finds himself pulled inside, as if entranced, as if lifted and carried. Just a pitch-perfect way to handle that scene. Just evocative in all the right ways.

And man, there's just beat after beat that Eggers handles with that kind of superb attention to detail. He just finds ways of making all the visuals and sound work perfectly for the story, while also speaking beyond the story, toward the mythological.

I'll end my review here because I could go on, but that's pretty much everything I wanted to say. I felt like the Robert Eggers version of "Nosferatu" wildly exceeded my expectations, and I haven't stopped thinking about it since I saw it.

Ah, but I guess there's one other thing you probably want to know. Would I call the film "scary?" This is a question which does not matter to me. I have watched and loved plenty of horror-films which I wouldn't call "scary." The word itself is a trap, because not everyone defines "scary" the same way. What I will say is this: the Eggers version of "Nosferatu" DEEPLY creeped me out, and I can't say that about either of the previous versions. This film filled me with so much dread and anxiety that there were times I wished I could pause the movie and go do something else for awhile. I was quite unsettled by it. But I was also dealing with some emotional stuff before I watched it, and that has its own influence. I will happily watch this movie again -- but probably not real soon.

reviews.author: adrianrhilge
reviews.body: Robert Eggers' Nosferatu (2024) promises to be a haunting revival of the classic vampire tale. With Bill Skarsgård as the sinister Count Orlok and Lily-Rose Depp as the doomed Ellen, the film reimagines the eerie world of the 1922 silent masterpiece. Early glimpses suggest Eggers' signature atmospheric style, blending historical detail with unsettling horror. Willem Dafoe's involvement adds intrigue, following his previous vampire-adjacent role in Shadow of the Vampire. If the trailers are any indication, this retelling will be a chilling, visually stunning exploration of obsession and terror. A must-see for horror fans.

reviews.author: pedroquintaoo
reviews.body:
The new version of Nosferatu (2024), directed by Robert Eggers, is a technically stunning work that, for me, fails to create an emotional connection with the viewer. The visual and sound design are undeniably incredible, showcasing Eggers' perfectionism. However, both the villain and the film itself seem to lack one essential quality: a soul.

More and more, I feel that Eggers creates films to be admired rather than felt. His works are like art galleries-visually flawless but devoid of any real emotion. No matter how much I tried, I couldn't connect with or feel involved in this production.

On a technical level, the film is remarkable. The dark and gothic atmosphere is crafted with extraordinary attention to detail. From the lighting, which recalls the aesthetics of German Expressionist cinema, to the sound design that heightens discomfort, Eggers' talent is undeniable. Yet, this technical perfection often overwhelms the narrative, making it feel secondary to his obsession with crafting a visually immaculate experience.

The biggest issue with Nosferatu is its pacing and length. At 2 hours and 15 minutes, the film becomes a test of patience. There are scenes that add nothing to the plot and dialogues that feel repetitive. Many of these moments seem to exist solely to showcase the production's technical brilliance but end up dragging the story's rhythm. Honestly, the film would benefit greatly from being 30 or 45 minutes shorter.

The protagonist's arc is another aspect that left me frustrated. A significant portion of the film shows her in a trance, contorting and groaning due to hallucinations. While these scenes create tension at first, their constant repetition quickly becomes tedious and predictable. The narrative loses strength and intensity, eventually becoming monotonous. To make matters worse, the justification for her connection to the villain feels weak, if it can even be called a justification.

The film is not slow; it includes jump scares and suspenseful moments. The issue with Nosferatu lies in its overly drawn-out narrative. Recently, I watched Heretic, which has a much slower pace, but it managed to keep me more engaged than this film did.

As for Nosferatu himself, I have mixed feelings. Bill Skarsgård delivers a memorable performance, with a chilling voice that gives the character a commanding and menacing presence. However, the vampire's design left me torn. At times, I appreciated it, but the strange mustache made him look like a fusion of the 1922 film's villain and Borat, which occasionally undermined the character's seriousness.

Nosferatu is not a weak film by any means. It's a technically impressive piece of work that lacks a tighter narrative and an emotional core. Robert Eggers is undoubtedly a master at creating atmosphere and technically brilliant works. However, in my opinion, he struggles to make his films emotionally resonant, to forge a genuine connection between the audience and the story. Perhaps this won't be an issue for everyone, but for me, it's an impossible flaw to overlook.

reviews.author: hlnasydy
reviews.body: Bill Skarsgård. The man you are. You better see yourself. You better trust yourself. And you better love yourself. You're the most talented actor in the whole world. I never doubted in you. You better never doubt in yourself. Will always love and respect you. You're a legend. And Lily-Rose Depp. Ma'am. I'm sorry. I wasn't familiar with you and your game. You're a legend too. The whole atmosphere of the movie was great. Cinematography was amazing. Willem perfect as always. I didn't like Nicholas Hoult that much. He was a little boring to me. Emma Corrin was brilliant. And Robert Eggers thanks again for another amazing movie!

reviews.author: ShootingStar82
reviews.body:
Nosferatu is a living nightmare. A 132-minute nightmare that never relents from start to finish. If you're not prepared to watch it, you might also find yourself have nightmares afterwards. This quality is partly achieved by the great lighting. A significant portion of the film is shot in shadows, and the nighttime scenes are filmed in a glorious silvery monochrome.

Make no mistake about it, Nosferatu is a beautiful film. The cinematography is up there with the best I've seen, and some of the shots are simply gorgeous. The sets are beautiful, and the costumes are stunning. The acting is also great across the board, save for a few moments where Lily-Rose Depp was a bit too OTT for my liking.

So where does this film fall short? Firstly, I felt that the story lacked a bit of cohesiveness, particularly in the second half. There's a bit too much jumping around, and on multiple occasions I found myself asking "why is this happening?". More importantly, though, there's a sterileness to this film. I just didn't find myself caring for what happened to any of the characters.

All up I think Nosferatu is a worthy film, if only purely for the visual aspects. Just don't expect too much depth beyond that.

reviews.author: ianzgreat
reviews.body:
He certainly knows how to make a pretty movie with pretty sets, but this film solidifies for me that I'm not an Eggers fan. I was hooked until about 25 mins in when I realized he knows how to decorate a frame, but tell a compelling story he does not. It felt as though his actors had no freedom to feel alive in their roles. The cast is fantastic. The only one that seemed comfortable to do his thing was Defoe. I'm all for a traditional telling of a classic story, but at least make it interesting. There's nothing fresh in this rehash of an elsewhere better told story. I was border line goofy. In fact our audience laughed when it ended.

I love slowburn, artsy films, but this huge budgeted film is strictly eye candy. Stagnant eye candy. I wish he'd leave the direction to someone else and just lend his talents to the camera and set decoration departments.

reviews.author: jamie_starr0503
reviews.body:
The new "Nosferatu" film is a stunning visual masterpiece that breathes fresh life into the classic tale of vampirism. The cinematography is nothing short of breathtaking, with each frame meticulously crafted to evoke a haunting atmosphere that pays homage to the original while introducing a modern sensibility. The use of shadows and light creates an eerie tension that pulls viewers into its world, making every moment feel alive with dread and fascination.

The performances are compelling, with the lead embodying the essence of the infamous vampire with a chilling intensity that lingers long after the credits roll. The film's pacing and direction keep audiences on the edge of their seats, intertwining dread with moments of eerie beauty. Overall, this "Nosferatu" is a fantastic reimagining that not only honors its roots but also stands as a remarkable achievement in contemporary cinema. A must-see for horror enthusiasts and film lovers alike!

reviews.author: danielceda
reviews.body:
Each frame is a work of art.

Robert Eggers' 2024 remake of Nosferatu is a visionary reimagining of the 1922 silent horror classic that not only pays homage to its roots but also redefines the genre for modern audiences. A director known for his atmospheric dread and meticulous attention to detail (The Witch, The Lighthouse), Eggers has crafted a chilling, artful masterpiece that stands as one of the most haunting films of the year. This Nosferatu is more than just a remake-it's a revelatory cinematic experience that will be remembered for years to come, and it deserves all the hype surrounding its release.

From the moment the film begins, it's clear that Eggers is in complete control of the material. The gothic aesthetic and haunting atmosphere are immediately striking. Shot in stark black and white, the film feels like a living homage to the silent horror era, yet Eggers' sensibility is undeniably modern. The cinematography, masterfully crafted by Jarin Blaschke, uses chiaroscuro lighting and long, lingering shots to create a visual language that is both mesmerizing and terrifying. The film's compositions feel like moving paintings, with the haunting presence of Count Orlok (played with chilling perfection by Bill Skarsgård) casting long shadows over every frame.

Skarsgård's portrayal of Orlok is nothing short of phenomenal. His performance channels the unsettling energy of Max Schreck's iconic turn in the original but adds layers of nuance and depth. While Schreck's Orlok was a grotesque and monstrous figure, Skarsgård's interpretation brings a tragic dimension to the vampire, making him a creature of pain, longing, and unholy obsession. His physicality is hypnotic-whether standing still or gliding across the screen, he evokes an otherworldly, almost spectral presence. It's a performance that lingers in the viewer's mind long after the credits roll.

Eggers excels in making Nosferatu a deeply psychological experience. While the plot follows the basic framework of the original-an eerie encounter with a vampire in a small, isolated town-the director uses the film to explore darker, more existential themes. The film meditates on the terror of the unknown, the fragile nature of the human psyche, and the horror of isolation. Eggers' trademark slow burn style allows these ideas to unfold gradually, imbuing the narrative with a sense of inevitability and doom. The pacing is deliberate, with long silences and minimal dialogue, heightening the sense of claustrophobia and dread.

The supporting performances, particularly from Lily-Rose Depp as Ellen, Orlok's tragic muse, are equally impressive. Depp brings an ethereal quality to the role, embodying the innocence and vulnerability of her character, while also conveying a sense of foreboding-an understanding that something sinister is at play. The emotional weight of her character's journey, tied to Orlok's curse, is palpable, and she balances the delicacy of her performance with moments of inner strength, giving Ellen a profound depth.

Perhaps one of the most striking elements of Eggers' Nosferatu is its sound design and score. The film's haunting soundscape, composed by Mark Korven, complements the visual eeriness of the film with a score that is both minimal and profoundly unsettling. There is a raw, almost primal quality to the music, using a combination of dissonant strings and eerie, unearthly sounds that heighten the film's atmosphere of creeping dread. The sound design is equally meticulous, with the film's quiet moments punctuated by subtle, unnerving sounds-the whisper of the wind, the creaking of old wood, the distant howls of something unseen. These elements immerse the viewer in the film's world, amplifying the tension and making the terror feel all the more real.

Eggers' direction is also complemented by his use of practical effects, which enhance the film's authenticity and nightmare-inducing quality. While digital effects are occasionally employed, Eggers' reliance on practical makeup, miniatures, and camera tricks recalls the tactile nature of classic horror films. This commitment to physical effects ensures that the supernatural elements feel grounded in the film's reality, lending them a sense of credibility and weight that CGI often lacks.

Ultimately, Nosferatu (2024) is a breathtaking achievement-a film that not only reimagines a classic but pushes the boundaries of what horror cinema can accomplish. Eggers has created a film that feels timeless, both a tribute to the past and a forward-thinking work of art. The haunting visuals, mesmerizing performances, and subtle yet profound exploration of fear make this Nosferatu one of the best horror films ever.

This Nosferatu is nothing less than a dazzling masterpiece that deserves all the attention and acclaim it is receiving. Eggers has once again proven his mastery of atmosphere and psychological terror, solidifying his place as one of the most exciting filmmakers working today. It is a film that will resonate with viewers long after they've left the theater, a reminder that true horror is not just about what we see, but what we feel.

reviews.author: sinscopefilms
reviews.body:
Nosferatu (2024) is a gothic masterpiece that hooked me from its introduction. The cinematography is absolutely fantastic, excels in atmosphere and style with exceptional color grading and a reliance on minimal cuts that allow the camera's fluid movements - panning, zooming, and tracking - to tell much of the story. Editing transitions are flawless, maintaining the immersive flow of the story. The natural lighting casts evocative shadows on the actors' faces, creating an eerie and authentic atmosphere.

The music is suspense and tension worthy with its blend of mystery, melancholy, occasional hope and loud moments. It's so effective that I had goosebumps multiple times. The acting is another highlight: Lily-Rose Depp's performance exceeded my expectations with its natural and immersive quality, while Bill Skarsgård brought depth and menace to Nosferatu. Admittedly, his overly Slavic-sounding voice initially made me laugh, but his talent shone through regardless. Willem Dafoe's character arc added a fascinating mix of humor and horror, keeping me thoroughly engaged.

The sound design is impeccable, loud and eerie, amplifying the film's unsettling tone. The locations are stunningly beautiful and perfectly suited to the gothic narrative. The horror elements lean into the grotesque and mentally unconventional, offering a deeply unsettling experience.

Robert Eggers has once again proven his mastery, crafting a film so immersive that I genuinely lost my sense of reality at times. The pacing, however, could have been tighter; a few scenes felt a bit slow, slightly dragging the otherwise engaging rhythm.

reviews.author: leonardooliva-16135
reviews.body:
Robert Eggers' films clearly have a legion of followers, including myself.

He has a very personal, very auteur-like cinema, but also has some mainstream elements that make it so that every time a film comes out, it is eagerly awaited.

"The Witch", "The Lighthouse" and "The Northman" are works of art for me, so the fact that he was in charge of this adaptation gave me a lot of expectations.

I'm not going to lie, I liked the film, but not that much, maybe I expected more, maybe I had higher expectations. I think the script was quite weak at times.

I feel that we have a first half where the horror represented in the features of Nicholas Hoult shines, which is incredible.

But I also feel that the second half, mainly the whole investigation plot, is a bit unnecessary for me.

The ending seems fine to me, in keeping with the aim of looking for some originality considering that it is about a toxic relationship between a woman with a high libido and a demon with whom she made a pact to satisfy her carnal desires... perhaps that is my biggest problem, going from the initial horror to that final tone.

I am not going to stop appreciating how magnificently set it is, how it involves terminology from the Psychology of the time such as hysteria to explain what happens to Ellen.

The shots are incredible, the colour palette is dazzling. Everything is extremely well taken care of, like the moment when the gypsies speak in a dead ancient Romanian language, it is really crazy.

Bill Skarsgard is sublime in his interpretation as Orlok, we never realise that it is him, his vocal work is beyond absurd in its forms. I also like the appearance, very faithful to a man from that time in the Carpathian region.

Lily-Rose Depp is also very good in her performance, as is Willem Dafoe.

A must-see for lovers of cinema and its technical prowess and the work of its actors. However, don't expect to find Eggers' best work, because no, it isn't.

reviews.author: Agent10
reviews.body:
First of all, I will keep this relatively short. I like the aesthetic and the look of this film, but it's hard to describe how I feel about the film.

For one thing, I just didn't like the lead characters all that much. Nicholas Hoult was especially dull, overacting his accent and being rather goofy in his role. And therein lies some of the issue with the film for me. While I have enjoyed Robert Eggers filmography to this point, something about the overacting in this film just didn't sit right with me. Maybe they were compensating for the weaker actors or maybe he wanted an older acting style to match the gothic aesthetic...I don't know.

And then comes the final criticism...Eggers didn't really try anything unique. While The Lighthouse and The Northman had some interesting shots, lighting and other aesthetics, this film didn't have any of that verve. It felt like the kind of film should have new technical ideas, but it was just more of the same for Eggers. It's a well made, well crafted piece of art with a relatively simple story and flat acting. I mean, that pretty much sums it up.

reviews.author: nick-64431
reviews.body: Vampires in general and Dracula in particular have been cinematically done pretty much to death since cinema started, hence the original 'Nosferatu' from over a century ago now...yes, it really is that long ago! There's not much opportunity for spoilers here, this new take on an old story doesn't bring anything particularly new to the genre but nevertheless it's a cracking movie and doesn't disappoint, even if you pretty much know what's going to happen right from the start. It's absolutely soaked in it's gothic atmosphere and settings, and I recommend, if you haven't done so already, going back to the original source material so to speak and reading Bram Stoker's book which sets the scene particularly for the opening part of the movie, the journey to the castle. If you've read the book you have the extra element of enjoyment by spotting the bits that are pure Stoker and the bits that aren't. I actually preferred it to Coppola's effort, it's nowhere near as pompous and overblown and the characters are far more believable and as vampire movies go it works and works well.

reviews.author: christopher-underwood
reviews.body: I liked it a lot especially at the beginning through the opening credits and begins as we find out about Lily-Rose Depp's character in her early days. I thought the Gypsies were fine but as we go on and into the castle I was worried that it might be too long and as for some reason I wasn't happy about the scary moments. Back home and we get Willem Dafoe as the professor and we love what is going on and of course Depp is brilliant, the dialogue gets much better and the two actors are excellent. Although I had thought I might even fall asleep early on and then it gets on so amazingly that I loved it and forget those slow bits as there was, for me this long spine tingling sensation. So she finally tells her husband, and us, about Bill Skarskard as Count Orlok or Nosferatu and there is an awful but thrilling ending.

reviews.author: aghostofachance
reviews.body:
As a 50 years old horror movie fan who watched almost anything and everything about Dracula and the vampires, I can say that I did not enjoy this movie except some cinematographic elements. The movie was like an overrated and highly exaggerated combination of all previous Dracula/Nosferatu movies. So that, it almost looks like Herzog's "Nosferatu the Vampyre" and Coppola's "Bram Stoker's Dracula" had been hybridized to create something "in the middle", minus the grandeur of each... Honestly, it was very disappointing for me mostly because of the hype about it, which also made me expect a lot from this movie that has so less to offer compared to its predecessors... Sorry but this movie is far from being an Eggers classic or even a horror classic for true horror fans.

I watched all R. Eggers movies in the past and I dare to say that this is the worst in so many ways which I can not understand why. By the way, my favourite Eggers movie was The Witch because of it's original scenario and atmospheric elements. Eggers is actually a very talented director and writer however there's the possibility that he may not really be good at making movie adaptations or remakes. It looked like Eggers had a vision on his own but he felt that he had to stick to the original(s) to make it more acceptable and viewer-friendly. I wish he had gone to the extremes like some of the scenes in this movie (no spoilers).

The Nosferatu cast are all good actors and actresses however they mostly look like wasted on a very bad script with an outdated formula. Lilly Rose-Depp looked like an utterly unhinged version of Isabelle Adjani's Lucy Harker from Herzog's movie. Her performance stands out among the rest because she goes to such extremes to portray Ellen Hutter character asd they tried to add a twist to that but did not fit so well in the context (vampiric and demonic possessions are two different concepts). The chemistry between her and Nicholas Hoult's character was failing at times and mostly depending on over-acting. I couldn't really see that "big love" if there was any... I liked Simon McBurney, Nicholas Hoult and Emma Corrin's performances too because they really tried their best to make their characters look believable and as original as possible. Bill Skarsgard was almost invisible as Nosferatu under the make up and even his Pennywise character from movie "It" was more scarier than this although it was even a clown(!). Willem Dafoe, could have delivered a much better Professor van Franz however his acting was so mediocre. Perhaps I'd prefer him to play Nosferatu like he did before in Shadow of the Vampire.

The cinematography was the only good thing that I enjoyed in Nosferatu and the scenes were very well-crafted mostly. Though some people might find it too dark or having such weird angles, director of photography Jarin Blaschke did his best as such an indispensable component of Eggers cinema.

Special effects were also mediocre and Nosferatu looked like a car-crashed version of Gary Oldman's Dracula. If Count Orlok is not supposed to be Dracula, why did he have to look like Dracula and not like the classical look of Nosferatu from multiple movies from the past? I think they should have created a modernized version of the original Max Schrek's Nosferatu to pay homage. Sound effects and Count's voice was good enough which created the other half of the horror ambience for the movie. But the dialogues were so kitsch and unbearable as if trying to make it look more artsy and less cheesy... After the movie, not a single note from the movie score was left in my mind... Was there even music? No?... Costumes were also rather boring, like a crossover between different eras: Amish, northern European, Medieval French and less Victorian perhaps... I won't talk about the story not to give spoilers but all I can say that it had no surprises at all, it was quite bland, and not taking too many risks for trying something new. The pacing was also sometimes too fast and sometimes too slow. I also didn't like how some scenes were pieced together, which creates a feeling that you miss the whole set of events like as the scenes kept skipping (especially in the second half of the movie, it was became more disturbing for me) Even if this was a horror movie, I have never felt scared during the whole time because there was nothing in there that wasn't done before. The scenes which were inserted to look scarier were all done in previous movies, not going to spoil any of them here. When you watch you will remember them from the previous movies... As a matter of fact, knowing where the story goes, I did not really feel any tension or a grip until the very end. It started and ended as it's expected. Which means this film can be quite boring for those who know the original story.

I think I would still watch Coppola's Bram Stoker's Dracula or Werner Herzog's Nosferatu the Vampyre which might fall in the same category with what Eggers tried to do here. And overall as a vampire movie, I don't think I might ever want to watch it again or even recommend it to vampire movie fans, that's why I gave it a harsh 2/10.

reviews.author: samcollier101
reviews.body:
A beautiful, yet horrific tale based on Bram Stoker's Dracula. It doesn't shy away from its source material yet it may well be the best adaptation yet.

A film that begs to be seen in the cinema with its dark lighting and excellent sound. It's probably Robert Eggers most accessible film to date and its duration flies by. I wanted to see more. The acting is top notch. Lily- Rose Depp in particular is outstanding in a difficult role to play. She is sympathetic and yet menacing at the same time. Bill Skarsgard brings a new a new approach to the well recognised character. He is both humane and menacing at the same time. The supporting cast never fall short. Eggers always seems to get the best of his stars performing the roles necessary for the period he portrays.

Aesthetically, Nosferatu is a modern day masterpiece. The lighting in the film helps to build up tension and atmosphere perhaps that Eggers only matches in The Witch. It stays true to its source material and doesn't divulge too much from it.

There are however slight tweaks and 'improvements' that's make this more than worthwhile watching for fans of horror. Above all though, this is a film that should be enjoyed by everyone and has certainly my favourite film of 2024.

reviews.author: andersmerrild10
reviews.body:
The cinematography of this film is haunting and beautiful. Robert Eggers has really outdone himself with this movie. There's a number of shots in this movie that I can only describe as hauntingly beautiful.

The performances in this film are all solid. There's not one single actor who didn't deliver on a solid and fitting level. So far I've been impressed by Skarsgaard but this was without a doubt his best performance. Lily-Rose Depp delivered a great performance and stole the scenes she was in.

The movie completely captured the oldschool gothic tone that you would expect and I view this movie as an instant classic. More than 102 years after the original Nosferatur came out this movie is a fitting remake and I hope it will be remembered for decades as well.

reviews.author: ipratt-12182
reviews.body: Can't understand some of the bad reviews this film is getting. This isn't normally my kind of film but went to see as my girlfriend is a fan of the vampire genre. The setting and acting was excellent, story was told brilliantly, kept me glued to the screen. Lily rose and Nick Holt especially were very convincing and acted brilliantly throughout the film. Didn't know much about Nosferatu and his story before I saw this film but I do after watching this. Well worth a visit to the Cinema, ignore the negativity reviews and go and see and make up your own mind. I always find that is the best thing to do.

reviews.author: shelliiaae
reviews.body:
I'm going to keep this brief. I'll just make a few points!

I liked it a lot. I'm very big on locations, & this was able to bring this old brooding world alive. It felt lived in. It didn't feel filmed on a set.

This is big for ME, others may not care... the sex. I get so tired of sex in horror, especially graphic sex. I am so happy to be able to say, it's implied more than shown. If anyone worries if they can watch with family or whatever due to that awkwardness? I'd say it's pretty safe. Even the topless scene, her hair covers her. I'm very conservative, but I'd be willing to let my 16 yr old nephew watch it. The gore may be another issue though lol

The monster. I'm a sucker for any cool monster design. They did a really good job here! The voice is apparently all natural/real too, and his voice gives off an aura of power, & ancient knowledge. I almost had a feeling of him as some ancient dragon.

I waited about 9 months for this film, & overall I'll say.... I wasn't disappointed. I do think we could've gotten more with Orlock, and I kinda selfishly wish he was like 12 feet tall haha. But...

If you're a horror buff, if you're into monster films, or non-traditional (which oddly, this traditional vampire is no longer the norm) vampires? I think you'll enjoy it.

Lilly Rose Depp was actually AMAZING!!!! I was worried removing Anna Taylor Joy would've been a big mistake ... Lilly killed it!

reviews.author: Lefteris-Anagnostopoulos
reviews.body:
Even though I had a terrible theater experience, with obnoxious people talking, eating, and flashing their phones every 20' because they were bored, Nosferatu is an excellent movie and offers something new and unique that separates itself from previous adaptations. Unfortunately, it's one of those movies that has a lot internet chatter and morons everywhere will flock to see it and then complain and annoy the rest of us.

Eggers' Nosferatu is more of a possession movie that explores the repressed nature of the protagonist. Comparing it with the rest of his filmography, I'd say that this is his most accessible film and if you ask me, I'd say that I prefer The Witch, The Lighthouse and The Northman more, since I think that he took more risks in these movies - especially the first two. And even though I like the direction the movie took, I don't think that's the definitive adaptation of Nosferatu/Dracula either. Herzog's version is far superior in my eyes and of course Coppola's is also excellent.

These aren't complaints that detract from the movie, just observations. Nosferatu has great photography, great acting (especially Lily-Rose Depp gives 100%), and manages to stand on its own in the rich filmography of the Count.

I can't wait see it again alone in my house... Movie theaters suck and years now have become the worst place for cinephiles. The irony.

reviews.author: tomasctinoco
reviews.body:
I really wanted to enjoy this film more than I ultimately did. I gave it a 7 out of 10 because, while it has its merits, I think the director overthought too many aspects and stayed too close to the original. There were subtle nods to the director's signature styles and influences, but they weren't distinct enough to set this adaptation apart.

The biggest flaw for me was the cinematography. While I keep reading praise for it, I strongly disagree. The film is dominated by a blue palette that bleeds into black and gray, creating a monotonous, washed-out look. For comparison, Tim Burton's Sleepy Hollow comes to mind-a film where the cinematographer masterfully lit scenes, giving actors their own distinct light while enhancing the overall atmosphere. In Nosferatu, however, the cinematography flattened everything, making both the actors and the sets blend into a single, unremarkable color scheme.

The second major issue was the editing. A stronger editor and a tighter cut could have done wonders for this film. It's overly long and drags in several places, which really undermines the pacing and momentum. Overall, while I appreciate some aspects of the film, it fell short of its potential.

reviews.author: matepolcz
reviews.body:
Nosferatu is an absolute beast of a movie. It has strong themes and technically near perfect.

The story is something I wouldn't think I like, but the strong themes make me enjoy it as well. The theme of evil trying to survive, presenting itself as attractive is something I loved. Ellen knew what she had done was bad, while she still had enjoyed it. My favourite character was Professor Eberhart, because he immediately understood what was going on, I love these kind of characters. The dialogues sometimes feel too much.

This is the first movie where I noticed several scene transformations. The editing was beautiful. The pacing isn't perfect though, I think the movie could've been a little shorter. The cinematography is award-worthy. Slowly moving, revealing camera all the time. Give me more of that. The lighting is the best I have ever noticed. The cast is amazing, Lily-Rose Depp was obviously the best, but Willem Dafoe is a powerhouse. He has a presence no one else does and he gave my favourite performance. The sets also looked amazing, I genuinely don't know how much they relied on CGI. The practical effects looked great. Robert Eggers is a master at crafting a film, I'm looking forward to watching his other films.

Nosferatu is damn good movie. The best shot movie of the year and the best lighting I have ever seen.

reviews.author: druss44121-1
reviews.body:
This newest version of Nosferatu is quite well made. There are some incredible shots in this film, including one trick shot that, if they did it practically, I'm not completely sure how they pulled it off. The cinematography and production design are as good as it gets. The performances are great. A lot of thought and effort clearly went into this production.

But after a solid first act, the film becomes more one you "appreciate" rather than one that actively engages you. It's never scary or even that creepy, except for the first scene when you meet Count Orlok, which was the highlight of the movie for me.

I've felt this way about all of Eggers movies so far, that they are very well made but they never quite engage me the way the best cinema does, so YMMV. The Witch is still probably his best work for me, but if you've loved all or most of his films then you'll probably enjoy his take on Nosferatu more than I did.

I actually think the 1922 silent movie is creepier, more engaging, and better paced. Even from a modern POV. If you've never seen it, I recommend that and Murnau's other films like Sunrise and Faust.

Anyway, I'd still say this is worth seeing at least once. If you're a fan of Eggers, try to see it in a theater.

reviews.author: TheeRealMonsignor
reviews.body: Nosferatu? More like No-thank-you-ratu! Stellar cinematography, sure, but this flick is a snooze fest masquerading as a horror. Zero scares, unless you count the vampire's mustache as a fright. Seriously, who on earth thought a 70's style mustache would add to the already horrible recreation of an already tired movie? Max Shreck was THEE creepiest vampire to ever grace the silver screen. This version was laughable at best. Oh, and the predictable jump scare? Yawn. I bailed after 2 hours and 15 minutes of pure boredom. The rest of the theater was moaning too, but I was the smart one who escaped first. Avoid this cinematic disaster.

reviews.author: TheVictoriousV
reviews.body:
Gothic horror, psychosexual fantasy, and a raving Willem Dafoe surrounded by pestilential rats in a flaming chapel. You'd think the reception would be more consistently positive here.

Once the sneak previews started, Robert Eggers' loving remake of Nosferatu (1922) quickly became the talk of the town, or at least my social media feeds -- and indeed, not all of it was terribly ecstatic. In one Film Twitter corner, David Ehrlich praised its purposeful darkness -- in the visual, tonal, and thematic senses of the word. In the other corner, Brandon Streussing wrote, "superfluous, tedious and deeply uninspired, Eggers is pulling from everywhere but his own imagination". Some say it is Eggers' best; others argue it's his worst.

No matter how you slice it, however, Nosferatu is a film made by someone who deeply reveres the work he has been tasked with translating -- recall the impassioned letter he wrote for the Critics Choice Association, where he describes how the F. W. Murnau original shaped him when he saw it as a kid (reminiscing how he watched it on "a VHS made from a poor 16mm print, the degraded imagery making it feel more real"). In a later interview, he also shouted out the SpongeBob SquarePants episode Graveyard Shift, which, let's face it, is probably where everyone below a certain age was first introduced to Nosferatu. Bottom line, the man is a "true fan", possibly to a fault.

In the role of Graf Orlok (the character whom Murnau created as an "unauthorized adaptation" of Bram Stoker's Count Dracula, winding up with a horror-film figure who is arguably even more iconic than any official Dracula iteration, including Lugosi), Eggers has cast Bill Skarsgård, who might one day be synonymous with "21st-century horror". Yet again, opinions have been mixed.

People have compared him unfavorably to Klaus Kinski's iteration in Nosferatu the Vampyre (1976); others have given the highest praise possible, speculating that Skarsgård may be a real-life vampire -- not unlike the urban legends surrounding the original Orlok, silent horror legend Max Schreck, as explored in the 1998 comedy Shadow of the Vampire (which, as it happens, also starred Willem Dafoe). I personally think he acts more than well in the role, and I appreciate the inclusion of a book-accurate mustache -- supposing a remake of the knock-off should be faithful to the "real" source.

Verdicts on the rest of the actors have been all over the place too. Lily-Rose Depp's performance makes up for the stinking she was made to do by The Weeknd in 2023's The Idol, but people seem a lot less enthused by Aaron Taylor-Johnson (I think he MOSTLY works). People are fairly fond of Nicholas Hoult (from playing Renfield in Renfield to the Jonathan Harker expy in Nosferatu, he seems made for all things Stoker) and, obviously, Willem Dafoe is a blast as Professor Albin Eberhart Von Franz -- Nosferatu's equivalent to Van Helsing. The scene near the climax where he acts opposite thousands of non-VFX rats is exactly as kino as you've heard.

The film looks absolutely fantastic. Yet, there are some issues here, and some of you will have feared them when you saw the trailers: the images don't always pop the way that a Nosferatu film ought to. In Ehrlich's review, he called it "luminously ashen where too many recent movies and TV shows have just been irritatingly dim", but I contend that a few of the shots are just that: simply dim. Yes, even during the breathtaking sequence where Mr. Hutter first arrives at Castle Orlok.

A movie that supposedly pays tribute to German Expressionism -- especially the most famous example thereof -- has no business shooting for a "natural" look, but this one sometimes does. (This means we don't get to see Orlok lug his coffin around like in the Schreck or Kinski iterations because, hey, that wouldn't look real.) However, the images are painterly and moody regardless, and the music is splendid.

Most importantly, however, the vibe this film achieves is transfixing -- derivative or not, it works. (I certainly never felt the tedium I was promised.) Its central Phantom der Nacht works as a personification of the ravages of the Black Plague, a manifestation of Mrs. Hutter's sexual repression, and as a simply memorable movie monster who has already inspired a slew of oh-so-funny TikTok impressions. What else to expect from good old Bill?

Granted, I understand if the film isn't for everyone; it certainly isn't for you if you're anything like the Zoomer seated a few rows ahead of me. Throughout the screening, this person whipped out her cell phone to (1) use Tinder for a little bit, (2) snap a few selfies with the flash turned on, and (3) use the calculator app. I have no idea what this math problem must've been that she absolutely couldn't wait until the movie was over to solve it, but the good news is that she eventually fell asleep and I was able to enjoy the film in peace.

reviews.author: Pairic
reviews.body:
Nosferatu: Cecil B. DeMille used to boast that his films had "a cast of thousands", well, Nosferatu features around 5,000 trained rat actors. Nicholas Hoult claims they were incontinent. They were certainly everywhere in Europe in this film. Robert Eggers re-imagines the F. W. Murnau's 1922 silent film Nosferatu, which was inspired by Bram Stoker's 1897 novel Dracula. Indeed many of the characters are similar albeit with different names. Thomas Hutter (Nicholas Hoult) is Harker, while his boss, Herr Knock (Simon McBurney) who sends him from Wisborg to meet the Count is also Renfield. He cackles madly, sits naked in a Pentangle marked out with candles as he hails his master Count Orlok. Knock has a taste for sheep, rats and pigeons, preferring to eat them alive rather than flies. For some reason he ends up in an insane asylum. Hutter's wife Ellen Lily-Rose Depp tries to dissuade him from journeying, in the past she had psychic encounters with Orlok but keeps them secret. As Hutter nears Orlok's castle, Romani and an Innkeeper advise him to turn back but to no avail. Orlok (Bill Skarsgård) is first seen in deep shadows, we only gradually see more of his features, he looks significantly different to Murnau's Count.

Anyway Orlok/Nosferatu arrives in Wisborg bringing the plague with him. Streets are strewn with the dead and rats chew on bodies. This is actually more cheerful than previous views of Wisborg where it rained as much as in Angela's Ashes' Limerick. Prof. Albin Eberhart Von Franz (Willem Dafoe) an enigmatic philosopher/scientist/alchemist joins in the battle against Orlok, along with Knock he provides some of the (very dark) humour which leavens this tale of terror. I won't go into the disturbing scenes of horror and violence which permeate the film, better that you experience them unfiltered. Great acting from an ensemble cast, the production design is superb as is the cinematography, prosthetics are used to good effect rather than CGI in many cases. It has flaws though, it could have lost 15 minutes from its 132 minute running time, there are too many declamatory exchanges in the second half of Nosferatu. Still there is a wonderful, moving Grand Guignol ending. Robert Eggers has Written and Directed an almost masterpiece of Horror, it is a worthy addition to the Vampire Film Canon. 8.5/10.

reviews.author: mwcharke
reviews.body:
I joked about seeing this movie on it's Christmas release date but waited until January 5th and it wasn't a joke. It blew me away. So many shots in this movie could be framed peices of art. The culture of 1838 was thick but the language was clear enough that you could understand everything.

The story was incredibly simple but the subtle influence of the villain was, well, it's hard to describe. There were no spoon-fed explainations to the audience. Instead everything was shown with sound, color and distortion. They made you feel the vampire's presence sitting there in your seat. And once they had you, they twisted you like a wet rag.

I want to complain about the ending but like those under the creature's influence, I can't. I wanted a different ending, a more modern ending but that wouldn't have worked, not for this movie. I haven't seen the original Nosferatu but you can taste it in this work of art. It's not like other movies today.

reviews.author: njrmbm
reviews.body: A dark, gothic gem that is more horror/fantasy than straight horror (not a criticism), this movie is a visual feast and immaculately made. I love the pervasive sense of dread throughout this film. Count Orlock's presence is felt long before it is seen, and Eggers wisely keeps him in shadows most of the time. Some will criticize Orlock's different look here, but I applaud the director for thinking outside the box. Robert Eggers has shown himself to be a writer/director to watch, and I look forward to what he brings us next. He is a unique talent. Definitely see this in a theater if you can. Mesmerizing.

reviews.author: gvqkfv
reviews.body:
I loved the Witch. It had that eerie atmosphere all the time. Unsettling. This however? I seem to have missed it. As a Dracula-ish movie it's quite nice. Great settings. But the Count just sounded like a parody to me. I never felt any dread or connection to the actors.

It's a dark movie, but it's shot in a way that you can still see what's going on. Or just enough.

Perhaps I was just trying to find a convincing feeling of impending doom. Just a version that makes you feel uneasy. And no, certain "weird" scenes failed to make me feel that way. For the most part the acting was good to OK. Unfortunately it was a bit of a miss for me personally.

reviews.author: artizsan
reviews.body:
The film masterfully immerses viewers in a tense and shadowy atmosphere, bolstered by a haunting score that accentuates its carefully crafted scenes. The cinematography stands out with top-tier visuals and meticulously designed sets that evoke both awe and dread. However, the film's reliance on overly dark sequences-perhaps as a nod to the 1922 classic-feels slightly excessive, potentially detracting from the overall visual clarity.

Nosferatu is undeniably a strong work, with several standout moments that resonate deeply. It is best experienced in a cinema, where the sound design and imagery can truly envelop the audience. The dialogues, enhanced by the clever use of multiple languages, feel authentic and well-executed, adding to the film's immersive quality.

In conclusion, it's a compelling reimagining of a classic that, despite its minor flaws, is well worth watching for its atmosphere and cinematic prowess.

reviews.author: thebrokenmap
reviews.body:
Look, I don't know who all of you are out there raving about this movie. Is this your first one?

Yes, the movie is done well. The imagery, mood, pace and everything is great. Now having said this, you should know that they did the same thing just as well or better back in 1922 for the original Nosferatu. That's over a hundred years ago. In 1931 they also did it just as good or better for Dracula (1931).

So to rave and go into hysterics about how wonderful this movie is just doesn't make sense. In this film they pulled off what should be the very bare minimum of expectations for ANY movie to be considered skillfully made. This makes me think that the artistic quality of film over the past couple of decades has suffered so much entropy, and audiences have become so accustomed to subpar trash, frankly, that the minute anything is released that is remotely of any quality, audiences think they've been blessed with something from the heavens.

The reality is that it's downright disappointing that after more than a 100 years, with all of modern film technology, gear, improvements, and resources, the best this film manages to do is just come close to being as good as the original. Nothing new or exceptional here, comparatively.

I'll tell you right now, the fundamental story is as tired as can be. It has been beaten like a dead horse. I was bored. I think I sighed audibly knowing that I would have to sit for two hours through a story I've already seen told a hundred times. Everybody knows this story - it's the same fundamental story from Dracula the book, Nosferatu the film (1922), Dracula the film (1931) and Bram Stoker's Dracula (1992). Same story.

Eggers strays from it in only one significant way, which I won't spoil here. But suffice it to say that it does not improve the story. In fact, the entire premise for this deviation in the story (a premise you are introduced to in the very first opening shots) is downright absurd and makes no sense whatsoever. The entire film is built upon a ridiculous premise that requires the audience to believe that any person could be so lonely that they would ever behave in such a way as depicted - behavior so far fetched that it bears no resemblance whatsoever to real people or real life. It's like they brainstormed for the most unlikely thing a person would ever do and went with that, working backwards, of course. "Here's where we want the story to end up... Ok, now how do we get there?"

I saw this movie last week, and I'm glad I did. But know that I have been pondering the experience for a while now and I'm not writing this review as some sort of knee-jerk reaction to it.

reviews.author: mclaughlin-98589
reviews.body: This movie does not live up to the hype. Loud swells of music is nothing more than a jump scare. Nothing "masterful" or special about this film. The acting was theatrical and uninspired and the music has been heard before. What a waste of time and money making a piece of garbage like this. This movie lacked suspense and true horror. The costumes were beautiful but that is the only redeeming feature of this film. That was two hours of my life I will never get back. Of all the Dracula movies made, this was one of the worst. Hopefully the producers will be able to recoup their investment. Stay away from this stinker.

reviews.author: ani-chalakova
reviews.body:
A masterpiece for the eyes. Beautiful and at the same time full of very authentic details (like the depiction of Romanian people, local gipsies, old ladies at the church, etc. I am from the Balkans and I admire this part).

Super scary, I think I will be afraid of the darkness for quite so many days after seeing it.

An amazing depiction of a haunted woman by the main actress. Although she was not so impressive in the "normal" scenes, she was absolutely amazing when she was playing the posseessed or sleepwalking parts.

The bridge she did! (Even if it was stunted or animated, it was just mind blowing.) But the best part of it all was the philosophical second plan idea of the movie, which spoke of the power and darkness of the female sexuality and how it was treated and is still being treated as something animalistic, evil, a disease. Also, the internal struggle for women who try to supress it, the battle to stay faithful to your husband and the inevitability of it overwhelming the love, even when you know that it will bring a fatal end.

And last but not least - the movie theater was full of people, some of them very young. Everybody watched the movie in silence and left the salon in silence. I rarely see so many people from different background being shocked and thoughtful simultaneously because of a movie.

reviews.author: HorrorDisasterGuy-90617
reviews.body:
I found this to be a great remake of the original. While the story is the same, it does something differently and expands on it. Like Ellen connection with the vamprie and the lore behind him. I really like how the movie expanded on these topics throughout, which is interesting to learn about and builds up the development. The movie is faithful to the source material, with it having the atmosphere of its gothic nature and moments from the original. I also found the movie to be pretty creepy with how they did the direction with the cinematography of it. It also does a great job with character development on how they give them more reason to feel for them throughout. The climax itself is pretty memorable on what happened during it, and the way the movie ends is really great. I found the characters to be really great in this movie and how they expanded onto them. There's are a lot of other things great with the movie, like the production design looks great on how it feels like the time period, the movie contains a couple of great practical gore effects, and the costumes looks great too.

Nosferatu is a great remake that is better than the 1979 one, and I highly recommend it.

reviews.author: ashsaysno-41032
reviews.body:
Robert Eggers' Nosferatu is an amazing rehash of the original. Well breathing "undead" life back in the oldest vampire film classic, he simultaneously revives vampires as scary horror monsters.

Nosfurto was of course originally a rip off of Bram Stoker's Dracula (1897), written and adapted for screen by Henrik Galeen and Directed by F. W. Murnau. Thankfully the film was not wholly destroyed, as was intended after a 1925 court ruling. This was brought by Florence Balcombe, Bram Stoker's wife, from a lawsuit against German production company Prana Film.

Well paying enough homage to the original Nosfurto: A Symphony of Horror (1922), stand out performances by Lily-Rose Depp and Nicholas Hoult made Eggers' movie stand on its own. These of course were accompanied by Eggers eye for detail in building a world that was lived in and felt appropriate given the time period it is set in. Jarin Blaschke lights up the setting to amazing affect. Giving great contrast to the day and night settings, well not stumbling into the same pit falls that The Northman (2022) suffered from.

In world where movies like Twilight and Dracula 2000 are almost a generation old, Vampires as a creature have lost their luster and almost become jokes of celluloid. I am thankful none of the trailers showed anything but a shadow of Bill Skarsgard's Cout Orlok. He is truly terrifying and is absolutely the embodiment of evil.

Given the award worthy production and note worthy performances, this will be a capstone for horror in 2024. Hopefully this will be reflected in the upcoming award season. Though the original is over a century old, I would recommend watching Galeen's 1922 original before seeing this astounding adaption by Robert Egger.

reviews.author: harveyj-11761
reviews.body:
Nosfeatu has generated mixed reviews, with some praising its artistic qualities while others express disappointment. Overall, it can be described as a film that falls somewhere in between.

The narrative closely mirrors that of the original film, maintaining the same characters and core elements. The cinematography features striking visuals, a compelling dark aesthetic, and commendable performances from the cast.

However, a notable concern is the film's lengthy runtime of over two and a half hours, which contributes to its slow pacing. While a deliberate pace can enhance character development and world-building, Nosfeatu seems to linger, often revisiting certain themes and elements without a significant escalation in tension or momentum.

To improve its pacing, the film could have benefitted from a reduction of at least 30 to 40 minutes. This would likely address some of the pacing issues that appeared to frustrate viewers, as evidenced by audible sighs at the conclusion of the film.

For fans of the original who appreciate a slower narrative style, this film may be worth watching. Conversely, those who prefer a more dynamic pace might find it less enjoyable.

In summary, while Nosfeatu is not a flawless masterpiece, it certainly has its merits, although it could have achieved a more effective execution with some judicious edits.

reviews.author: kosticns-1
reviews.body:
Few films dare to revisit a cinematic landmark as audaciously as the new Nosferatu. Building upon F. W. Murnau's haunting 1922 classic, this reimagining both honors its predecessor and redefines the vampire mythos for contemporary audiences. Directed with surgical precision and steeped in aesthetic grandeur, the film is an uncompromising vision that melds folklore, body horror, and historical dread into a mesmerizing tapestry of terror.

From the first frame, it's clear this Nosferatu isn't a mere retelling but a rebirth. While Murnau's version relied on shadowplay and silent-era expressionism, this rendition bathes in atmospheric richness, preserving the dreamlike unease while enhancing it through modern filmmaking techniques. The choice to retain much of the folkloric authenticity-particularly the Romanian language spoken throughout-cements the narrative in a chilling realism that feels both timeless and immediate.

The addition of Count Orlok's attire resembling Vlad the Impaler is a masterstroke. It connects the vampire mythos directly to the historical figure whose reputation for brutality still haunts the European imagination. This visual parallel roots Orlok firmly in the legacy of Dracula while preserving the original film's spectral menace. The gypsy rituals that ultimately lead to the vampire's demise evoke ancient fears of curses and superstitions, grounding the film in Eastern European folklore with an authenticity that feels both respectful and chilling.

Perhaps most remarkable is the film's embrace of body horror to heighten the existential dread that pervades its story. The grotesque physicality of Count Orlok-gnarled hands, elongated limbs, and a cadaverous frame-feels disturbingly organic, as though the vampire has erupted from the earth itself. Every inch of his appearance reinforces the narrative's themes of decay and corruption, making his presence almost unbearably oppressive. The sequences involving transformation and feeding push the boundaries of visceral horror, reminding viewers of the genre's ability to confront mortality and deformity head-on.

The performances are uniformly exceptional. The actor portraying Count Orlok disappears into the role, embodying both predatory elegance and primal terror. The supporting cast similarly delivers layered, emotionally raw performances, grounding the supernatural narrative with a sense of tragic inevitability. The film's human characters are not mere victims but flawed, complex individuals whose fates resonate long after the credits roll.

Visually, the film is a feast. Every shot seems meticulously composed, recalling Murnau's German Expressionist roots while layering in sumptuous textures and shadows that feel almost tactile. The chiaroscuro lighting, often echoing the interplay of light and darkness in the original, deepens the film's psychological unease. At times, it feels as though the audience is peering through a cracked window into another realm-an effect that mirrors the voyeuristic nature of the vampire's stalking.

Yet, what ultimately sets this Nosferatu apart is its refusal to lean solely on nostalgia. While it pays homage to its source material, it also carves out a distinct identity through its exploration of existential horror, folklore, and human frailty. It dares to be as unsettling as it is beautiful, a balance few horror films achieve.

This Nosferatu is a masterpiece-a rare sequel and reinvention that not only honors its lineage but elevates it. It's a triumph of filmmaking, a reminder that some nightmares, no matter how ancient, remain eternally fresh. As the vampire dissolves into ash, so too does the boundary between past and present, leaving behind a cinematic experience that lingers like the echo of footsteps in an empty corridor. This is, without a doubt, one of the best films of the decade.

reviews.author: notfunnyiam
reviews.body:
To start with the positives, the cinematography is beautiful, the feeling the scenes give you are exactly what you would expect, the feeling of dread, the fear of the unknown. The actors, all great, they did amazing in their roles and played their parts as expected.

However, as much as i wanted to love this movie fully, i could not. The pacing of the story is all messed up, the story should be spanning over weeks/months however it feels as if everything happened in 3 days. The movie suffers from alot of telling and not showing, i wont spoil it but certain relationships and backstories should have been shown in a brief throwback scene or even a montage. The movie didnt do that, in the last third of the movie it just explained the nature of their relationship and in not much detail either. The nature of the relationship in question was left very vague and not in a good way, but in a way which leaves the story superficial. The star studded cast, in my opinion, was partially to blame for this because it felt like the writers/director wanted everyone to have a line and everyone to be important which left every character kind of bland and with not much depth to it.

TLDR: a good movie to watch for the beautifull scenes or if youre a fan of one of the actors, but the story will not give you what you want.

reviews.author: covaciaurora-41054
reviews.body:
It's been far too long since we've had a true Gothic horror movie that captures the essence of shadow, dread, and tragic beauty. Nosferatu delivers all of this and more, proving once again why this genre holds a timeless appeal.

This film pays homage to the silent-era classic while breathing new life into the Gothic aesthetic. The atmosphere is drenched in eerie, almost hypnotic visuals-decaying castles, misty graveyards, and candlelit chambers that evoke both beauty and menace. The performances are mesmerizing, with a haunting blend of terror and melancholy that's rare in modern cinema.

The film doesn't rely on cheap jump scares or excessive gore but instead builds a chilling, slow-burn tension that keeps you captivated from beginning to end. It's a movie that respects its audience, crafting a story that feels both poetic and deeply unsettling.

Nosferatu is a reminder of why Gothic horror endures-it explores themes of mortality, forbidden love, and the eternal struggle between light and darkness. If you've been yearning for a movie that embraces the haunting elegance of classic Gothic storytelling, this is it.

A must-watch for fans of atmospheric horror and lovers of cinema as an art form.

reviews.author: derek-duerden
reviews.body:
Unlike Herzog's remake of 1979 (featuring the stellar pairing of Kinski and Adjani), after this I ended up thinking "why did you bother?"

There's very little that's innovative and, for me, lots of jarring elements which were just distracting - not least the pointlessly VERY LOUD segments which had us thinking of leaving fairly early on. As others have noted, Orlok's voice and mustache were laughable rather than scary, and some of the acting was very poor (e.g. Aaron Taylor-Johnson). Mind you, I think everyone was struggling with the poor script and dialogue. You can't make a great film on cinematography alone...

Hoult does well with the first half but then he's rather sidelined and the film also seems to lose its way until the fairly predictable climax - by which time, like Lily-Rose, I was ready to go also.

Disappointing.

reviews.author: lndkent-93989
reviews.body: This movie tried to be artistic and visually interesting but instead was just long and boring. No real plot. The vampire was cartoonish (including his vampire accent). Way too much vomiting. (Why do shows insist on so much vomiting? It just gets tiresome. It is so overdone.) Unconnected elements and extended scenes made this movie painfully too long. None of the characters was sympathetic (except maybe the little girls). Plus it was WAY TOO LOUD!!! Thankfully I brought earplugs but it was still WAY TOO LOUD! The dialog was hard to understand. When it went to black at the end, I was just so hoping for the credits...best part of the movie!

reviews.author: sharkme94
reviews.body:
It's finally here, and now it can be undoubtably declared the finest horror movie of 2024, and possibly even years past. It was everything I hoped it would be.

The movie is terrifying in ways I wasn't expecting, with a level of surrealism that is both titillating and disorienting, removing a sense of time. It really does create an effect of the characters, and thus for the audience, of being trapped in a nightmare.

Nosferatu contains some of the most beautiful imagery to date by Robert Eggers. The production value is incredible, and his cinematography continues to put most other contemporary films to shame.

This film also has the most stacked cast of an Eggers film to date; every single person deserves an award. Nicholas Hoult was phenomenal in his earlier scenes with Orlock, and Lily-Rose Depp deserves all the acclaim she is getting for her emotional turn as Ellen and the extreme physical performance she delivered. To me though, far and away the star was Bill Skarsgard. Having seen other films of his, when you first see Orlock and hear him speak, the famous actor we know is gone and replaced by something monstrous and inhuman. The voice work he did was absolutely incredible.

This was the film I was most excited for in 2024 and it did not disappoint! Robert Eggers has once again proved himself to be one of the most original and powerful voices, not just in horror, but in cinema as an art.

reviews.author: ethanbresnett
reviews.body:
Robert Eggers keeps up his golden streak with another expertly crafted and gripping tale, cementing him as one of horror's finest auters. A passion project of his for many years, he can't have hoped for a better finished article.

Visually this film is masterful. The way the camera moves, the framing, the colour palette, the attention to detail, everything about it is arresting for the eyes. It's not just the visuals that demand your attention though. There is something about the tone of this film that also commands attention. It is uneasy, chilly, sinister, but you can't look away. Anything could happen and it makes for such a thrilling experience.

As we've come to expect with an Eggers feature, a stellar cast is assembled. The lead pair of Nicholas Hoult and Lily Rose Depp are superb. They bring such raw physicality and emotion to their characters that bring real stakes to the whole piece. A supporting cast of the likes of Aaron Taylor-Johnson and Eggers muse Willem Dafoe are in fine form. Then there is the titular performance from Bill Skarsgard as Count Orlok in a truly transformative role. The character design is incredibly chilling and effective. Add in the physicality and terrific voice work from Sakrsgard and you have a horror character for the ages.

As if all of this wasn't enough, the story is also thoroughly gripping. I was a bit concerned going in about the runtime and was worried that the story may feel drawn out, but it really works. It is paced well and the themes are perfectly explored.

To sum it up I think this film just simply engulfs you. Visually, mentally, physically. I just felt sucked into Eggers' vision and relished every second of it.

reviews.author: biancayo-73369
reviews.body: This movie is more than just a remake. I feel like Eggers capture the essence of a girl with depression, who thinks that she is not fit for love. In the end, she finds her one true love, Thomas, whose willing to risk it all and fight for her but we all know that Ellen has to realized the evil within her and fight it herself. I want to thank Robert Eggers for making this movie as not only does it represent a lot of girls but also for making this more refreshing with thrilling moments, pleasing-to-the-eye costumes, and appreciation for history and the art of darkness. I truly enjoyed the 2 hours 12 minutes of pure of art.

reviews.author: dngoldman
reviews.body: This is another fantastic Eggers film-dark, grotesque, and thematically rich. The late 19th century was a time when science, reason, and commerce were ascendant. However, the old country had something to say. Eggers doesn't make period pieces for their own sake. And the only way to combat evil is to embrace the irrational that had been disregarded throughout. It is only when Van Helsing, played by the William Defoe, arrives that the film takes off, unfettered from its somber beginnings. Defoe immerses the viewer in the social milieu of the day, and the West must sacrifice one of its own to fight off the horde from the east. Eggers' melodrama sometimes blurs the line between humor and camp, which works in the lighthouse but makes the Northman an embarrassment. There are some effects (Nosferatu's breathing) that elicit chuckles when they shouldn't. But the movie works because of its beauty, its ability to shock, and its capacity to make us think.

reviews.author: Dreamyweaver22
reviews.body:
Eggers' "Nosferatu" is both beautiful and haunting, a perfect blend. It is a cinematic masterpiece down to every last delicious and gory and grotesque detail. This is beautiful retelling and reimagining of Bram Stoker's "Dracula" and the original 1922 "Nosferatu".

It is rare that a film can bewitch me as this one has done.

This is everything I could have ever wanted out of a Gothic horror (and dare I say a Gothic romance?) film. The vibes and the tone were immaculate.

Everything about this film was artfully woven and perfectly placed. The costumes and set design masterfully set the scene and built the world. This is something Eggers has a forte for, with "The Witch" and now "Nosferatu", amongst others, under his belt.

The cinematography was particularly outstanding and one of my favorite parts of the film. There are so many scenes that will stay with me purely because they were so striking.

The cast was also perfect in every way. Depp and Skarsgård delivered award worthy performances of Ellen and Orlok. Hoult and Dafoe also did particularly well with their characters.

Simply put, there aren't enough words at my disposal to describe this film. This was a masterpiece and it definitely deserves the hype it is receiving. It is easily in my top five horror films, and probably in the top three films this year. This film definitely won't be for everyone, but I suspect it will be a big hit for true horror fans.

Do not miss out on catching this one in cinemas for the full experience. If you can see this in IMAX, it is an absolute must.

reviews.author: tmcmaster031405
reviews.body:
This is a decent movie. I don't understand the endless amount of praise every aspect of this film is getting. Yes the cinematography is outstanding & most all the technical aspects are great. But what about the script, what about the acting?

The script is the same Dracula story told numerous times. I know you want to stay faithful to the German silent rip off but no artistic liberties could be taken to liven up the story. We've all seen this story a million times.

The acting was by far the worst aspect of the film. Lily Rose Depp is awful. Terribly miscast and she just doesn't have very good acting chops. Also Aaron Taylor Johnson, while not terrible he really is giving a satirical performance. Ever word out of his mouth is spoken with such punctuation I couldn't help but laugh every time he spoke. Bill Skarsgard is pretty good under all that make up and a goofy mustache but nothing special.

Robert Eggers is a very good filmmaker and this film is beautiful and the film is decent enough but towards the end I was laughing at it. So it's good but not great. I do look forward to what Eggers does next but hopefully it's more original.

reviews.author: icminindy
reviews.body:
Nosferatu is an amazing re-telling of the original 1922 classic film. The director has taken the opportunity to utilize today's advances in cinematography to take the audience to another time, place, and reality that is authentic and engrossing. The misty, snowy, muted colored environment, along with authentic set design and costuming places the audience alongside the characters in each and every beautifully haunting scene.

Every performance is excellent, although in my opinion, Aaron Taylor-Johnson felt somewhat miscast. Lily-Rose Depp was spot-on in her role as Ellen Hutter, giving us a convincing understanding of the vampire that mystically torments her throughout the film. Bill Skarsgard portrays Count Orlok in a deliciously evil, haunting, yet sensually unique way.

The performance by Nicholas Hoult as Thomas Hutter, particularly in the first half of the movie, is so engrossing that you feel his feel every ounce for his sheer terror. He takes the audience to the height of his paralyzing fear, but never overacts a single moment. I found myself hoping he would pass out just so his torment would stop. He is brilliant.

I expect to see this film win many awards this year, and you will feel rewarded for taking the time to see it. It was worth the wait.

reviews.author: waltermwilliams
reviews.body:
"Nosferatu" is a 2024 remake of a movie that's over 100 years old and I was so keen to see this movie when I heard it opened on New Years Day, I changed my booking from Peru to Germany....figuring Vampires beat Bears all day long...that bear being Paddington.

Was I wrong?

The Good: Movie Mythology has it that the director of the OG, "Nosferatu" (1922), F. W. Murnau, made a Faustian pact with a true "vampire" to get him to star in his silent black and white classic, whereas director Robert Eggers only had to hire Bill Skarsgård as the titular character.

Bill was great in "It" 1 & 2, but his make up & prosthetics (including his penis) make Bill unrecognisable in "Nosferatu" as he casts his other worldly shadow (mocking the original) but in 2024 he comes complete with gigantic moustache and scaly old body that seems to be channeling "Rasputin" more than a vampire.

This is the second time that Bill Skarsgård portrayed a vampire.

The first time is in the Netflix show, Hemlock Grove (2013).

Meanwhile Nicholas Hoult as "Thomas Hutter" in "Nosferatu" also starred in another loose adaptation of Dracula, the dark comedy "Renfield" (2023) and I honestly enjoyed that so much more.

The Bad: According to Bill Skarsgård, his voice was the aspect of the part he worked hardest at, spending six weeks before shooting lowering his voice an octave.

He achieved it doing exercises that sound kind of like Mongolian throat-singing.

The result?

Bill sounded like a chronically asthmatic Darth Vader minus the deep voice of the late, great James Earl Jones.

The Fugly: Director Robert Eggers co-directed a stage production of "Nosferatu" in high school and it was probably scarier than this movie adaptation.

Eggers has always been interested in dark stuff.

He's best known for freaky feature films "The Witch" and "The Lighthouse".

If you want to see one of his better movies, stream "The Norsman" starring Skarsgård's older brother.

Watch out for: "Nosferatu" is a reimagining of Gothic legend and Johnny Depp's daughter, Lily-Rose Depp as "Ellen Hutter", is terrific as the haunted victim of the Transylvanian parasite.

It get's all Hammer Horror as she's trapped in a supernatural romance of sorts with "Nosferatu" since she was quite young, which makes her "melancholy", doctor speak for strap her down and dose her with ether and opiates.

Hubby Hoult hopes to break off this heavy petting passion obsession with the help of demon-hunter Willem Dafoe as the mad "Professor Albin Eberhart von Franz".

The creepiest character is Simon McBurney as "Knock" who swan dives from successful lawyer to demon worshipper including a scene worthy of Alice Cooper or Ozzie Osbourne.

This could have been a lush, old-school retelling of a stone-cold classic, but it misses the mark with it's M rating.

If thousands of rats, a couple of wolves or old castles give you jump scares then have I got a movie for you.

"Nosferatu" was not the fantasy, horror, thriller I thought it should be even with an historically accurate director in the big chair.

I did not succumb to the darkness!

reviews.author: kindle-82514
reviews.body:
I believe this is my first movie review, I can't not comment on Nosferatu. Whatever I thought this movie would be going into it, I was wrong. It tries to be artsy, but falls flat. The characters attempt to be compelling, but are one-dimensional. The sets, costumes, locations are stunning, but there's nothing of substance to fill them. It suggests a backstory between Ellen Hunter and Count Orlok, but never explores it.

In lieu of seeing Nosferatu, I highly recommend seeing its forebear, Bram Stoker's Dracula with Gary Oldman and Anthony Hopkins (1992). It's the same story, only done well, and Oldman's Count Dracula and Hopkin's Van Helsing are both captivating and iconic.

reviews.author: MrGrinch46
reviews.body:
