reviews.author: qkgsrhdx
reviews.body:
Just saw this at the Lincoln Square IMAX and was really impressed. The whole experience is so visually striking. The scenes and the way they portrayed the occult, and the sets, the costumes, and the dialogue made for a film that was truly greater than the sum of its parts.

I actually thought the dialogue was very enjoyable on its own merit. It's the kind of writing you would see in a theatrical play so the feel of the whole piece felt true to how people probably spoke in that time. It was nearly poetic and while is a bit less straightforward than modern English, it has a really great sort of luxuriously complicated quality. Hard to describe really, but listen to Count Orlok speak and you'll understand what I mean.

I especially enjoyed the way they held off on the full reveal of Nosferatu until more or less the end. One of the things I also really liked was how he spoke and the way Bill Skarsgard brought out the evil in the voice.

Same for Willem Dafoe, he was hilariously quirky and brought a refreshing bit of contrast to the scenes through humor through his character.

Overall a very worthwhile film, but do expect some gore, which I guess is part of the whole experience.

reviews.author: kevin_robbins
reviews.body:
Nosferatu (2024) is a film I caught tonight in theaters. Set in 1830s Germany, the story follows a financially struggling man working his way up at a local firm. When tasked with traveling to a remote mountain region to finalize a property contract for a mysterious Count, he reluctantly accepts. However, upon meeting the Count, he becomes both a food source and a pawn in the Count's plan to secure the property and return to the German village.

Directed by Robert Eggers (The Lighthouse), the film features a stellar cast, including Nicholas Hoult (Warm Bodies), Lily-Rose Depp (Tusk), Bill Skarsgård (It), Willem Dafoe (Poor Things), Aaron Taylor-Johnson (Kraven), and Ralph Ineson (The Witch).

This is a meticulously crafted production, feeling every bit like a high-budget Hollywood feature. The cinematography is outstanding, utilizing smart camera angles, dramatic lighting, and shadows to enhance the eerie atmosphere. The period-accurate backdrops, costumes, and dialogue effectively immerse the audience in the era. The horror elements are top-notch, delivering gruesome kill scenes, chilling "exorcism" sequences, and well-executed jump scares.

That said, the storyline is overly straightforward, lacking the twists and turns that could elevate it to a masterpiece. The ending, while serviceable, feels underwhelming and predictable.

In conclusion, Nosferatu is a beautifully produced film with much to admire, particularly in its visuals and horror elements. While the narrative lacks complexity, it's still a highly enjoyable addition to the genre. I would score it a 7.5-8/10 and strongly recommend it.

reviews.author: Junreviews
reviews.body:
Vampire movies are always intriguing to watch because it builds a contractual relationship through conflicting emotion between the vampires and the humans, which leads one of the two endings. Does human end up killing the vampire first or does the vampire strike beforehand?

"Nosferatu" has one of the top performances in terms of acting without relying too much on visual effects by starring Nicholas Hoult and Lily-Rose Depp as main characters along with a wicked vampire played by Count Orlok. Each actor exceeds their role by playing out of their mind in several interesting environments such as castle, village, and forest set in late 1800's in Germany. The costumes and cinematography are well done that they bring authenticity and realism as if I am taken back in time by a time machine.

Unfortunately, there are more cons than pros in the movie. The horror scenes constantly get cut short every time a fight or an event ensues. I can hardly remember a battle scene that lasts more than 30 seconds. The dialogue is also hard to understand, especially the vampire's unique tone and enunciation, which differentiates him to emanate a scary mood.

The story is hard to grasp as someone who watches Nosferatu for the first time without experiencing previous films from 1922 and 1979. There is not enough explanation on some key elements such as why certain characters do not die despite getting sucked their blood in the same way as others who end up dying.

This film is enjoyable for the most part if you don't pay attention to the backstories of characters as the movie does not do a great job on connecting the dots. That is why Nosferatu is not so for adults who tend to decipher the plot.

reviews.author: weinstockdanny
reviews.body:
I am not naturally a fan of scary movies. Jump-scares do not entertain me. Horror and gore are not concepts that I normally find fulfilling. But I am a grown-up now and I feel compelled to go watch great cinema!

Having seen this movie in Dolby, I don't think you can have a better sensory movie-going experience. The 10/10 aspect of this movie is the sound design. Following as a close second is the cinematography. The movie is, a cliche, hauntingly beautiful. Two days on from seeing the film, there are so many frames and sequences just frozen in my mind. That's not a novel thing for an Eggers film, two years later there are many frames still frozen in my mind from the Northman. But this film is somewhat unique in making a dark and bland color palette pop.

It is difficult to rate this film, as it is in a genre I do not have much exposure or appreciation for. All the choices come across as tasteful. One note I think should weigh heavily: the theater I went to was huge, and it was packed. When the credits rolled and the lights turned on, everyone turned to their group and smiled, laughed and immediately started talking. Same for me! Everyone clearly had a great time watching this. As a movie-going experience and piece of art, this is a great film.

reviews.author: paultreloar75
reviews.body:
Was so much looking forward to this one, after loving The Lighthouse and the imagination that bought to the screen. However, having to sit through almost two and a half hours of leaden plodden CGI, where we're told again and again "He's coming", we were both so disappointed as the credits rolled and the yawns were stifled. It's not a bad film as such, although the two female leads are drawn so thinly, you almost wonder why they bothered. But it's style over substance, all fur coat and no knickers as my old boss used to say.

If you want something bombastic and macho, this will probably satisfy but don't expect any consistency in the story telling, there are some many continuity errors, it's remarkable, and maybe some old things should be left undead. Worst of all, it really isn't very scary or sexy at all. And for a vampire film, that really is a curse.

reviews.author: Kuplinks
reviews.body:
This new version of Nosferatu is basically Robert Eggers saying "Hold my pint this is how you make a gothic vampire film"

It's beautiful to look at, it has genuine moments of terror and horror and for me a definitive telling of well told story. It even makes the bit where the vampire is in the city not boring rubbish or silly which for me most other versions do. Gary old man in sunglasses is stylistically awful in my opinion a problem this film does not suffer from. The vampyre is genuinely grotesque creepy and scary at times.

It's downsides are it suffers from we have seen this story a million times already and inevitably you find yourself going "when's the boat bit" etc etc

Aaron Taylor I don't rate him at all as an actor, overrated and in this film he does nothing to change my mind and I wish it was a bette actor in the role,

But minor quibbles as the film as a whole is a masterpiece as far as I'm concerned. The cast are brilliant with Dafoe stealing every scene and walking that fine line between eccentric Dr and over the top cheese which as it's Dafoe means the character is believable and not cheesy.

There are shots in this movie that will stick in my head for evermore. The arrival of a coach in the woods a particular highlight for me. Cannot wait to see it again. A film made for the largest screen you can find.

reviews.author: grigoraaakis-889-295918
reviews.body: A gothic fairytale. Eggers created a very atmospheric film with "Nosferatu". Every frame looks like a painting, every scene looks like it really belongs in Victorian era. I haven't really watched the original or any of the classic Dracula movies. Still I really appreciate the atmosphere of the film as it really transports you into the era and sets the pace. Eggers has some really visually creative scenes and at points the cinematography is captivating. My one issue with the movie seems to be the characters. I really was not able to feel for anyone on screen or connect with them. Depp actually hasn't enchanted me with her performance and Hoult while good almost felt like not a part of the movie. Skarsgård was completely unrecognisable, and while his character is the main event he still felt almost absent. The story is actually a classic gothic tale and still something couldn't let me connect. "Nosferatu" for me is a visual Victorian gothic fairytale without any depth.

reviews.author: amirseta-31655
reviews.body:
Nosferatu is a perfect example of how not to remake a classic. This film takes the eerie charm and haunting atmosphere of the original and trades it for a bland, lifeless mess filled with every horror cliché imaginable. Predictable jump scares? Check. Paper-thin characters? Check. A plot so pointless that even the vampire seemed bored? Double check. If you're looking for a movie that sucks the life out of you, just like a vampire, this is it. Do yourself a favor and skip this one.

Save your time, staring at a wall for two hours would be scarier... and more entertaining! Rewatch the 1922 masterpiece instead, and you'll thank me later for saving your time.

reviews.author: JohnDeSando
reviews.body:
"My dreams grow darker." Ellen Hutter (Lily-Rose Depp)

Freud and Jung would applaud this most recent adaptation of Brom Stoker's Dracula, directed by Robert Eggers, Nosferatu (2024), because it evidences the rich psychic territory that sexuality and death invade. In this iteration, Ellen has more clearly than ever seen her haunted sexual desires and awareness of death's primacy. She is horrified about her dark mind, like us wondering from where evil can come

Meanwhile, the ultra-desaturated cinematography, helmed by Jarin Blaschke, is as scary as any cinema has ever been. Eggers has restored material illegally taken from Stoker by F W Murnau in 1922 and made it refreshingly and scarily new. The difference between Orlock now and Kinski's and Schreck's then, is his remotely plausible addict not totally foreign to the aud.

Bill Skarsgard's Count Orlock is more fully exposed in his homely visage, much more accessible than most other Nosferatu's. Seeing even his flaccid member while the dialogue, especially Willem Dafoe's Professor von Franz (the new von Helsing) discounts the plague as the answer to the devastating recent population deaths in favor of the evil residing within the melancholy and uncontrollable Ellen, for instance. Fully available is her attraction to the bad-boy Orlock. "We are here encountering the undead plague carrier... the vampyr... Nosferatu." Professor von Franz.

The fact that Orlock is quite homely, not seriously ugly, gives credence to the universal original sin of weak human beings. That we see him frontally naked with his flaccid member is as new as ever seen for a mainstream Gothic gore fest. "Psychosexual" is only one of the many lurid adjectives to describe what's going on here.

This current Nosferatu relies heavily on atmosphere, a persistent fog suggesting pervasive evil yet allowing the aud to see it easily in Orlock and his minions. Nicolas Hoult's Hutter displays a vulnerable youthfulness that's easy prey for the Count. Hutter also has the accessible human quality of being clueless at the wrong times.

This iteration is careful to include the weakness of humans. Consider Ellen's primal attraction to Orlock, whom we see in shadows but understand better than ever-he's hungry for her and her blood. Stoker's mantra is repeated: "The Blood is life." It becomes clear that death, like the Count, is unstoppable, regardless how much blood one may have.

Don't fear the rising sun because it can bring the end of death for the moment. Just ask the Count, or wait for the next variation of Stoker's immortal bringing plague and damnation in around two horrific hours.

"It is the bloody business which informs." Macbeth.

reviews.author: c-57622
reviews.body:
At first, I had to keep reminding myself that this was a not one of the "present day style" movies I've been watching a lot of lately. Once I was able to surrender to the fantasy, I was drawn in. Beautiful costumes, cinematography, the film's texture and colors, the script, the actors' performances brought me the story on a platter. I love horror stories but this classic was delivered with just the right amount of old school jump scares to satisfy my need for an adrenalin rush. Yet, it was well balanced with humanity's strife with self, religion, belief systems, love, societal stature, etc. I love the use of different languages: German, Romanian, Dacian, Roma, Russian, Latin and English. It definitely added to the vibe.

I had some issues with the old time Hollywood view from a man's lens, where women easily moan and groan, and can be freely exposed but the men kept fully clothed. Then there was Count Orlok; I had to control my giggles with his over-wheezing. I would have offered him a puff from my Ventolin puffer so he could get his asthma under control and get on with his "business".

Other than that, I did enjoy the movie with its subtle hints taken directly from the classics. My English Literature teacher from my younger days taught me well to read between the lines. This film captured those unspoken words and hints. I'd go back for a second serving.

reviews.author: baksibakovic-207-122979
reviews.body: An excellent explosion of the masterful way of building tension and a charged gothic atmosphere that envelops the film with a superior mystery. The visual momentum that is presented is hypnotizing and spooky. And some scenes are so striking that they remain etched in the head for a long time. This effect was achieved most when Thomas set off on the road to the infamous Transylvania. The uncertainty and sinisterness of such an undertaking were perfectly captured, with eerie surroundings such as snowy mountains or enigmatic rocks that look more like some lined up statues. From ancient times. And while the dark ride in an unsafe and magical carriage will hardly leave anyone indifferent. Lily Deep did very well as Ellen. Her non-stop duels that she leads within herself between the tenderness of innocence and the loneliness of surrendering to darkness were convincingly portrayed. Skarsgård is an electric Orlock with a piercing magnetic voice and an evil disgusting appearance, a merciless cruel force. Who successfully evokes discomfort every time she is on screen. Hoult is likable in the role of a caring husband who does everything to build a better life for them, he contributed a couple of good scenes, especially when he was with Orlock on the screen, then the tensions were very high. The soundtrack is melancholic and gloomy, it gives a useful shape to the narrative and is remarkably intensified when the violence appears. While the finale was an impressive combination of great massacre and seductive elements.

reviews.author: serenamason
reviews.body: This film did a very commendable job bringing the legend of Nosferatu back to the silver screen. Nick H. Is wholly believable as our lead character, not knowing what he's got himself into when going to visit Count O. On business. The trip to reach the counts Castle is well shot and crafted. Some of the scenes are just absolutely visually stunning. The real interesting part of this movie is the performance by Lily. Johnny Depp's daughter has got some acting shops to be sure. Also, the work of the make up team, set design, and costume Departments all need to be mentioned and applauded. The movie grabs you from the opening scene and doesn't let go until the ending. It is well constructed and it is worth your time to go and view it. Job well done all around and a respectable addition to the vampire canon of movies overall.

reviews.author: sherwoodbandit-1977
reviews.body: I've been excited to see this ever since I heard it was happening! The trailer only made my anticipation that much greater. I'm a huge vampire fan and this looked to be a hopeful return to form from a genre that has grown stale and often obnoxious. The film lived up to my hype and much more! Not only is it the best vampire movie I've seen in years, but it is one of the most perfect all around movies I've witnessed in a long time. I'm new to Robert Eggers. I haven't seen any of his celebrated filmography but you can bet I will watch it all now. His vision for this movie was masterful and he carefully selected each shot so as to tell the most provocative story possible. He succeeded on every front. Even Count Orlok's new look, which I was skeptical of at first, made sense in the world that he created. Had he tried to emulate the original silent film's design, it just wouldn't have worked with his more realistic take on the story. Bill Skarsgård may well be the premier character actor of our time. He embodies every character he takes on to the full extent and the things he is able to do with his voice are astonishing. The rest of the cast is marvelous! Nicholas Hoult is always good and Lily-Rose Depp is fantastic in her breakout role. I've always enjoyed Willem Dafoe and while he isn't bad in the role of alternate universe Van Helsing, it didn't really seem like he belonged here. That is a miniscule complaint as he is still successful and considering Robert Eggers seems to really like working with him, he can get what he wants if the result is him being more comfortable to create when he has a friend on set. Which it clearly was! It is a rare thing these days for me to be completely satisfied when leaving a movie theater but Eggers and his gang of vampire hunters really hit a homerun with this one and gave me hope for the future of cinema!

reviews.author: liverimplant
reviews.body:
Let me get one thing clear. By no means do I think this is a bad film. It's extremely well made and at times enthralling.

Each of Egger's previous films captivated me from beginning to end. Their creepiness, the unravelling mysteries that they had to offer. Their tension built and built until it spilled over in an exciting climax.

That is really where Nosferatu stumbled for me. The plague ship began to run aground around the beginning of the second half, where the haunting atmosphere gave way to horror movie tropes that I've seen a billion times. We finally see Count Orlock, the dark cloud himself and he looks so damn goofy that It made me think twice about getting Lasik.

I didn't see the original movie but was told that this is a faithful adaptation. That's cool but I think it needed some updates.

All in all, like I said before, it's not a bad film, I just didn't find it as groundbreaking as everyone else. I saw multiple couples walking out of the theater and someone behind me was snoring at one point, also in the second half. The actors all did a great job though and I'm happy that they all get to be a part of a film like this, I'm sure it will be huge for their careers.

6.5/10.

reviews.author: cdjh-81125
reviews.body:
Nosferatu comfortably continues the trend that Robert Eggers has established for me in that every new film he's made I've liked more than the last. It truly does feel like everything his career has been building towards and not only do I think it's his best movie to date but it's also one of the best horror movies I've ever seen.

Robert Eggers truly is an auteur in every sense of the word because this entire film from top to bottom feels like something only he could make. He has such an unparalleled ability to immerse audiences into whatever time period he explores. Without sounding too hyperbolic it really does feel like cameras shooting real locations and characters from the 1830's. The dialogue feels totally authentic in how it's written and delivered by these actors but also in how it's shot.

The visuals are absolutely jaw dropping in a way that never felt like it was drawing attention to itself and feels totally right for the aesthetic that Eggers is trying to capture. Nothing about it feels modern in any way in large part because of the use of shadows and candles to light a majority of these scenes. Eggers loves a long take and the way in which he directs these scenes is so satisfying to watch unfold. The scene transitions make everything flow so well and for as long as some of these scenes and sequences are everything felt like it was building towards something meaningful and I can honestly say that I haven't felt this satisfied by the slow, deliberate pace of a film since Blade Runner 2049.

It's a horror movie first and foremost and I can't remember the last time I felt this much unrelenting dread watching a film. There's an element of mystery to it as well and the way that Eggers spoon feeds the details of these characters backstory felt executed in a way I would consider to be perfect. But like the best horror directors, Eggers understands that what you don't know is far more terrifying and I was left satisfied by all the things we didn't know for sure by the time the movie concluded.

We get very few proper looks at the Count Orlok character and for that every scene in which he was present for in some way had me genuinely glued to the screen. The highest compliment I can give the portrayal of that character is that I never saw an actor giving a performance. Part of that is how Eggers framed him and the outstanding makeup work but none of that works without the levels of menace that Bill Skarsgard exhibits.

His voice is absolutely on point and it's kind of performance where I kept wanting to see him interact with new characters. Every one, and I mean everyone, is great here but this thing truly belonged to Bill Skarsgard and Lily-Rose Depp to me. The physical feats she pulls off have to be seen to be believed and she really is the emotional centre of this entire film. She has to portray an overwhelming amount of despair from basically her first scenes and I honestly don't believe this film works as well if it wasn't for her. I know it doesn't have a hope in hell, but the Academy really should be looking at this for Best Actress and Supporting Actor nominations.

Everything about the first two acts felt perfectly depicted to me. There's a constant sense of tension and that truly horrific events are inevitable and to be fair to the film it mostly kept to that promise. Every character feels as if they're there to fulfil a specific purpose and even when I wasn't always clear what it was I couldn't wait to find out. Most of the film feels intimate and as if it's ultimately about the drama between a few characters but it's when the script starts to move away from that intimacy is when it started to lose me a bit.

The stakes get larger in ways that made sense to me but it really did start to affect the pacing. The whole thing feels like it's building and building for so long but when something of a world ending threat comes about it started to feel like the film became bogged down in exposition. It feels like the character drama takes a bit of backseat in favour of building up a whole new threat when I already felt as if there was more than enough dread to lead directly into a wholly satisfying climax.

Nosferatu ends up delivering on everything I wanted it to and then some. It's dripping in atmosphere and an almost overwhelming sense of dread but it never but it mostly manages to keep the character drama at the forefront. It's overbearingly tense and genuinely creepy in a way I haven't seen in many other horror movies and it's an acting showcase for everyone involved. I already knew that Robert Eggers was someone to get excited about but this movie puts him on a whole other level for me. He's one of the best directors working today, a true auteur and every studio in Hollywood should be lining up to finance his next film whatever it may be.

reviews.author: zombie134
reviews.body: Magnificently filmed and wonderfully spun Gothic horror story. Eggers film, from beginning to end, knows what kind of film it wants to be and maintains it's consistency to the final shot. At no time does he go off the rails with this film as I believe he did with the Lighthouse, blurring the line between reality and madness. This is a solid film. Count Orlock is a real villain here and has quite a bit of screen time and dialogue. I'll have to admit both Eggers and Skarsgard version of Orlock/Dracula is a fresh take. He's way less supernatural and more like a repulsive walking corpse. Honestly, Eggers really steers clear of many horror tropes like excessive gore and sex, over the top special effects and jump scares. Nosferatu prefers to creep out the viewer with perfect ambiance and unsettling visuals. Both the relationship between life & death and the setting of early 19th century European culture create an amazing pallette for this oft told tale. The darkness and loneliness of 1839 come to bear on the viewer and you begin to understand how a dark house or a lonely woodland path at night can invoke the reality of vampires or werewolves or witches. His depiction of Transylvanian villagers and clergy is very realistic as well not reducing them to goofy caricatures like previous films. They are both sympathetic and foreboding and the embodiment of ancient superstition. The standout of the film, though, is the brilliant acting of Lilly Rose Depp and Bill Skarsgard. Depp's Ellen is both haunting and beautiful and vile. Her depiction as both innocent and malevolent play perfectly against Skargard's dead and hollow Count Orlock. The directors depictions of death on the screen associated with sex and love stir feelings of both passion and abhorrence in the viewer touching on taboo imagery bordering on necrophilia and cannibalism and sadism but never crossing that line to make it cheap and exploitive. Overall I was very happy to see a work of art on the screen and beautifully adapted rendition of Stoker's Dracula and FW Murnau's Nosferatu 1922. Eggers made this film his own and brought his mastery of dark beauty to the screen for us. Although the film isn't perfect it's imperfections for me honestly are not worth mentioning. Definitely want to rewatch on my home cinema when it comes around and really explore the layers of this film. Gorgeous movie and not disappointed.

reviews.author: Josh-GenX
reviews.body: GenX reporting in. My wife and I are huge Dracula and vampire fans, ever since we were both kids, we'd watch dracula films on black and white TVs; so we went on a date to see this new Nosferatu. We were excited. The film starts out great. It is well cast. The style of the cinematography was good. Nice costumes. Then comes the vampire / count dracula design, which totally fails and isnt scary. It's a goofy looking 70's western mustache on a zombie. The best part of this film was the poster, ads, and trailer, all beautiful! There is one scene with Renfield that is excellent. reviews.author: djoenzy

Me and my husband really enjoyed this movie. I liked the tone, which was grotesque but not gratuitous. This was because there was an actual plot beyond a man stuck inside a castle. I enjoyed these plot lines into the regular society as it contrasted the Dracula scenes very well. I thought the acting was good and William Defoe nails it as the quirky alchemist who gets pulled in to attend to Ellen, the protagonist. There is cool lighting effects used to differentiate Dracula scenes. Overall, it is a good gothic, tragic film that isn't overly artsy/intangible and in terms of storyline.

reviews.author: cscottstapp
reviews.body:
This movie was another take on vampires and has a story line where you have a general idea of how it'll end. With that said, it's definitely a movie worth watching. Going into this movie, I knew there was a 1922 version of this movie but didn't get a chance to watch it prior to watching this one, so I'm unsure how similar they are.

The start of the movie was fantastic and took on a different take to vampire movies where a guardian angel turned out to be the devil. Whoever did the casting did an amazing job because it had an array of great talent who put on a stunning performance. The filming was on a whole other level. Changing between color and monochromatic/black & white and the use of shadows only hesitated the tension of the movie.

reviews.author: josephbrewster-88279
reviews.body:
Should you see this? If you're not a fan of slow burn films, films which are decidedly more "artsy" than accessible, slow camera pans, over-the-top acting and a splash of blood and sex, skip this one.

If you grade horror based on how scary it is, you might find this a bit underwhelming. There's tension, suspense and horror, but I wouldn't put it on my top 10 scariest ever movies list.

You might enjoy this movie if: you're a fan of vampyr lore (but don't expect elaborate plot justifications for the creature's existence), a fan of film noir, classic Vincent Price or Lugosi films, a cinephile who drools over cinematography and art direction.

I believe Eggar's gives us a love letter to classic horror in Nosferatu (2024). Lily-Rose Depp overacts, and I felt it was exactly what Eggars asked her to do. He intentionally injected some camp, refusing to bow to the new order of psychological horror (although he plays that game well), providing a window into a world which felt part broadway stage acting, part big-budget b-movie.

Each character did what I felt was needed for their role, bringing a sufficient level of Psycho energy to the screen, ramping emotional tension and providing a stage for some strong performances, such that are rarely called for in modern horror cinema.

The plot was lacking in some areas, possibly due to scenes still gathering dust on the editing room floor, but I felt satisfied overall that this movie was what I expected it should be, given both the director attached and the source material being referenced.

It was well worth the price of admission, but isn't everyone's cup of tea. For me, it was a welcomed bitter winter delight.

reviews.author: ThereelscoopwithKK
reviews.body:
If I were to describe the film as succinctly as possible I would describe it as very well polished and yet shallow at the same time.

In an age of cinema where sets and poor CGI have seemingly been cheapening the feel of film I admire and appreciate the high level of detail that director Robert Eggers puts into his work. The cast performs well, the camera work and overall cinematography is beautifully done, and overall lighting and atmosphere superb. No expense is spared on the costumes either. All of this helps the viewer immerse themselves into the desired world and time period.

Now with all this said why am I not giving it a higher score? Despite how technically sound it may be there is something a bit soulless about it. The dialogue is fine but I can't say I'm truly ever fully invested in the story. Many moments are spent dragging on for an ending most viewers of the genre are already familiar with. For those who weren't , the conclusion probably felt even more underwhelming.

reviews.author: Terryweaverjr
reviews.body:
Story ~ 8 ⭐ This was a story re-told. The legend has it Nosferatu was an unofficial adaptation of Bram Stoker's 1897 Novel - Dracula. After the film was released, the widow of Stoker sued the production company, but the film prints were already in distribution and the film had taken on a cult following.

The script is very good. Could it have left a little more room for mystery? Yes, but it will be known as a masterpiece, without a doubt. It's a true horror film ~ for more on that, read the commentary at the end.

Acting ~ 9 ⭐ A few weeks ago I reviewed The Order with lead actor Nicholas Hoult I explained why he was not a great cast pick for the antagonist in that film. In this film, he was perfect. Hoult was exceptional in every way and was an excellent cast selection for Thomas Hutter. It's hard to say who stole the show, Hoult or Lily-Rose Depp, daughter of famed Johnny Depp. She was incredible. The weakest performance came from Aaron Taylor-Johnson, which was just, well, not special. Willem Dafoe, Bill Skarsgård and Ralph Ineson rounded out the spine-tingling performances.

Cinematography ~ 9 ⭐ Hat's off to Cinematographer Jarin Blaschke. His work pulled the viewer into the scene. Every shot was framed remarkably, like a master painter had first storyboarded this film and turned over the paintings to emulate. The film was artful, cinematic and stunning in every frame. This movie transports you to a cold, dark, visceral world.

Robert Eggers There is something to be said for this director Robert Eggers; this film is stunning. This is my first watch of his work, but I want to see more. He wrestles with massive themes, symbology, and the greatest stakes in story, that is eternity. He's one of the scriptwriters and he's clearly a special filmmaker with the ability to bring unique expressions to life.

One look at the scenes that take us to Count Orlok's say, you are entering a different world. Bravo to Eggers; you've gained a new fan.

My Advice If you are a fan of horror or want to try something new, you've got to watch this in theaters.

reviews.author: diaaasky
reviews.body:

reviews.author: johannes2000-1
reviews.body:
In spite of (or due to) my high expectations, I was slightly disappointed. It sure is visually very impressive: the atmosphere is spot-on gothic, the photography is beautiful and at times very inventive, the settings and costumes are perfect, and the abundant CGI is convincing. The story is a faithful remake of the 1922 Nosferatu (in fact a German version of Bram Stoker's Dracula novel) and it has all the needed suspense, violence, chilling and sinister scenes, and a very effective score.

What pleased me less was the theatricality of it all: the characters all talk in almost pompous Oxfordian English, and act like they're playing on a stage for a far-off audience, with constant raised voices, wild gestures and rolling eyes. Especially William Dafoe goes totally over the top as the eccentric doctor Franz. Lily-Rose Depp has the ungrateful task to act most of the time as a deranged and possessed woman, the effect was - I'm sorry to say - at times more ludicrous than realistic, seeing her madonna like face constantly wide-eyed and gasping. Nicholas Hoult however did a great job, keeping his emotions just inside the borders of reality.

Bill Skarsgard was as Nosferatu unrecognizable in yet another of his grandiose metamorphoses, playing him with a grave authority. For some reason they decided to radically change the 1922 appearance of Nosferatu, from extremely skinny, vulture-like to a blown-up professional wrestler with a gigantic mustache. It only worked (for me at least) in the first half of the movie, when he moved as a menacing silhouet in the shadows of his castle. The more he came into full view, the less convincing it became, and the last scene of his bulked body on top of frail Lily-Rose was almost grotesk.

I recently saw Francis Ford Coppola's "Dracula" (1992), a dazzling cinematographic experience, that almost overwhelmed the underlying story and the actors. I definitely like this 2024 Nosferatu better, but it has more or less the same problem, of the form too much dominating the substance.

reviews.author: Muddymilkshake
reviews.body:
I read reviews before viewing so I went into this movie with low expectations but was pleasantly surprised.

The gothic asthetic and cinematography kept me intrigued and even though I knew where the story was going I still felt an element of suspense.

I thought Lily Rose gave an exceptional performance as Ellen. I could feel the vulnerability of her character , especially in the end scene which finished with beautiful detail.

Every character invoked a feeling in me and I felt especially stimulated by Orlok who conjured all the things you would expect a vampire to be.

Seductive , powerful, terrifying.

The whole film carried a macarbe artistic flair which I was able to appreciate, however I could tell other audience members around me were getting restless.

Im glad it stayed true to the bones of the original and didn't venture away from that. I feel it's a film that will be met with much pleasure from the right audience.

reviews.author: hougejoel
reviews.body:
Nosferatu is not without its strengths, with incredible performances throughout its runtime, especially from Depp and Bill. Apart from the acting, the film is gorgeous. Seriously some of the best cinematography I have ever seen. The style is gripping and a future Oscar for the outfits and clothes is sure to come.

Although there are some serious strengths within the movie, I found it to slow down significantly after Nosferatu makes landfall in the new town. This movie should be 20-30 minutes shorter easily, and this added time creates opportunity for repetitive scenes. Similar to other Eggers works Nosferatu is also incredibly strange. This however works somewhat in its favor in building an uneasy tone. I also found that the dream sequences reduced stakes and made the film difficult to follow.

Overall a mixed bag of a film. It's a 6/10 for me with clear Love it or Hate it potential.

reviews.author: tommy-97761
reviews.body:
I've come to love the works of Robert Eggers for a couple reasons. His nerdy attention to detail and adherence to historical accuracy appeal to me very much. If you'd seen any of his previous works than this is no different. Contrary to other Artsy-Auteur directors with Eggers I understand the point he is trying to make.

What was the point of Nosferatu?

To make a Vampire story based on the folklore of Vampires rather than to recycle the same depiction we'd seen depicted countless times already. Personally I love the various permutations of the Dracula/Orlok story and this one definitely sets itself apart from the rest. You might not like the new approach, personally I loved it.

The plot remains very true to the original 1922 Nosferatu. If you watch that movie in advance, you'll notice a couple of lines taken straight from the title cards. The Original Nosferatu, if viewed as if it were a current movie have a number of plot holes, character flaws, very crude exposition and other narrative problems. These are IMO addressed and fixed in the 2024 version. The characters get fleshed out better and their reactions seem more realistic. Everyone praises Lilly-Rose Depp and Bill Skarsgard, and for very good reasons, though the most relatable character IMO was Aaron Taylor-Johnsons Harding, who portrays a supportive wealthy friend who gets pushed far beyond his comfort zone. Seeing a behind the scenes video about the costumes, I'd like to draw your attention to one thing I missed during my first viewing. Harding is in fact wealthy, while Hutter is rather middle class. This can be also seen in the costumes where Harding own multiple top hats and has more jewelery compared to Hutter.

The tone of the movie is slow burn, with about 3-4 jumpscares. Some would call the movie unscary, personally I found it atmospheric. The Imagery, the character interactions, sense of doom. It is very similar to the Witch or Lighthouse. If you enjoyed those movies, I believe you will enjoy this as well. If I were to rate the movie against other adaptations, this will land amongst the top ranks. I have to give it some time though, because I can feel recency bias affecting my judgement, placing this movie at the to position even above the Coppola movie.

P. S. The whole movie I kept thinking, Aaron Taylor-Johnson has a pretty good english accent, which shouldn't be surprising upon learning that he's english.

reviews.author: 210west
reviews.body:
After so many adaptations of "Dracula" (including at least two of "Nosferatu"), did we really need another? This new version is certainly handsome enough, but it's stiff, stilted, and artificial as a set of waxworks. It is chilly -- but not in a good way -- and ultimately so tedious and uninvolving that you can almost hear audience members stirring impatiently in their seats.

The color is muted (when there's color at all). Scenes are either shot in dimly lit interiors or else beneath bleak grey skies, so that everything is bathed in a cold blue-grey light. The effect is artistic, in a showy way, but also looks a little fake, like illustrations created by A. I.

The worst thing is the language, so self-consciously old-fashioned and ornate, like the stilted dialogue in fairy tales, that I felt sorry for the actors, saddled with the impossible task of making their lines sound natural. As for Count Orlok, he speaks with exaggerated slowness -- liiiiiike theeeeessss -- in a low, guttural, electronically amplified voice. Who knows if it's really young Bill Skarsgard underneath all those prosthetics?

It's hard to imagine anyone finding much joy in this grim, dreary film. And yet, though a couple of well-known critics have, correctly I think, chided it for being "self-serious," most of the reviews have been unaccountably respectful. Damned if I know why, or why it was even made.

reviews.author: outahand
reviews.body:
Eggers has worked on the presentation of Nosferatu through a number of live play performances in his younger years, and was able to beautifully concentrate his best ideas that added a deliciously dark atmosphere and an imposing sense of terror, from which the viewer cannot escape.

Lily Rose Depp was captivating from the first scene where her turmoil only amplified until the glorious finale.

Willem Defoe brought a much needed gift of humour within the ceaseless dread.

Now to Count Orlock. Bill Skarsgard's make up is absolutely incredible. As much as I love Herzog's version, I could never get past Kinski's look, with his protruding ears and rabbit teeth. I absolutely loved Skarsgard's soft introduction (pun intended) where he is mostly shown in shadow until his disgusting visage is revealed.

I will save you from any spoilers but I will say that this film has brought new heights of class to the horror genre. Bravo to the entire crew of Nosferatu!

reviews.author: ElCinefago
reviews.body:
Eggers takes us on a journey to darkness. This film exists in the shadows on the lights of torches and candles. Its titular vampire is more of a zombie and a Demon than a classic cinematic fang wielding vampire.

I just walked out of the cinema and I feel I have seen a simpler yet more terrifying version of Coppola's Dracula.

The work of the actors is absolutely magnificent, they do succeeded in selling the audience their struggles and their fears. Regarding Orlok himself it works beautifully when it exists in the shadows but once it is revealed (quite soon in the film) it loses most of its visual power. The fact that he's covered in proscetics makes his body look too rubber-like and will remind you of a generic bat-like vampire. I wish Eggers would have hold the reveal until almost the very end of the film and just let that vampire be hands and shadows and scare us with that powerful voice. The coat he wears becomes almost an obstacle to make him a visually imponent figure towards the end and the lack of fangs made it look a bit just like a zombie.

I very much enjoyed the design of the face and moustache but I think it was a missed opportunity to making him scarier.

I know it's a re-telling of Nosferatu but I really missed the other elements and scenes from Stoker's novel. He wrote them for a reason. I really missed the brides, I really missed the count turning others into vampires and I really missed a story that was written to feel much bigger.

Eggers's Nosferatu is so beautiful and horrifying and yet it story feels rather small for a two hours movie.

reviews.author: kjproulx
reviews.body:
The 2024 remake of Nosferatu was a fascinating experience for me. Despite my love for cinema, I never managed to see the original 1922 version, though I'm familiar with the story. As someone who is impressed with director Robert Eggers, I didn't feel the need to have seen the classic before diving into this remake. While films like The Lighthouse and The Northman didn't completely blow me away (I tend to appreciate the filmmaking and visuals of his works more than the films themselves), this Nosferatu might just be my favourite work from Eggers so far. The way he brings the story to life, set in the 1830s, is both hypnotic and terrifying, and the film does a fantastic job of blending old-fashioned gothic horror with modern sensibilities.

The plot follows Thomas Hutter (Nicholas Hoult), who travels to Transylvania to sell a manor to Count Orlok (Bill Skarsgård). Meanwhile, Hutter's wife, Ellen (Lily-Rose Depp), remains at home, troubled by unsettling visions. Orlok, who has a haunting history with Ellen from her childhood, returns with sinister intentions. The atmosphere of the film is where it truly shines, thanks to the work of cinematographer Jarin Blaschke. The visuals, along with Robin Carolan's eerie score, engross the viewer in a sense of dread. Eggers' style is always meticulously crafted, and is on full display here, with the film feeling both timeless and modern at the same time. Every frame pulls you deeper into the haunting world of Orlok and his terrifying hold over Ellen.

Nicholas Hoult and Lily-Rose Depp both deliver incredible performances, with Depp's portrayal of Ellen being a standout. I was genuinely surprised by how powerful her performance was, as this was my first exposure to her work. I wasn't sure what to expect, but she elevated the film. The chemistry between her and Hoult works well, but it's really Depp's nuanced portrayal that anchors the emotional core of the movie. Skarsgård's Orlok, meanwhile, is every bit as unsettling as you'd expect, adding an extra layer of menace to the character. The film's acting, coupled with the masterful direction, makes it an immersive experience.

While Nosferatu completely captivated me in most areas, I do think the film's final moments might push things a little too far. There are certain moments and insinuations throughout the film that I feel could've been toned down, as they border on excessive. However, these are minor nitpicks in an otherwise fantastic film. Overall, Nosferatu is one of the standout films of 2024, and for fans of Eggers' horror talents, it's a must-watch. It's now playing in theatres and if you know what to expect from a Robert Eggers film, I highly recommend it.

reviews.author: lindsey-steindler
reviews.body:
I will commend the visuals, most of the acting, and Bill Skarsgard's eerie Orlok voice. That being said, I really thought I would be leaving the theater more shivery. Gothic horror films obviously punch a bit differently than the typical horror, and Rogert Eggers certainly gave us something fun to watch on a Tuesday night. But man, I was in the mood to really get scared. Must be the winter chills...

Seeing it in theaters was a plus; we all felt like we were trapped in the castle for a while with Nicholas Hoult. Heart racing and knowing darn well sooomething just ain't right with "my Lord" and his raspy breathing. No question- the first few scenes with Thomas and Orlok are my favorite parts.

Looking forward to what darkness Robert Eggers will bring to the table next.

Sidenote- hope you like rats!

reviews.author: sportsfrikaf
reviews.body:
Right now, Robert Eggers, is the most authentic, original film-director Hollywood has had in a very long time!

To attempt the daring attempt to make a Remake of the cult pioneer horror classic ''Nosferatu'' film from 1922.

Didn't any of us hardcore horror-film fans think that anyone could possibly do it today, especially with the thought that we live in a bad film industry that only makes terrible remakes and reboots of old film classics.

But there, Robert Eggers proved to everyone that he could do it.

The entire film scenario was completely based on the Original Nosferatu film, from the setting of single scenes, the historically correct historical costumes, on authentic settings in 1830s Germany, to the gothic setting of the film which was completely based on Bram Stoker's novel.

Actor casting was absolutely excellent, it was like seeing people right from the historical period even though the story was a fiction.

To witness Bill Skarsgård as the iconic ''Count Orlok'' was to see a haunting demon trying to possess you to create something evil.

And even though Count Orlok sent out was not as hauntingly terrifying as the previous Nosferatu films from the 1922 original and the 1979 version.

Skarsgård's acting was a haunting fear of a masterpiece of an acting performance.

reviews.author: Jeremy_Urquhart
reviews.body:
I didn't see this under perfect circumstances, but even if I had, I still feel as though I might've come away from Nosferatu just a little bit disappointed. It rides the line between a 3/5 and a 3.5/5 for me, whereas all his other movies hover closer to 4/5 territory, sometimes even a little higher. It feels the least essential of all his films to date, in part because we've had a couple of very good Nosferatu movies already that still largely hold up. I appreciate how it felt like there were a few shoutouts in this to other horror movies from the 1920s (possibly The Phantom Carriage and Faust), but it's still kind of what you'd expect. In good ways and bad ways, it is a Robert Eggers Nosferatu movie through and through.

There isn't a ton of passion to this. There are a few points where it really comes alive, and I guess technically it does impress, when you can see what's going on at least. The murky darkness does feel like a confident deliberate decision, sure, but it's still just a bit too dim. Some performances go through the motions a little, and a few individuals find moments to shine. I don't think I can call anyone here bad at least. I wouldn't have known Bill Skarsgard played Orlok if I hadn't been told beforehand, so seeing someone that recognizable disappear into a role is cool. I was underwhelmed by how Orlok ultimately looked, though. There was a lot of secrecy around his appearance, which I guess built up a level of hype that couldn't do anything but disappoint eventually.

It is a perfectly fine vampire movie. My gut is telling me that 3.5/5 is too high, but part of that might be just the other stuff going on at the moment influencing enjoyment. If I ever see this again during a more peaceful time in life, and it still disappoints in these small but noticeable ways, I feel I'd lower my rating. Negativity aside, a lower-tier Eggers film is still going to have interesting things within it, and though Nosferatu is a bit too long, if you wade through its murky 2+ hour-long runtime, there are some unsettling, striking, and bold moments to be found... maybe just not as many as I was hoping for.

reviews.author: gracesophia-47412
reviews.body: This movie was aesthetically beautiful, and the acting was great! But it was so boring. Of course, I know it's supposed to be a slow-burn, but Egger's 'The Witch' from 2015 was a fantastic slow burn that had me on the edge of my seat the whole time. I don't know what happened with this film. The silent film version is 10x better and more entertaining, and it doesn't even have dialogue. It also wasn't even scary. It's supposed to be a slow burn, a creepy and eerie scary, not a jumpscare scary. But it wasn't even that; the movie didn't make me uneasy or creep me out at all. The film had amazing cinematography, and the acting was great overall, but those are the only things that I liked about it.

reviews.author: mjanelle-24974
reviews.body:
I've been trying to piece together a coherent review of this, and frankly, I'm not entirely sure it's possible. But here goes.

This is an extremely atmospheric piece, dark, menacing, seemingly in black and white, but actually in color. All the tones are muted, including costumes and light. This is supposed to be Christmas time (though not specifically stated, such is shown with lighted trees, and such - unless I missed something). You can tell that a lot of care went into the filming of this movie. The set pieces are elaborate, but also a little bit stock, as in, we've seen these sets before somewhere - can't quite place my finger on it. There are brilliant pieces of camerawork, for instance a scene where Lily-Rose Depp's character sits up in bed, and the camera pans out in anticipation of her movement and then follows her as if you are rising yourself.

Performance wise, Ms. Depp is a standout, exposing the depths of her character's madness and fear. Also notable is Willem Dafoe's Professor von Franz, just crazy enough to be sane and just sane enough to be crazy. (please someone give this man an Oscar already).

The rest is just meh. The writing is so flowery in a strained Victorian way as to be WAY over the top. The other performances are of perfunctory stock characters performing as you would expect those stock characters to act and react. Changes in attitudes come and go with these characters on the turn of the proverbial dime without making a lot of sense. A stern task master immediately changes position without a even transition, just kind of like, oh, now i'm supposed to be sympathetic instead of outraged and put upon - OK, here you go.

This film was no improvement on the previous two versions, nor on its predecessor source material (the original Dracula - the similarities being extremely obvious). Worth seeing on the big screen for its visuals. Otherwise, if that's not your thing, i'm not sure I'd even look for it in a streaming format, as most of the visuals would be lost on the small screen.

reviews.author: birdlion77
reviews.body: Do not understand the complaints. Thought the movie was scary, intense, and emotional. Just because people were expecting something different, does not mean it will come to pass. The direction and cinematography were flawless. If you are on the fence, do not go to see this film, and miss a really great film. If you were so bored, stay at home, and read the Brahm Stoker book. The sound design, and score were outstanding as well. I remember when they used to guarantee satisfaction when you paid to see a movie ... oh wait a minute ... that has never happened. I saw the Robert Pattinson Batman Movie, and did not care for it, and did NOT spend valuable time whining about the fact that I did not. Art is subjective, no guarantees, that you will like it.

reviews.author: ddevilsaadvocate
reviews.body:
A visual masterpiece, with haunting beautiful locations, a good script and solid performances (especially from Willem Defoe who is brilliant in all of his movies) .

This moder remake of the original 1922 movie is a great tribute to the first and to the original story. Bill Skarsgard is great impersonating Nosferatu, as he did with all his villain roles he had before this.

Lily Rose is beautiful and also dark and macabre when needed. Brilliant performance from her as well.

A bit slow paced but i was more than happy with that as i wanted to see more of all the details and all of the locations and the great editing/coloring of the footage.

What a great experience this was.

reviews.author: charlottegilham
reviews.body:
First Film Review of 2025

Robert Eggers delivers yet another strikingly beautiful film, with Willem Dafoe delivering a standout performance. The cinematography is taken straight from a dreamscape, capturing the stark, atmospheric world of the story with precision.

Eggers' ability to elevate such dark folklore into something both captivating and revolting desirable is a testament to his craftsmanship.

However, the film's deliberate slow pace and lack of narrative momentum ultimately left me feeling somewhat unsatisfied, despite Count Orloks feastings.
