Eggers' ability to elevate such dark folklore into something both captivating and revolting desirable is a testament to his craftsmanship.

However, the film's deliberate slow pace and lack of narrative momentum ultimately left me feeling somewhat unsatisfied, despite Count Orloks feastings.

reviews.author: ztpbrmhw
reviews.body:
Conceding that this film is evocative, if not superior, to Francis Ford Coppola's Bram Stoker's Dracula (1992), the film is impeccably staged and acted and at times visually mesmerizing. That said, with a story and plot points that are now largely familiar, it's hard not to not simply recall all the iterations of this story that have come before it.

Relying heavily on mood and atmospherics, the movie, sadly, lacks much conventional "action", and everything and everyone move excruciatingly slowly. There are very few sequences of flashy quick editing, and nearly all the set shots are painfully slow zoom ins and zoom outs. For these reasons, movie goers less appreciative of "high art" will likely find the film tedious and boring at times.

However, on balance, this is an enthralling masterful movie to watch that I would otherwise rate a "10" were it not for the overwhelmingly somber sensibility.

reviews.author: robertayers-1967
reviews.body:
I found this version of Nosferatu to be too long and tedious. It was quite dull, but was very artsy. I thought the cinematography was quite good, and the way they used shadows to add some tension, but it wasn't enough for me to give this movie a good rating.

I didn't find it that scary but it did have some creepy atmosphere. But that creepiness wasn't enough to overcome the films dullness. It was quite bland.

William Defoe's character was probably the best of all the actors, but he always plays eccentric characters quite well. I found all the other performances just average. Nobody was bad, but other than Defoe, none of the other actors really stood out.

A little too dull and boring for my taste, even though the film had a few things interesting that I mentioned previously. All in all I give it a 6 out of 10. Not horrible but not quite recommended.

reviews.author: jvillarreal-81273
reviews.body: I absolutely loved this movie. From the moment it started to the last scene. I especially loved the scenes in Transylvania. Going back to vampire folklore with "where" Orlock sucks the blood of his victims, the castle. There are a few jump scares during this part of the movie that truly freaked me out. Skaarsgards voice, transformation, the set designs, the acting, the story, the attention to detail. Everything was truly incredible. I don't understand the hate se people have on this movie. It stayed with me after I saw it. I even dreamt about it. Very haunting movie and I can't wait to watch it again.

reviews.author: dlmiley
reviews.body: A remake of 1922 German copy of "Dracula", this film stars Lily-Rose Depp as Ellen Hunter (ala Lucy in Dracula) who is haunted by visions of Count Orlok. Soon her husband (Nicholas Hoult) is summoned to Orlok's castle to handle an estate sale. I am sure you can probably guess the rest if you have read or seen "Dracula". The movie is beautifully filmed, and the period recreations are excellent. However, I found the movie's pace tediously slow and the acting suspect - particularly by Depp who doesn't seem quite right for the role. And Willem Dafoe as Prof. Albin Eberhart von Franz (read: Van Helsing) overacts to a degree that becomes comical. In summary, I found the film needlessly slow - only recommended for the cinematography and production design. 6/10.

reviews.author: huantecon
reviews.body:
Just went to see NOSFERATU with my brother and sister in law. Save your money and wait for streaming. VISUALS: If you do stream at home, make sure it's pitch dark because the cinematography visuals are dim and hard to see. OVERALL: Storyline was choppy, dialogue was weak, music was reductive and unimpressive, and it was 30 minutes too long with a lot of unnecessary scenes. They tried so hard to build up the suspense so much that they struggled to "land the plane." I dosed off half-way through the movie. ACTING: Lily Rose Depp and Simon McBurrey were excellent in their roles, but everyone else was mediocre -- yep, even Wilhelm Dafoe who looked like he struggled to get into his character.

Sorry, but I think Francis Ford Coppola's "DRACULA" still remains the #1 masterpiece - hands down in the Vampire genre.

reviews.author: PaulSkirzyk
reviews.body: I have the pleasure of working on some major films and I appreciate when the art and lighting are so well done. The imagery is unique. The lighting is shadows and negative space. Everything has a purpose, everything has a plan. It is a joy to watch from a technical perspective. The story is a bit hard to follow and the language can take a second to become accustomed to the style and era of the words. Lily Rose Depp transforms herself from young wife to tormented soul in a manner that defies explanation. Nicholas Hoult as the husband isn't as strong as I would have liked but he was convincing as a confused husband. It was a bit of a shame Bill Skarsgard didn't have more screen time, What we had was creepy, and disturbing. A Skarsgard specialty.

reviews.author: aquableecs
reviews.body:
What a film! Robert Eggers delivers again with another banger. From the first 3 minutes you know what you're in for. Either get with it or get out of the way.

The cinematography in this film is simply breathtaking. There are so many beautiful shots in this film, it's hard to decide which is my favorite. The snow falling when Thomas is in the castle, the close ups of Lily-Rose Depp, and the final shot is one of the best final shots I've ever seen in film. It actually reminded me of the final shot of Robert Eggers' "The Lighthouse" which is another movie with a fantastic final shot.

This film pays homage to the 1922 original, from the classic vampire shadow look, to quoting the book with narration from Willem Dafoe.

I love the use of some of Robert Eggers recurring cast, Willem Dafoe and Ralph Ineson. You can tell he's found the cast that works well with his style and it works.

The last thing I loved about this film is the use of color. Color whenever it shows the innocence of children or purity, and pale or black and white whenever something is sinister or demonic.

In my opinion, this film is a masterpiece. It's my second favorite of Eggers films, the Northman being my favorite. Absolutely fantastic, and one that benefits from being on the big screen more than most.

reviews.author: Mykhailo98
reviews.body:
The film "Nosferatu" is a true cinematic masterpiece that combines horror and artistry. The atmosphere is so intense that it's impossible to take your eyes off the screen.

The visual component is particularly impressive: every scene looks like a work of art, rich in detail and beautifully lit. The director has masterfully crafted a chilling yet mesmerizing world.

The performances by Lily-Rose Depp and Bill Skarsgård are outstanding. Their characters are deep and alive, and you can feel their tension through the screen. Skarsgård is so convincing in his role that his character will stay with you long after the credits roll.

The film includes several genuinely terrifying moments. This isn't just your typical horror movie - it's a story that makes you feel, worry, and stay on the edge of your seat.

I highly recommend this movie to anyone who appreciates quality in the genre. It will definitely leave you with lasting impressions!

reviews.author: ubik-79634
reviews.body:
There was every reason to be excited in the lead up to the release of this new "Nosferatu": the brilliant writer/director behind such gothic gems as "The Witch" or "The Lighthouse" remaking one of the absolute classics of horror cinema. I was thrilled to be surrounded with warm bodies in a large auditorium on a wintry Friday night, and glad to have survived the stupefying 20mn showing of mind-numbing ads. Multiplex Nosferatu at your disservice.

Alas, maybe these stultifying ads did affect my brain, but I cannot say I had such a good time sitting through Eggers' "Nosferatu". Perhaps because I very recently rewatched Murnau's original on a big screen (with a live band accompaniment, which was glorious), but I thought too much of it was way too familiar, more of a retread than a reimagining. This "Nosferatu" is way too similar to what has been done before, without the director providing a new angle or perspective on the familiar story or characters, the way Coppola did in his brilliant "Dracula" (perhaps because of the emphasis on the relationship between the vampire and the wife, that's the movie I kept thinking of while watching "Nosferatu"). When watching Coppola's film you had the feeling of rediscovering a familiar story made new again; when watching Eggers' "Nosferatu" you just get the weary sensation you have seen pretty much the same scenes dozens of times before (including in last year's much maligned "Last Voyage of the Demeter").

Only in the focus on Ellen Hutter did the film show any signs of wanting to go in a fresh direction. The film opens on her and her "animal" desires, and there is a lot to like in her scenes. But at the same time there's a sense that it doesn't fully go the distance, just hinting at what the film could have been if it had taken more liberties with the source material. We never really get to know this woman, her personality and the reasons for her "melancholy" (sexual frustration seems like an overly vague diagnosis). Good vampire stories really are about sex and sensuality, letting our animal longings come to the surface, which is even more interesting in the case of a married woman in 19th century Anywhere. But the film still devotes too much time to a rather unremarkable Count Orlok, who leans heavily into the standard horror baddie and never into the seducing, charismatic creature you'd expect - how the wife can be attracted to him remains a mystery to the end.

Other characters never grow beyond their status as side characters and do not bring anything very valuable. Like every sane person I worship Willem Dafoe (including his own gig as Nosferatu in the underestimated "Shadow of the Vampire"), but his character doesn't contribute much to the story or atmosphere. He should have been a Freud rather than a Van Helsing alter ego, just like the movie should have focused more intently on sexual repression.

For instance, there was an interesting parallel being drawn between the two couples, the Hutters and the Hardings. The thirsty sex lives of both are alluded to, for a long stretch they share the same house and even the same bed, and of course the necrophilic end of the Hardings is a striking one. Yet it feels like the parallel has not really been completed, we never get to care much about any of these characters, and their suggestive moanings when being sucked dry are not as memorable as could have been.

I still enjoyed the cinematography, especially the scenes where dread is created by ghostlike gaslighting, as well as the various tracking shots and pan shots that help create an atmosphere of dread throughout the narrative (I liked the various creepy ways Orlok entered the frame, as well as the multiple frames within frames). Lily-Rose Depp was pretty impressive as a possessed Frau, and I liked how you felt sometimes as though this was a crossover between "Dracula" and "The Exorcist". If only that had actually been the case... in the metaphorical, psychosexual way this version was already going for.

reviews.author: ffhckbw
reviews.body:
Robert Eggers' Nosferatu (2024) breathes new life into the legendary 1922 silent film, offering a bold and atmospheric reimagining. Bill Skarsgård is captivating as Count Orlok, embodying terror and vulnerability in equal measure. Lily-Rose Depp and Nicholas Hoult bring depth to their roles, making the story's human tragedy resonate even more.

The cinematography by Jarin Blaschke is breathtaking, blending gothic visuals with Eggers' signature realism, while the haunting score amplifies the sense of dread. Eggers remains faithful to the original's eerie spirit while infusing the narrative with fresh energy and complexity.

Though the pacing is slow at times, it enhances the suspense, drawing the audience into the film's dark and mesmerizing world. This remake is not just a tribute but a cinematic triumph in its own right.

10/10.

reviews.author: branflakes4547
reviews.body:
The movie is 90% convincing, with great attention to historical and linguistic detail, but Bill Skarsgård deflated the movie . Not sure what Robert Eggers was thinking with his casting. Bill sounds like someone doing a scary monster voice for a child. His Nosferatu "performance" is akin to a bad imitation of Bela Legosi and Dr. Claw from Inspector Gadget - When you're the son of one of the greatest actors of our generation, and can't hold a flame to your siblings, what do you do? Answer: hide yourself in 80 pounds of makeup. He doesn't sound like an old man, nor a monster. He sounds like a kid trying to tell a spooky ghost story, and it's borderline awful. The movie was pretty phenomenal otherwise. Probably the weakest of Robert Eggers's films.

9/10 without Bill Skarsgård, and 7/10 with Bill Skarsgård.

reviews.author: Scodelli
reviews.body:
Because Robert Eggers has made such exceptional films (The Witch, The Lighthouse, The Northman) I went into this film with very high expectations. Especially due to all the buzz and hype surrounding this movie.

And I'm glad to say I wasn't disappointed.

This film is drenched in dark, brooding, unsettling atmosphere that is extremely well done and is very consistent(perhaps relentless) throughout the film.

Even benign scenes are directed in such a way that they're so creepy.

And this is all due to Robert Eggers' exceptional directing which most filmmakers can't reach.

Now when it comes to the Dracula story, I've seen many, many Dracula films. I'm so familiar with the story and seen so many adaptions of it that it's become wearisome. Especially with the slower pace of the Dracula story.

Don't get me wrong. It's an incredible story and the pacing is fitting.

But I've seen so many adaptations that it's become wearisome.

But not this movie. Despite the inherent slow, measured pace of the Dracula story, this entire Nosferatu film is riveting.

Every single scene is gripping. The beautifully done, consistent dark atmosphere drips from each frame.

However this film has alot going for it aside from atmosphere. The script is impeccable. The acting is incredible. There's so much this film does using the incredible dark atmosphere as a foundation.

This film is truly horrifying. I say that as a seasoned horror fan. This one got under my skin. It's just incredible.

Now when it comes to the film as a Nosferatu or Dracula remake, this film truly makes the story it's own and departs from just the standard story we're all familiar with.

And that's a good thing. It's done in good taste with obvious respect to the original.

So when you see this movie, it's more than just regurgitating the exact same story we're all familiar with. And that's a good thing because we've had so many adaptions and retellings and remakes of this story.

This movie makes the story it's own in a valid, respectful way. And it does so in such a well written way.

When you combine the incredible acting with the incredible directing, there's some deeply horrifying aspects of this movie where you really feel the character's fear.

While being a horrodrama, there's some savage moments of violence peppered into the film. Made all the more potent by the directing, story telling and script.

This movie further cements Robert Eggers' as a master film maker.

I highly, highly recommended this film.

reviews.author: Tzanidis_
reviews.body:
Having seen countless horror films and nearly every adaptation of Bram Stoker's Dracula, I must say this one was a disappointment. The scenes felt exhausting and lacked any sense of realism, with an overreliance on AI effects that made them appear artificial. The scene transitions were subpar, failing to maintain a coherent flow.

Lily's performance in the lamentation scene was particularly weak, lacking the emotional depth needed to make it convincing. In films like this, a touch of realism is crucial to fully engage the audience, and that element was entirely absent.

As for the allegories people are raving about on social media, I'll say this: stop looking for depth where there is none, wannabe intellectuals.

Lastly, the inclusion of cheap jump scares in a film like this was deeply disappointing. Such a classic story demands subtle, atmospheric horror, not gimmicks. I also forgot to mention how underwhelming Dracula's appearance was-a truly missed opportunity to create an iconic and memorable character.

reviews.author: ZeeEnds
reviews.body: Francis Ford Coppola's take on Dracula took Bram Stoker's book and added romance; this movie takes Coppola's film, nukes the romance, ignores the book, hat-tips Nosferatu by setting it in Germany, and says, "So what if it were, like, the woman's fault?" Great. Just what we need. Another two-hour slog through, "If he hadn't married a vampire's ex, we could have avoided this plague..." Brace yourself for totally unnecessary self-sacrifice to apologize for teenage hormones and the crime of wanting your own place to live. Does Eggers have a second trick, or is he just stuck on naughty teenage girls who dare experience sexuality, and therefore owe the devil a debt? Is that really what we need to see right now? Nicholas Hoult plays Keanu Reeves and hopefully fired his agent after this, and Lily Rose-Depp plays Perimenopause As a Person, which is most effective when she's doing butoh. William Defoe can't stop laughing at how Nosferatu got rebranded 90 Day Fiance: The Underworld (don't give TLC any ideas) and he gets to play his character from Poor Things again (but a bigger paycheck probably). This movie will post impressive numbers at the end of Christmas weekend, but only because every single option out in the biggest theaters is a remake or sequel, and there's an element of narf in watching a vampire movie on this holiday. Our libraries are full of books, and it's time for Hollywood to choose another one and stop beating this one to death.

reviews.author: eoinageary
reviews.body:
The gothic adaptation I needed, leaving me wanting more.

This tale sees Ellen, a newly wed to her husband Thomas. From the outset we see Ellen is plagued with a curse, a demon, Nosferatu. He holds a darkness over her and a lust for her blood. When Thomas is tasked with selling property in Germany to a count in a far away land, the lines start connecting. As her husband is gone, Ellen falls to her melancholy, by others seen as madness. When all seems lost, they seek the help of an unorthodox professor, who dabbles in the occult and other ritualistic studies. Count Orlok wants Ellen's soul, nothing will get in his way in capturing it.

I have been extremely excited for this, and it did deliver at about 85%, let me explain.

Firstly Robert Eggers has created another visual masterpiece in an era that allowed his vision to shine. The acting from everyone in the movie was top, Lilly Rose Depp and Willem Defoe I most enjoyed, and of course Bill Skarsgard as Orlok, which if you didn't know prior it was him you never would.

The story itself was good, a very sexually heavy movie in terms of what visually happens and the lust and desire you feel from the characters. Of course the meaning of the soul and blood routed in this but quite graphic, leave grandma at home.

What pulled me out was the pace, for 90% it was perfect but there was a tad too much of Ellen being "sad" I don't think this needed fleshing out as it's extremely clear what's happening, I would have liked more time in the castle which felt quite fast. Also there were maybe 2-3 scenes that felt unnecessary, shaving 15 minutes would have been great.

Along with that was the end, anticlimactic is a lot but I did kind of feel something grander could have happened. This also is preference but I would have liked seeing more vampire, more death/kills/blood. He is an absolute menace don't get me wrong but I would have liked to see his power at play more.

Those are my only complaints because I really did love this, it's an era and genre when done correct is a delight and this is that, I highly recommend this one, 8/10.

reviews.author: rgkarim
reviews.body:
LIKES: Atmosphere Strong Dialogue Feels Like A Book Brought To Life At Time Creepy/Scary Elements Strong Cinematography Incredible Dialogue Acting Is Amazing Summary: Eggers is all about his visual style, and once more, he has accomplished a fantastic visual style that embodies the Gothic-horror combination quite well. With a period pace that is mixed with a spooky twist, Nosferatu is loaded with an atmosphere that feels like the pages of a book brought to life. The costumes and scenery are strong representations of the times and establish some of the confines that represent the personality of the party involved. The strong visual elements provide a foundation that builds into a lore-driven horror, where shadows hold just as much life as the characters that travel around them. The constant grey filter adds a foreboding nature to the tale, where light only provides a shallow sanctuary from the encroaching horrors of the menace orchestrating everything. That lack of safety, the layering of dread alongside stronger characters establishes stakes, assisting with the suspense and thrills that I came looking for in my viewing. Eggers' visual choices to play close to black and white are advanced by his visual storytelling, with so many pieces coming together to establish the connection between everyone involved. And though this might not be the biggest scare movie we've seen in the past, its twisted aspects and gore arrive to add this realistic and savage edge that makes the creature even more sinister than your average fanged freak. Wrap all this up with beautiful angles, dynamic camera work, and masterful shots that utilize all of these elements into a stylish set of sequences and scenes. It's a risk at times, but those risks paid off for me a lot of times.

Past his direction of visuals, the story and dialogue come together to help bring the twisted tale of the count to life. Strong dialogue that conveys such terror is poetic at times to reflect the soul, yet not so lost in old English to be confusing and condescending. I was able to follow much of the story while also seeing how the lines were curtailed to the character alongside the actor selected to be that character. It's filled with emotion, yet not to the point of soap opera theatrics (to most the extent), all while testing the foundations of truth with science vs. Faith, all intelligently written in trying to stop what is at play. To help unleash the full potential of the lines, Eggers has assembled a talented cast with impressive skill in handling old-world stories and occult-based lore. Skarsgard adds another role to his belt, the mannerisms of the creature captured in his movements and twisting of words in his regal and acidic tone, such passion in each uttering word as he weaves in and out of the tale. Hoult's complex character is done well as his character goes through the motions and tries to adapt to the situation at hand, often keeping his tone in check and elevating the quality of young Thomas. Depp is astonishing as well, a bit more dramatic, but fully immersed into the maiden role trying to make sense of her life. Her screams punch the heart and the ears, her tears so raw and natural, while her words change with each personality quirk she adapts. Add in her nonverbal abilities, and you have another solid performance for an Oscar. Taylor-Johnson, Dafoe, Ineson, and the rest are all stunning, with incredible chemistry to make this complex congregation come to life.

DISLIKES: Graphicness Inconsistent Lighting Elements At Times The Story Feels Truncated At Times Slow As Dirt At times Summary: As with most artistic components, though, sometimes there are limitations that come with it, and I found a few with Nosferatu. The graphicness component is a big part of the movie and a major essence of Nosferatu's terror. Such savagery adds so much to the villain and the suspense of wondering what other tricks he will extend to get his desires. Yet, for viewers like me, this aspect gets excessive, sometimes to levels I didn't need to see in the theatrical cut and could have been in a director's cut. I don't enjoy some of the more "intimate" bouts of gore that Eggers seems enchanted with putting in his movies, though I feel this was still tamer than some of his other movies. Still, those who aren't fond of realistic twists to such dark material need to avoid this film. The story at times also struggles, some of the elements feeling blunt and unfinished in their portrayals, or perhaps even rushed at times. Nosferatu sometimes was not present as much as I thought he would be, and I felt that there was more to adapt from the tale than what we got. Add in the pacing at times, and you get a story that sometimes feels a bit bloated and missing some of the thrills earlier parts held, and the film gets lost in the dialog that it got stuck for me once or twice. Finally, the lighting gets inconsistent at times, though nothing like Game of Thrones, and it was hard on my eyes from the varying brightness.

The VERDICT: Nosferatu is one of my favorite works by Eggers and, quite honestly, one of the best movies of the year when it comes to style and story. A wonderful cinematography leads the charge with creative visuals and settings to bring the authenticity of the period to life. Savage tones, an ominous presence, and intense dialog all continue to wrap you into this dark cloud of dismay to see how such an ominous presence can be stopped. With incredible acting that brought the characters to life and an edge that keeps the debate of science and mythology are as much an enemy as the count himself. This film will bring a lot of people into the mix, dividing many in the common age, most likely, but many should appreciate the rich visuals that he made. Yet, the movie does have some artistic limitations that may dilute your enjoyment of the film, especially if you invested in the original tale. The graphic elements are vicious and can be a tad too much at times that sensitive viewers will not like it. The story still has elements that can be improved, perhaps in a director's cut that gives him more time to delve into the lore of the vampire lord. And the pace could use some sprucing up if you aren't just about bathing in the grotesque world Eggers has crafted for us to see. Add in a little technical sprucing and a few balance issues, and you will help this movie shine further. With all this in mind, those seeking the dark thrills of this tale should see it in theaters for the balance of story and strong visuals. However, those who can't take the risks of the expense of movies for such a violent epic might need to wait at home to watch this one.

My scores for Nosferatu are: Fantasy/Horror/Mystery: 9.0 Movie Overall: 8.0-8.5.

reviews.author: tjjannak-66655
reviews.body:
I would recommend this if you're into horror, particularly gothic horror. If horror isn't your thing, OR you aren't into slow burns, you might not have a good time with this one.

I was enthralled the entire time, from first shot to last. If you are going to do a remake, THIS is how you do it.

Lily Rose Depp was shockingly good, Oscar-worthy good. She proved that, given the right director and script, she can do great things. Nicolas Hoult, Bill Skarsgård, and Aaron-Taylor Johnson also gave Oscar-worthy performances. Nobody gave less than a good performance.

The costumes were top-notch and, again, Oscar-worthy, as was the score, cinematography, and screenplay. This is the kind of film where everyone and everything is firing on all cylinders.

reviews.author: hellraiser7
reviews.body:
This is one of my personal favorite films of all time, it's sort of ironic considering most of the personal favorite films are from the vampire subgenre in horror; "Fright Night", "The Lost Boys", "From Dusk Till Dawn", and "Bram Stokers Dracula" (Francis Ford Coppola movie) and I'm proud to say this film is that new edition I've been searching for a long time and now it has finally found me.

Of course, I'm aware this film is the second remake of the original silent film which I've reviewed, and I have seen and own the 1979 remake which I also like and maybe a story for another time. This film though is personally my favorite version of the old story, though probably for now as I have a feeling in the far future there might be another remake of the film. But that possibility I don't mind because it just shows how timeless the story truly is; a story that will be retold to both old, current and the generations to come.

This isn't just a film, it's an experience that is breathtaking (to me anyway), where description and words can't do it justice. One of the things for me about the film is it really has a bit of a throwback feel, not just for being a period piece, but in a way reminds me of some of the films from my favorite movie studio "Hammer" as of course they were famous for their horror most of the time set in gothic and Victorian settings. Just seeing this film felt like a breath of fresh air as this is a practice in the horror genre that has been sorely missing and now has made a comeback.

The visuals in the film are just spectacular, it really feels like most of the shots and everything you see looks and feels like an oil painting come to life, or each of the scenes could easily be pictures for the art gallery. There are just a lot of memorable visuals, like how they use shadows. From seeing the shadow of Orlok's hand just come over the city, just on how it moves gives you a chill as its just shows how the evil is growing and has a complete stranglehold. Or even seeing Orlok's shadow simply open a simple door, it also sends chills knowing from this how invisible and almost untouchable Orlok can be.

But I also like the settings like Orlok's castle which looks spectacularly foreboding and beautiful in it's gothic glory. Even the weather really enhances the dark beauty, the winter weather in a way represents the coldness of fear and evil. It's true the pacing in the film is one of those slow burns which make this film not entirely for everyone. But for me I honestly don't mind slow burn films if it works to the story and film's benefit which it does. The pace of the film really does add to the dread, because throughout the film, despite moments of peace you know they won't last, as they can end almost in a heartbeat.

The characters are also good and well-acted, from William Defoe in the Van Helsing role, though here he's named Albin Eberhart . It's ironic considering he was in the fictional comedy docudrama film "Shadow of the Vampire" where he was in the Norsferatu role. Anyway, his character I really like as he's you can say could almost be old man Fox Mulder but in Victorian times. He's open-minded, kind of funny as he's got a few clever funny lines. One of my favorite lines is when he makes a statement on the weakness of modernized thinking which I believe is true as that line of thinking doesn't have all the answers nor the truth.

Really like that he has a sense of commanding presence when he's doing his paranormal investigating work as it's his wheelhouse after all. But you can also tell the guy does obviously have a couple of screw looses, though from how long he's been in his business I can imagine that would make anyone lose it a little.

Two of the others are Nicholas Holt is solid as Thomas Hutter, whom you can say is just your ordinary joe that was simply trying to his job, only to get caught up in things he never planned for and wishes he headed the warnings. I really love how scared he acts, which makes him easy to emphasize with as in some parts of the film we would feel the same way. It's understandable as he and we know he's dealing with something outside of his area and beyond his own comprehension. This makes him more human and sympathetic as we see him just being put under the ringer but has the iron will to go on to protect his wife.

But really love Lily Rose Depp as Ellen Hutter who is a lovely actress that just knocks it out of the park. Her character you really feel deep sympathy for as she's a psychic that is tortured from little control over her untrained powers, but also from Orlok's psychic reach that is constantly trying to seduce and come to her.

This girl is another that going thought the ringer from what's happening, her psychic ability which she never asked for, and a hint of her past which wasn't good as she was possibly abused. She's simply a person that wants to live out and experience life and what it has to offer, there is this one scene where she gives out some comments on the beauty of the sky and other things of nature; I like that as I like those things too.

I really like the chemistry between both Thomas and Ellen, you really get a good feeling for them as husband and wife as you feel both are deeply in love. Really like this one scene they have where both um let's say do business together, I found it strangely erotic and beautiful as you can tell both are just going though lots of feelings together negative and positive which is understandable due to the circumstances but yet we see the connection they have remains strong both physically and spiritual. Their connections just make the most of what happens to them in the film all the more tragic. There's this double-layered suspense as one part of you hopes both will survive and get that happiness they desire, but another part of you from how much the danger grows and a grim discovery we make near the end, make are uncertain and dread grow and that happiness further out of reach.

Of course, we are here for the main man himself Count Orlok/Norsferatu. Bill Skarsguard is another of the actors on the rise and to me this is probably my favorite role from him at least for not. I really love the makeup job on Orlok, it's a different take on the vampire, I won't say what it is as it's something you must see for yourself, but it makes sense to the vampire lore as vampires are the undead after all.

But I really love the voice which is a very deep cold German accent which makes sense as the original silent film was made in Germany and Orlok is located in the European region after all. But also, what they did with the audio in the film which reminds me a little like with the film "Candyman". Every time he talks it just game me chills as it just was constant coldness and evil, but also in the times he talked with the characters it felt almost like he was talking to me, like he was trying to get into my head. His only motive and function is to simply destroy everything that's good, and his prime target is Ellen, whom is a representation of that, as long as she's alive and her soul is good she'll always be a threat to him, just as he's a threat to her.

I really like how he's made out as an otherworldly being, I wouldn't be surprised if he was a demon straight out of hell he probably is. He really doesn't look nor feel like a human being, but a fiend that is just pretending to be one. He's a little like the Xenomorph from "Alien" as we only get flashes and glimpses of Orloc, sometimes we see him and sometimes we don't, but the film as it progresses slowly but surely reveals more of him.

But also, he's a force of evil, from his otherworldly powers. From his voice and psychic influence and how far it stretches, commanding the unpleasant vermin, the darkness how it seems to always be a part of him, and possibly plenty of powers we don't know but it even more shows how evil knows no bounds. Even when we don't see him or in the peaceful moments, we feel no peace because we always know he's out there watching and waiting to make his move soon.

Even if you don't believe in the existence of evil, it always believes in you.

Rating: 4 stars.

reviews.author: tigrina-31134
reviews.body: Robert Eggers had me excited with his Lighthouse which made me watch The Witch and I was blown away for sure. When heard about Nosferatu it heightened my expectations but somehow this remake did not met them. Sure this is a breathtaking visual treat just like other films of Eggers but somehow this one lacks the edge that Lighthouse had. Maybe because we have seen the classic by Murnau and how he plays with the shadows. Overall the theme of vampire and Dracula is so overused that making anything new with it is indeed challenging. I am glad that the challenge is accepted by someone like Rober Eggers. It has it's moments that will make you go awe. But there are many other places where I thought the screenplay could have been materialized more effectively. The visuals do help you keep spellbound but then how is it different from watching postcards or still photographs. The performances from actors is top notch though and that is no wonder when the captain of the ship is Eggers himself but then again the screenplay matters. That is why it is a Near Perfect remake which is of course watchable yet it lacks at a few places.

reviews.author: business-33778
reviews.body:
Nosferatu is an absolute love letter to horror cinema of the past, giving us amazing visuals that shine with old-school techniques & styles with a modern flare. Nighttime visuals are gorgeous, focusing on a stylistic black-and-white approach that sets the film apart.

Lily-Rose Depp and an unrecognizable Bill Skarsgard lead the way with fantastic performances, giving their all to this dark and graphic retelling of the 1922 classic. There can be plenty of debate if this accurately portrays the Dracula story, but was it really trying to?

Overall, Nosferatu is a gorgeous film with fantastic cinematography that pays great attention to detail in all aspects. It's a throwback to the horror cinemas of old, and it nails it in nearly every way.

Brad: 9 Josh: 9.

reviews.author: antide-42376
reviews.body:
I went in with very high hopes about this remake of 'Nosferatu' but when it ended I felt kind of flat about it. The best way to express my thoughts is to list what I thought was good and not so good.

GOOD The cinematography is excellent and the soundtrack is good too. The atmosphere is very depressing in the castle and this felt right. The build up was quite good too.

NOT GOOD There is no doubt that the movie is overlong by at least 20 minutes and there were times when it's just plain boring as hell. The acting and some of the scenes are hammy in places, almost parody I thought. One of the biggest gripes is Count Orlok. The accent is ridiculous and he just isn't scary enough. He just looked like a large version of Fagin from Oliver Twist to me and don't get me started about his moustache! It was an extremely disappointing representation of Orlok especially when compared to the Max Shrek version.

I feel this movie has been overhyped and will continue to be. It does have some fine scenes especially when set amongst the snow but overall this was a bit of a let down.

reviews.author: YT-Mayor_N
reviews.body: I didn't really find this movie to be that scary, and I didn't necessarily find the story to be very engaging or the characters to be that deep or interesting, but what I did find was some of the most incredible presentation in a movie I've seen in a while. Not surprised at all that the guy who directed the Northman and the Lighthouse is able to capture so mant aspects of the 1800s perfectly, be it speech inflections, clothing styles, or one of the many sets used throughout this movie. The lead in particular was amazing with his 'ye olde' accent, even if a lot of the supporting cast weren't selling it as well to me. The movie plays with darkness a lot, and it makes for an extremely suspenseful atmosphere. The way this movie is shot looks fantastic, and the overall presentation is amazing, but the story itself falls short for my liking.
