reviews.author: liamthefailure
reviews.body:
Robert Eggers has left very little room for criticism, as his adaptation of Nosferatu is as breathtakingly gothic as it is harrowing.

Frank Miller-esque shots with a matured and modern finish accompany Eggers' vision of the classic vampire tale, creating one of the most convincing and memorable worlds in modern horror.

While the first act unfolds at a deliberate pace, the remainder utterly nails the narrative's true essence: fate, obsession, love, lust, doom, sacrifice, and the fears of the ominous unknown.

On an aesthetic level, Eggers' use of color is notable-from the completely achromatic sequences to the haunting depiction of a classic vampire sunrise. Most of the runtime features a subtle "Ozark tint," but with much-needed saturation that adds a great layer of depth and contrast to the visuals.

Lily-Rose Depp delivers the strongest and most haunting horror performance since Toni Collette in Hereditary. Though I loved Anya Taylor-Joy's work with Eggers in 2015's The Witch, I can't imagine her delivering a performance that parallels Depp's quality in this casting.

Every major performance in the film is fabulous, from Nicholas Hoult and Willem Dafoe to the apparent modern master of horror monster portrayal, Bill Skarsgård. While Count Orlok's costume design and appearance feel slightly dated, Eggers' intent to depict him as a historically accurate Transylvanian nobleman is clear. The "Stalin-stache" (for lack of better reference) and balding combover might not be as terrifying as fan made depictions, but Skarsgård's vocal performance-whether in accent or delivering lines in Dacian tongue-elevates the character to something unforgettable.

As Nosferatu goes through its inevitable cycle of praise and criticism, I remain convinced it's one of the most chilling and poignant horror films of the decade so far, and I'll be revisiting it again to appreciate it's modern take on classic horror and existential terror.

reviews.author: LongTimeMovieLover
reviews.body:
I went to see this movie alone, because everyone in my house (incidentally, my wife and two college-age daughters) thought (or heard) it was too scary. I don't think it was that scary, it was just about right, which is to say dark, eerie, and gothic, but not too scary. A couple of moments of gruesomeness, but that is to be expected.

I thought the cinematography was superb, with a sort of gray/blue filter that gives that cold dead feel. Again, just right. There were a few scenes that were really beautifully eerie. A first Oscar nod for cinematography.

Next, the score was excellent, setting the mood without intruding. Just right. A second Oscar nod for score.

Next, Lilly-Rose Depp did a great job with a wide range of acting emotions, perhaps an out-of-gate acting nod for best Actress. There was actually acting here, not like in the sullen Gladiator II.

Scarsgard did a great job as Nosferatu, although with that much makeup, I'm not sure a lot of good actors could not do as well. His gurgling voice might be a tad tough for someone who is not able to listen attentively.

I'm not sure that there is enough here for an adaption Oscar. Some of the plot was not developed sufficiently to have real emotional engagement, which I expect is a function of a long story that could not go longer. Hoult did well, again nothing exceptional required or delivered.

The only sore spot that I have (and I really hate to say it) was Willem Dafoe. He was probably cast because of his "cheekbone look," which was ineffective, and his acting was quirky and off for me. Perhaps not as bad as Jason Robards in Julius Caesar, but still a very bad spot. I thought he delivered it all wrong, and without proper gravitas. His character failed to deliver the tension that was needed for his character. Perhaps not as bad as Joaquin Phoenix in Napoleon, but pretty bad for me.

The pacing was good, sort of, if not a few long moments, with about 2.5H running time. The focus was on the timing before Nosferatu is in Germany, with the climax coming late and a tad of a flub, since the tension had not held sufficiently, and Dafoe sort of killed the intended mood. Someone old and doomy would have been way better than Dafoe's quirky, fast and weak performance. (I really like Dafoe, but not in this one...)

This is a movie to see in the theater, because it should be watched sort of captive and without interruptions. It's Holiday time, but that does not matter. My theater had more people in it than usual, which I was glad to see.

Now, if I had to do a comparison with, eg, the Bela Lugosi or Coppola versions, I would still prefer those, but this is an entertaining gothic horror that is not silly like a lot of other horror, well told and delivered, and worth of a watch with adult family at the theater. There are some gruesome parts, but I don't think there's so much or it's so extreme that any adult should not be able to handle it.

reviews.author: tomtalker2000
reviews.body: For starters, I wish people would stop comparing this to Gary Oldman's Dracula portrayal. Dracula and Nosferatu are completely two different characters. Dracula is far more powerful relying on his ability to be a handsome cunning human to attract his prey. Or turn into a creature at will. He looks to expand his army of vampires through his bite. Nosferatu is a walking infection period. He has no desire to change others into what he is. Light will kill him instantly and he has limited telekinetic powers. Where as Dracula can tolerate limited light and has VAST telekinetic powers. Nosfeartu's bite kills instantly and his sole purpose is to feed to satiate his hunger. He can command rats to spread his infection further or do his bidding. While the stories of both characters are similar they are also completely different. I think Nosferatu is FAR more intimidating and scary being the creature that he is. He cannot turn into something attractive and suave like Dracula to lure his prey. People should appreciate both portrayals for what they are. Gary Oldman nailed Dracula and nobody in my opinion has done it better since that film. And i believe Bill Skarsgard is probably one of the best character actors of our current time. He proved that in both "IT" films. And nailed this role as Nosferatu being the best i've seen yet. And i'll argue that point with anyone.

reviews.author: gavinp9
reviews.body:
'Nosferatu' is Eggers' 4th film and continues his examination of the darker side of humanity. I haven't seen the original Nosferatu (from 1922) since high school, but I believe this is not a direct remake, but more a retelling, set in 1830s Germany, but filmed in Romania/Czechia. We follow newly-weds Ellen (Depp) and Thomas (Hoult) as they deal with Count Orlok/Nosferatu (Skarsgard) occupying their dreams/nightmares.

When Thomas is sent to Transylvania to close a house sale, Ellen moves in with friends Friedrich (Taylor-Johnson) and Anna (Corrin), where she relapses into having "fits", so doctors Sievers (Ineson) and Franz (Dafoe) are called and get on the case. It's not overly gory, but there's definitely some blood, violence and a few gross moments. The final 45min or so are quite hectic and the ending is somewhat predictable but also well-executed. Doesn't feel like the film goes for 130min.

Every actor is great, with Dafoe having fun, Depp showing all the torment on her face, and Skarsgard literally unrecognisable. As per the original, the use of shadows, black/white and colour, in concert with the score, is really-well done and means there's always something to capture your attention. While possibly not the best ever vampire film, it's enjoyable and fun to watch.

reviews.author: movie_maakenic
reviews.body:
Nosferatu (2024) features an ensemble cast including Nicholas Hoult, Bill Skarsgård, Johnny Depp's daughter Lily-Rose Depp, Willem Dafoe and few more fantastic actors in a reimagining of the 1922 German silent Expressionist classic. Helmed by Robert Eggers, a modern eerie visionary and macabre storyteller, this marks his fourth directorial venture. Eggers, known for his ability to fuse folklore with horror and mystery within meticulously crafted authentic historic settings, has built an unparalleled reputation in just a decade. If you haven't seen his top works (The VVitch, The Lighthouse), you're missing essential benchmarks of modern dark cinema backdropped in the historic era.

The Nosferatu tale traces its origins to Bram Stoker's 1897 Gothic novel, Dracula, a cornerstone of English literature and cinema, immortalized by wonderful adaptations from Tod Browning in 1931 and Francis Ford Coppola in 1992. Eggers' adaptation reclaims the legacy of the unauthorized and unofficial 1922 German version, which transposed the British Lord Dracula into the sinister Count Orlok amidst German locales. That creative liberty sparked controversies then including accusations of antisemitism, leading to legal orders to destroy all copies. Despite this, Nosferatu endured, evolving into a cult phenomenon that profoundly influenced many over a century including Robert Eggers whose early days influenced him to an extent that all of his work reflects a dark and gothic aesthetic.

His version of Nosferatu took almost a decade to make and the final product is an immensely gripping, authentic, creepy and chilling depiction of an Evil Lord which aligns to the original premise of the movie.

I am not diving into the plot details to allow the viewers to fully enjoy this Gothic Tale unfolds its mystery, horror and suffering itself.

Merits:








Demerit: Lily-Rose Depp delivers a commendable performance but perhaps the original choice Anya Taylor Joy(who became a star after Eggers' first flick and immensely popular The VVitch) would have lifted the movie higher since her personality and skills match well to the premise. This isn't a demerit but a tantalizing "what if." Nevertheless the entire cast performed really well, especially Nicholas Hoult and Simon McBurney(Knock, Count Orlok's eerie aide).

Obvious special mention is for Count Orlok, played by Bill Skarsgård(brother of Tarzan: Alexander Skarsgård who also played the arrogant yet amusing villain of John Wick 4: Marquis). His transformation will obviously not let you recognize him but certainly he is utterly & genuinely scary yet fascinating even where his presence just lingers in the background or voice overs and virtually every scene of him uplifts the movie and makes a chilling impact.

Cinematography is by Egger's regular Jarin Blaschke who photographed all his previous films and again did really well by capturing the world which Egger envisioned and Nosferatu's old & rich history demands.

Conclusively, Nosferatu (2024) is another feather on the cap of Egger that breathes new life into Gothic horror, deserving your time and full immersion.

Prepare for a journey into darkness, suffering, and the enduring legacy of a story that refuses to fade.

Enjoy the nightmare!!!

reviews.author: wghume
reviews.body:
The attention to detail in the costumes, attitudes, and locations was incredible.

The portrayal of the time of reason fighting its way out of superstition was well done. The example of the interaction between the sexes and classes was on point. The landscapes, the architecture of the different areas were beautiful.

The issue for me is it was very slow. I have read that it followed the original movie well. The problem with that is the original movie was a nearly direct knockoff of Bram Stoker's Dracula, without the 'elegance' of that story. While Dracula is, in his own mind. Trying to redeem his past by recovering his reincarnated love, Nosferatu is just hunger. Dracula is of course wrong in what the outcome will be for him and his 'love' Nosferatu is only concerned with consuming his 'bonded' and everything else in the world.

reviews.author: alessandrodrago
reviews.body:
With an all-star cast and solid performances from all of them for the most part (save maybe for ATJ), this film sets the tone and mood early. This tone is the films biggest strength, along with its dark visuals. Probably Eggers third best film (though his filmography so far is so strong).

I have never seen the original film, though some of the shots in this film (particularly its use of shadows) is clearly an homage to the 1920s silent classic. Its titular character is shrouded in shadow for most of the film, and this is used to great effect. The monster itself is not the scariest part of the film, rather it's its effect on others. Solid film, recommend watching on the big screen with enhanced audio.

reviews.author: glennmeerten06
reviews.body:
Nosferatu has been in the works for years. After battling and pleating to get it made, Robert Eggers finally got his vampire epic in theaters. Though it's not quite perfect, Nosferatu proves it's teeth are still sharp in 2024.

Ellen Hutter, portrayed by Lily Rose Depp, dreams of a demonic force that haunted her as a child. This entity might be returning to collect on a forgotten contract, followed by in it's shadow, death itself...

Acclaim should be directed to the cast. Lily Rose Depp surprises friend and foe with a career best performance. It's captivating, daring and unquestionably demanding of the young actrice. She showcases a great faith in herself and her director. On that note, there is not a single performance that fails to impress bar one... Aaron Taylor Johnson does an amazing job, unless he doesn't. In one scene, he's sweeping me up and away with his performance. In the next he stands out and falls short when measured against a legend like Willem Dafoe. The lather, by the way, whose mere presence elevates the entire proceedings. Bill Skarsgård is simply unrecognizable as the titular devilish Nosferatu. Not just through make-up effects but more so through his performance. From his accent, through is cadance, all the way up to his posture and breathwork. You'd forget he was once a cackling clown demon.

Robert Eggers has a background in production design. A filmmaking expertise he puts to horrificly gorgeous use once more in Nosferatu. Aided by the dark setting, Oscar worthy production and costume design, the sexual violence the monstrous Nosferatu rains down upon his victims is unnerving, infectious and sinister. Special accolade should be granted towards the sound design and mixing. From cracking staircases, to fearful breaths. From glutinous swallows of blood, to crackling fires that still seem as cold as death. The world of Nosferatu feels unwelcoming and ominous.

The film does so much to damn near perfection. Though it's not Eggers best nor bravest flick. That honor still falls upon The Lighthouse. What Nosferatu does succeed in though, is bringing a character that first horrified audiences over a century ago, into the 21st century without losing that terror and dread it carried. The long and insidious shadow the soulless Count casts, will linger just a while longer, thanks to Robert Eggers.

reviews.author: calummacleod-51310
reviews.body:
Horror is a genre unlike any other. The feeling it evokes can be the most powerful in film if done right. However, in this era of shock horror where we are subjected to anything and everything, classic horror has become a rare breed.

Nosferatu has shown the world that horror needn't be all about jump scares and gore and gives us a character that holds power over his victims just from being in his presence.

There is a classiness about the film and director Robert Eggers has clearly thought about every element. This isn't just about scaring the audience but more about the atmosphere that is created. On this point the look of the film is stunning, with such detailed cinematography that allows the audience to immerse themselves in to a fantastical story while being a wholly believable setting.

The cast is top drawer with pitch perfect turns from Nicholas Hoult and Aaron Taylor-Johnson, while Willem Dafoe is his eccentric best as Professor Albin Eberhart Von Franz.

Bill Skarsgard is at his most devilish as Count Orlok, showing he really has become the go-to as the most monstrous characters in Hollywood. Nosferatu, however, would be nothing without it's beating heart, Lily-Rose Depp who steals the show with her portrayal of Ellen, a woman consumed by darkness from the awakening of the creature in her earlier life. The way she shows herself to be forever troubled by this demon while trying to keep her love alive for her husband, is mesmerising and thoroughly engaging. Depp shows the vulnerability and strength of Ellen with clarity and ease and it is clear that she is a star in the making.

When looking at flaws in Nosferatu, it is easy to focus on the storyline itself which at times is quite thin while the obsession that Orlok has with Ellen is never quite explained. Despite its 135 minute running time, there are moments that feel rushed and more of the backstory that has brought us to this moment, would be a grateful addition.

However, these elements never deter from the enormity of the setting and the world that Eggers has created, with a suffocating air that never lets up and doesn't allow its audience to lose focus. In an era where franchise horror has taken root, here we have a refreshing change in the genre, that takes us back to what the true conventions of horror should be.

reviews.author: tiaskyelandish
reviews.body: Ever since this was announced, this became one of my most anticipated films. Robert Eggers is one of the best filmmakers working in Hollywood, though I haven't seen The Northman yet. On top of that, it has a star-studded cast. But, I've avoided the trailers. The 1922 film will always be a classic but I haven't seen the 1979 one. The question is: how does this version compare to the original? I must say that it didn't disappoint whatsoever. It's an elegantly touching movie. Once again, Robert Eggers does a masterful job in the director's chair. The cast does an amazing job but Willem Dafoe and Bill Skarsgård (who looked completely unrecognizable). The slow-burn narrative is effective. The visuals are stunning and it's incredibly atmospheric and gothic. The music is fantastic and the production design is stellar. Also, some scenes will send chills down your spine. As a whole, it did resonate with me. It's one of my favorite films of 2024.

reviews.author: r96sk
reviews.body:
'Nosferatu' didn't quite hook me, but there is enough about it that I can consider it as a good film. The visuals are splendid, as are the gothic horror elements. On the cast, Lily-Rose Depp impresses, as does (more minimally) Emma Corrin and I'm always happy to see Willem Dafoe.

I do continue to feel quite nonplussed by Nicholas Hoult. I did like him in fellow 2024 release 'Juror #2', but in this I've kinda reverted to feeling unmoved by him onscreen. I'm not entirely sure why as he seems a likeable chap, yet his performances just don't really register - which admittedly sounds harsher than I intended.

Bill Skarsgård as Count Orlok is also a part of this flick that I'm unsure on. Does he look the real deal? Absolutely, no complaints there, but I particularly found the dialogue with him to be a borderline bumbling mess. I found the scenes directly with Count to be the least interesting.

I would also say that the movie goes on for a bit too long, though I admit that probably is more of a personal shout than one that is to be set in stone; because if you love this, it'll be the perfect length I'm sure. For me, I feel like they went around the houses a tad. With that said, I did highly enjoy that final scene with Depp - very good!

Those last paragraphs make it sound like I have a dislike for this film. I do not. It just has some noteworthy points that I felt the need to mention. As I type, having not looked at how this has been received, I'd be shocked if this wasn't rated high. Either way, this is worth a watch.

This is my third Robert Eggers film. I loved 'The Northman' (9/10) but I, honestly, hated 'The Lighthouse' (4/10). Safe to say this falls exactly down the middle, in terms of how I think of it. Quite a stark contrast even so, kinda fascinated to see how 'The Witch' hits me when I get around to that at some point.

reviews.author: shyamkrishsai
reviews.body: Watched #Nosferatu at a 4K laser non Atmos scope screen today. I didn't have much idea what level to expect, but then the movie was a piece of art. It stirred my souls with fear, melancholy and wretch for the hours it played. The whole cinema hall was silently watching with their breath held. The story of damned evil nosferatu and it's lustful covenant with Ellen Hutter was not easy to watch. Lily rose Depp has done a phenomenal job in perfecting this role. Prosthetic covered BillSkarsgard proves once again that he is the master of physical horror after Lom Chaney. Robert Eggers revisits his style of color movie with less colors and more of a black and white color tone. The cinematography and editing is amazing and it definitely adds beauty to the eerie ambience of the movie. Willem Dafoe effortlessly aces his character as usual. Worth watch in theatres if you are a fan of this genre. I wish it was released in #IMAX screens here in India. Also watch it in a flat screen if possible. #Atmos also might help when it comes to hear the dreaded labourous breathing of count orlock.

reviews.author: jon_pratt12345
reviews.body:
Nosferatu is based on a story that is ingrained in film culture. It's difficult to imagine how a film maker can bring something new enough to make it a worthwhile endeavour. But Robert Eggers manages to do just that.

What we get is a story we all broadly know, presented in the most beautifully gothic and stylised fashion. Eggers shows us the story in how I can only imagine it was always meant to be shown.

The locations, the constume design, the cinematography, the score, the dreamlike off-kilter feel. It all contributes to what could be the most impressive version of this story yet. I can't imagine what more I would want.

What is most noticeable is just how much of the story and it's previous film iterations have become familiar troupes or even cliche. Doors opening by unseen hands, shadow figures looming, but Eggers executes them with such skill and craft that they have renewed impact.

Overall, Nosferatu is unlikely to deliver twists and turns for it's audience, and I think it knows it. But if you go in prepared to experience something familiar through an exquisite lens then this should be thoroughly enjoyable.

reviews.author: frankde-jong
reviews.body:
In 1922 Friedrich Wilhelm Murnau adapted the Bram Stoker Dracula story and called it "Nosferatu" to avoid copy right issues. He didn't succeed. The widow of Bram Stoker won a lawsuit in which she demanded the destruction of all existing "Nosferatu" copies. Fortunately she also didn't succeed and today the 1922 version of "Nosferatu" is one of the highlights of the German expressionist movement.

After 1922 there were made a lot of Dracula movies under the original name. But also het "Nosferatu" movie from 1922 generated various remakes under which most notably the 1979 remake by Werner Herzog and, recently, the 2024 remake by Robert Eggers.

Despite being based on the same literary source there has remained (or grown) a difference between the two. Dracula takes the form of a charming gentleman while Nosferatu looks much more like an undead, often with an appearance reminding of a bat. As a consequence of this Dracula films generally have a sexual undertone that is lacking in Nosferatu films.

How does the 2024 Robert Eggers remake fits into this scheme? Well not very well I think.

In the first place the eroticism is in this movie much more explicit than usual. This coincides with the character of Ellen Hutter (Lily Rose Depp) playing a more important role than usual. Ellen Hutter is portrayed as a woman who has become possessed by Nosferatu. Owing to this possession some scenes of "Nosferatu" (2024) reminded me of "The exorcist" (1973, William Friedkin).

Does this greater emphasis on eroticism goes hand in hand with a more plaeasant appearance from Nosferatu? Not exactly. Nosferatu is not the charming gentleman we know from Dracula films but he is neither the bat like creature from the 1922 movie. He reminded me most of an ugly version of Golem from "The Lord of the rings" trilogy (2001-2003, Peter Jackson). Also the voice of Nosferatu, more exaggerated than scary in my opinion, did me think of "The Lord of the rings" trilogy (although I don't know exactly of which monster, in any case not Golem).

All in all In my opinion the greater emphasis on eroticism doesn't quite fit in with the rest of the film. This doesn't mean however that the 2024 version does not have its merits. The part of the film in which Thomas Hutter travels to Transylvania is really beautiful, with the highlight of the pagan ritual concerning the virgin and the vampyr. This is a real Robbert Eggers scene comparable of some scenes in "The Witch" (2015).

Directly related to this scene is a strong point of the "Nosferatu" version of Robert Eggers, the contrast between rationality / enlightment on the one hand and supernatural beliefs on the other. In most of his films Eggers chooses the side of the supernatural, and "Nosferatu" is no exception.

The reason behind the move of Nosferatu from Transsylvania to Germany is more explicitely explained than in previous versions. Because Germany is enlighted nobody beliefs in Nosferatu and nobody will oppose him, this contrary to the population of Transsylvania, who still belief in the supernatural.

The same theme lies behind the two docters in the film. Rational docter Wilhelm Sievers (Ralph Ineson) understands nothing from the symptoms of Ellen Hutter. The alchemist Albin Eberhart von Franz however correctly diagnosis her as possessed. As he says: "We are not so enlightened as we are blinded by the gaseous light of science. " and "If we are to tame darkness, we must first face that it exists!".

reviews.author: MixedFormula
reviews.body:
Let me start by saying that this review is written from the perspective of someone interested in the remake rather than the horror. I don't like horrors, I don't watch horrors, I have nothing to say about how this film fits into the modern horror genre so I accept that for this reason it is a limited perspective on the film.

Having said that, I was surprised how little this film made me feel fear. It made me uncomfortable in many places and I failed to anticipate one jump scare but otherwise, for a person who is very sensitive to watching pain, suffering and gore, I was not being subjected to fear. I was watching other people's fear, dread and suffering and I was sitting there wondering if I believed it.

There is no question that this film is really well produced. It's not monochrome, it's silver. It's incredible how silver it looks. The casing is good. The acting is good. The effects are impressive. So it is really a shame that the story leaves you cold.

I think one of the problems is that it doesn't seem to have anything to say to a modern audience. After decades of popular psychology, after the horrors of modern history, in the midst of the current political dread, this film isn't connecting with me with anything urgent, relevant or cathartic to say about the experience of a personal, historical or political trauma that wasn't said in the original. Maybe there is a message but it's hiding too deep under the Victorian theme park costume and archaic language ("Untie this child!").

Theoretically there is one theme which should make me excited because it's right up my street, and that is the question of consent, its remits and its limits. I can see it, I can engage with it on a logical level, but I'm not excited to do that. I can't even figure out why that is the case. And that is where, in my view, lies the biggest weakness of this remake. What was its purpose? Why did it need to be made? People who have never seen the original, who are not interested in old black and white films or in history of the cinema are not going to appreciate its relationship to the original or to the period. If I wasn't scared, I doubt people who like horrors were scared. So who was this film for? New generation? To tell them what? Because the consent message is just too subtle for the demographic who analytically can't deal with antiheroes, even if it's Walter White, or with straight up villains even if it's Homelander.

Kudos for allowing cats to finally break onto the big Hollywood screen. Can't wait to see them on the red carpet :)

reviews.author: Mrsteinfeld
reviews.body:
I went into this movie expecting it to be, not only one of the best horror movies of the year but also just one of the best movies of the year in general and while I don't think it's the best movie ever made, it definitely got me quivering in my seat.

I'm going to start with the positives. This movie constantly keeps you on edge throughout the entirety of its runtime. There was never a moment in this movie where I felt safe from a jump scare. Bill skarsgard as count Orlok was one of the best parts of the film. All of the actors in this movie do a superb job. Especially lily-rose depp. The scenes where she is getting possessed are some of the best in terms of acting. Another thing I love about this movie is the visuals and the cinematography. Each scene looks incredible and could easily be some of the best cinematography I've seen this year. Also the movie perfectly catches that 1800s type feel to it. Another thing is that the horror scenes were very scary. I thought this movie would be more about the characters than the scares but no. It was almost the complete opposite. On that note, I didn't really care for any of the characters that much. I did like them but nothing to make me cry over somebody's death but enough to make me like them. The only one I really liked was willem dafoe's character and maybe Ellen (the main character)

Now to start with the negatives, I have a few. One of them being the fact that time in this movie kind of doesn't exist. Either that or characters can fast travel because they go to places so fast, it is unbelievable. For example, there is one scene at the beginning of the movie where someone says that the location the main character is supposed to go to takes six weeks to get there, but when we do get there, there are little to no shots of him actually riding his horse there so it looks like he travels there in an afternoon. And when he is leaving count Orlok's castle, he is injured (he jumped off the castle) and when we see him, he can barely move but then it just cuts to him a few months later back to his town. And when he got to the town he was in really bad shape, so in that case, that means he had to feed himself, water himself and clean himself while also trying to survive and stay warm all while being very injured. This also happens multiple times throughout the movie. This movie is said to take place over multiple months but it felt like it took place around 4 days at most because everyone is just zipping around. There is another scene where nosferatu basically says to the characters "you have three days before I come for you" and on the first day literally nothing happens and on the third day at around 2:00am somebody dies. I'm not going to say due to spoilers but they have time to grieve, bury and have a funeral for these people and plan for Nosferatu all in the same evening. Keep in mind the person who died, died like 6 hours ago. Bit unrealistic just skipping over the grief and just skipping to the funeral. It's also pretty out of character for the people who planned the funeral as you'll see in the movie. This next one isn't really a complaint but is scary if your going to see it with family. There is alot of nudity in this movie. The amount of times during this movie where I had the awkwardness of watching a nude scene with my family while also being on the edge of my seat incase a jumpscare appeared was... something. At first I didn't think there was much nudity in this movie and then when the first nude scene came on I was like "that's a naked guy" then the second one came on which was probably the nudiest nude scene. Then I began to lose count. The amount of sex scenes in the last 30 minutes of the movie are very awkward if your with family (although you might enjoy it if your alone) it's nothing like "Fifty shades of grey" but it's still dirty women on screen.

"Nosferatu" is a great movie. Nothing that will blow your socks off of your feet but probably one of the scariest horror movies this year. While it does have a few flaws (specifically the management of time) it's still a really fun time for horror fans. Just don't watch it with family. Overall: 7.9/10.

reviews.author: Kademan-02092005
reviews.body:
Nosferatu is Robert Eggers' reinvention of F. W. Murnau's classic unlicensed adaptation of Bram Stoker's novel Dracula. And it's a hauntingly gorgeous film that manages to terrorise and fright with restrained delight.

The cinematography is absolutely awe inspiring, featuring incredible usage of natural lighting, silhouette shots, clear-lit scenes for night sequences, and a plethora of other technical aspects. The costume and set design are thoroughly constructed to say the least, fitting into the style of the time as well as the overall gothic aesthetic the film achieves. The performances are incredible across the board, with the most notable being a committed Lily-Rose Depp, a devilishly entertaining Willem Dafoe, and an absolutely unrecognisable Bill Skarsgård. Skarsgård's voice and appearance as Count Orlok are astoundingly contorted, as his vocals commit to the Transylvanian dialect and the prosthetics and makeup create much more of a monstrous and undead vampiric appearance, compared to the more humanistic iterations in the past. Furthermore, Orlok is an incredibly and simplistically evil antagonist that acts more as a force of nature and as a plague on the community rather than the typical singular dark force. This then has much of the film be committed to exploring the effects of his powerful presence and keeps the action relatively minimal, creating more build-up towards confrontations between the Count and the protagonists. Moreover, elements exploring the sexual nature behind several characters was equally as unexpected as it was interesting, comparing the more socially accepted relationship between Nicholas Hoult's Thomas Hutter and Depp's Ellen Hutter with Orlok's mystically seductive advances towards Ellen. And the dreamstate sequences were eerie as much as they were disconcerting, with the build up to Orlok's castle being a particular stand-out sequence of horrifying anticipation. All all of it is cloaked with a subtly haunting score that, perhaps not particularly memorable, is able to compliment the terror on display.

As notable nitpicks, however, the old 19th century English dialect can be difficult to understand at times. The pacing is very patient as the story takes its time in building up the threat, and the protagonists take their time in figuring out what the vampyre is. And Eggers' typical abstract storytelling is, although more streamlined, still present and definitely not for everyone.

But it was very much for me. So regardless, Nosferatu is an excellent film that manages to inventively reimagine the classic creature's goal of acquiring a house and bride, while also revisiting the depiction as an undead animal that uses its humanistic qualities to seduce and lure its prey, making for a fantastically horrific experience to be had.

reviews.author: daoldiges
reviews.body: Having see the original Nosferatu I was already familiar with the story, although having not seen or being familiar with is not a serious hindrance to one's enjoyment of this version. This version's visuals certainly are the star here including the cinematography, sounds, sets, costumes, all present a highly stylized and cohesive world. It's very dark and somber and that is mostly to good effect. On the downside the beast is hidden in dark shadows and isn't truly revealed until the near end of this film. I understand why that approach might be taken and don't completely disagree in theory but the viewer should have given a little more sooner in the film. As for the performances everyone turns in solid performances but it is Depp who really shines here and is the true star of Nosferatu. The basic story is very good but at more than two hours it was not fully supported and nourished/reinforced that entire time. As such I think Nosferatu could have genuinely benefited from some prudent editing down to keep the viewer more wholly engaged. For fans of the genre it's a must see and for almost everyone else it's also worth checking out.

reviews.author: joshuawarrenmedia
reviews.body:
I went into the movie theatre with complete faith in Eggers but unfortunately this is the first time I've been anything but awed by his work. Much of the film did live up to my expectations, and then some, but in other parts I was actually a little disappointed. Overall I came out of the theatre feeling very conflicted about it.

Maybe I'm a bit biased as I've never been able to connect with the original silent film. I sometimes feel like I'm the only person who don't regard it as a masterpiece, and I've even seen it "properly" with live music and all, twice, and yet I've always found the plot and dialogue kind of hokey and nonsensical. Herzog's remake from the 70s, however, I did find quite interesting in its quiet, almost melancholic approach to the original Dracula/Nosferatu plot, but in the most recent remake I feel that Eggers has been burdened with many of the flaws of original. Much as with the silent version I found myself shifting from loving it to being frustrated. Now, Bill Skarsgård is as excellent a Count Orlok as Max Schrek was in the 1920s, the visuals were absolutely stunning, the effects seamless, the performances leagues beyond the melodrama of Murnau's "original" (it was a 'bootleg' of Dracula after all), and yet, during the scenes with Ellen Hutter, Lily-Rose Depp's character, much of the magic often disappeared for me, and at times I even found her scenes tedious to get through. Now this is no slight against Depp's performance, but the character was at best vaguely defined (also a problem in the original) and at worst excessively grotesque. After a while her possession scenes began to feel painfully repetitive.

Now, I realize that an exploration of evil must by its very nature be shocking, but there were many times where I felt that the film was shocking just for the sake of being shocking, especially in the aforementioned possession scenes. I also felt that the film needed more breathing room between all the scares, and despite some people complaining about the slow pace, I personally felt it was a little rushed at times, though this is a very minor complaint. Probably my biggest frustration was that Egger's has taken to utilizing jump scares, something which he brilliantly managed to avoid in his first film; The VVitch. With that film he brilliantly let a sense of dread slowly creep in and never had to rely on gimmicks to frighten the audience. With Nosferatu, however, I found the somewhat frequent use of cheap scares and jump cuts to be below his former high standards and more in line with modern Hollywood horror tropes. Granted there was more finesse at display here than with your usual generic Hollywood jump scares, but it still felt oddly uncharacteristic of him. It is of course possible that this is another case of studio interference (a bit like what happened with The Northman).

Now I want to stress that the majority of the film is very much on brand for Eggers. As already mentioned Bill Skarsgård gives a fantastically creepy performance oozing with evil menace, and the slow build up to Count Orlok's reveal was masterfully executed. Jarin Blaschke's cinematography is probably his best work as of yet, and I cannot stress how much I appreciate Egger's commitment to the expressionistic look of the original film and how he somehow managed to make it feel completely natural within his trademark historically accurate settings. One of my favourite characters in the film, who incidentally is also a huge improvement over the original silent version, has to be the character of Prof. Albin Eberhart von Franz, the film's vampire hunter, who was played with a perfect blend of quirky humour and sober gravitas by Willem Dafoe. In the original film this minor character contributed practically nothing to the plot. Here Egger's wisely chose to create his own, slightly more eccentric interpretation of the now quite familiar Van Helsing character.

Despite my frustrations with certain aspects of this film, I still very much regard Eggers as one of the most talented and original directors currently working, and I anticipate his next project with great interest. I suppose his perfect streak was bound to be broken at some point and in a sense it was appropriate that it happened with a remake of someone else's film. Compared to the current era of gimmicky horror movies this is still a massive improvement, and as such I hope it will do well at the box office, as Hollywood can learn a whole lot from films like this. My critiques mostly stem from expecting more from Eggers, perhaps even too much, but in the "grand picture" of horror films I still think it is flawed and doesn't quite live up to its full potential.

reviews.author: breaker-71598
reviews.body: Took a point off because I didn't like how the story was resolved and I wish some actors opened up more (were more dramatic). Felt a bit cheesy and ridiculous at times, and deeply wrong at others. Could use a bit more thriller-action but it was more about tragedy and corruption. Looked great, sounded better, be ready for gross eating sounds. There was a lot of nudity and profanity, relative to mainstream horror movies. Willem Dafoe was great. A lot of small jokes about the time period which were fun. Set and costume were great. So many rats. A couple accents were hard to understand at times but everything essential was always conveyed. Beware there is sexual violence.

reviews.author: a-j-kelly
reviews.body:
Pre-Nosferatu Experience

In a few hours, and after a year of anticipation, I'll finally see "Nosferatu." Robert Eggers has not let me down with his movie output, with "The Witch," "The Lighthouse," and "The Northman" all being 10/10 masterpieces, in my opinion. It doesn't hurt that the cast is stacked and all-talented. I wanted to see it sooner, but Christmas is Christmas, so I had to wait a day longer. I haven't seen the original interpretations of this story, but I will after seeing this remake, no doubt.

Additionally, Focus Features lifted the review embargo over three weeks ago. Talk about confidence! I can guarantee that this will be one of my favorite films of the year and may even surpass "Anora" as my pick for the best. Just "how" is the only question left to be answered.

Post-Nosferatu Experience

Very is the answer to "how" great this film was. I don't think it beat "Anora," but I'd be lying if I said it didn't come close. It's going to be in my Top 5 favorites of the year. Check my 2024 Movies RANKED IMDb list to see exactly where, but for now, let me talk about what makes this experience so unreal.

To start, Robert Eggers, you have just made me a die-hard fan, and I saw your other films only this year. His direction and screenplay are unlike any other I've seen in 2024. It helps that the story he is reimagining is rich in execution, and again, I've never watched any other take on this narrative. It can be overwhelming, but it can never be described as bad, thanks to Eggers' mystical direction.

Next, the acting from every actor is unfathomably solid. Willem Dafoe, Emma Corrin, Nicholas Hoult, Ralph Ineson (it took me a bit to recognize him, and I'm glad he's here), and Aaron Taylor-Johnson all give potential career-best performances. However, Lily-Rose Depp and Bill Skarsgård as Ellen Hutter and the titular Nosferatu, Count Orlok, deliver some truly atmospheric work. Skarsgård, in particular, is unrecognizable as Orlok, thanks to the stellar Oscar-worthy makeup, and I don't think I could guess it was him if I didn't know beforehand. The richness of the narrative also helps, as Hutter finds herself and those closest to her threatened by the Count. Without Depp and Skarsgård's performances, I don't think the story would've been as strong.

The 2-hour and 13-minute runtime almost rarely drags. Perhaps the only semi-negative I could give is some stretches of the film drag but never cease to provide meaning to the story, like the ending of "The Substance." A remarkable feat is how I was the most immersed in a film the entire year with "Nosferatu." "Wicked" and the aforementioned "Anora" both had me engaged, but I don't think I've been this invested in the world and story of a film in a long while.

Furthermore, "Nosferatu" is the best horror film I've seen all year. I thought "The Substance" would hold that crown through to the end of the year, but no. I was consistently tension-filled throughout, with many sequences having me floored by how terrified I was. Eggers knows how to do horror and takes those talents to the next level here.

For the remaining positives, the practical effects are remarkable alongside Beatrice Brentnerova's set and Linda Muir's costume designs. Jarin Blaschke's cinematography and Robin Carolan's score enhance the story and the creepy nature of its contents.

I'm not surprised that I loved "Nosferatu" to the extent I did. It's one of the few horror films this year that deserves to be nominated and win many Oscars. I still firmly think that "Anora" is more deserving to win Best Picture, but I wouldn't mind if "Nosferatu" takes an upset victory.

Eggers' directing and writing are grand, the acting is groundbreaking, the score is haunting, and the visuals are unbelievably perfect, making for a 10/10 technical masterpiece.

For the enjoyment score, what a Christmas present! Of course, it's a 10/10 for the enjoyment score, for me at least. Whatever Eggers does next, this instant classic guaranteed me seeing it!

reviews.author: makdrenski-78643
reviews.body: Let me start with the positives: Beautiful cinematography, great costumes, perfect atmosphere capturing the madness. Some solid performances. The hype for this movie was a lot. It certainly delivers on some aspects. However the movie is slow at times, maybe because everyone know the story and what follows next. For me the most important element of the movie Count Orlok was weak. Max Schreck and Klaus Kinsky were creepier, even without the ton of make up used here. Eggers tries too hard to show a scary and brutal version of the count but it would have been better if he used a more subtle approach and a more natural vision. And no I don't mind the moustache.

reviews.author: edhou
reviews.body:
The film has two sides to it. One of non-supernatural normalcy in 19th century Prussia with typical European costume design, sideburns, horsewagons, and the other the mysterious, gloomy castle of Count Orlok and the nearby frightful, religious peasants who live in terror of the devil itself.

Which is more interesting, and should be the direction of the film?

As you have correctly guessed, Count Orlok and his castle as the setting! The first half is around 40% Prussia, and 60% castle, and those latter sequences were truly haunting, with the Count as this mythical, undead monster subjecting and manipulating mere mortals with ease. Disgusting dreams that cross and make you question reality, corpse rituals amongst the peasants adding historical layers, amidst classic horror themes of normal objects but behaving unnaturally... Hoult sells his terror in the castle - his rising anxiety makes for a thrilling frightfest, giving us a glimpse into the madness of horror we expect from Nosferatu in the 2nd half.. only for it all to disappear in bland nothingness.

The castle/Count Orlok/horror side of the first hour should have been the entirety of the film, with simply brief scenes from Prussia to introduce the story, but what we got was Count Orlok to leaving his haunting castle and traveling to Prussia, where the movie blandly resides for the rest of the film!!

In the 2nd half, Count Orlok is brought to Prussia, and suddenly the plot shifts to how to realistically kill the vampire?? Setting up a plan to find out when he sleeps, bringing in Willem Dafoe is this formerly top doctor turned prophetic heretic to rave about how scary Nosferatu is (which wasn't even in question - we witnessed it firsthand!), and a full 20 minute sequence of Hoult and Depp arguing about their love was so dishearteningly bland.

Nosferatu tried to do something classic, excellent horror films lack: create a gripping horror film but also with some historical context, and a more somewhat-realistic story having less "oh well, that's just the way horror is" plotholes. But the effort in making an actual story detracted from the elite terror that Nosferatu displayed initially. So instead of a frightening horror movie that was teased in the first half, we got mediocre 'slay the monster plot in 19th century Europe'. What a bore.

Nosferatu tried to save itself with the twist that Dafoe is actually an anarchist and wanted Orlok to succeed this whole time (it did not land), and acts of straight disgust, like copulating with your dead wife's corpse, or monster sex, which might have worked in a truly freaky fashion if it kept up its A-game horror in the first half but now its bad plot AND disgusting. The scenes of disgust were truly next-level, it could assist a whole sub-genre of disgust if the revulsion I experienced was not intermingled with my disappointment of the 2nd half of the film.

Potential of an elite 8/10, but I'll confirm at least a 7 in the first hour. 3/10 in the 2nd. Overall a disappointly average movie. 5/10.

reviews.author: TheRealPDoddsy
reviews.body: This is how a horror should be made. It puts everything else made in this modern era to shame. I'm sure a lot of die hard horror fans will disagree as it's a re-hash of a classic and a genre that has taken many forms in cinema, but I found it really enjoyable and well done with beautiful nods to the classics whilst not neglecting the benefits of modern film making. The atmosphere is dark and foreboding and I was hooked from the start. Costume and make up excellent and the performances of Depp, Hoult and Defoe are very engaging. Also, Skarsgard plays a convincing villain caught between the living and the dead. A character you see just enough of to keep you engaged with him but who also disappears into the shadows to allow for the thrill of the jumps and scares. Overall, for me, it's the horror movie I've enjoyed most for many years and I would definitely recommend watching.

reviews.author: fatfil-414-451797
reviews.body: First up, I have to say, this will not be for all horror fans. It is a very, dark, gothic and relatively faithful retelling of the classic black and white original. Also, not an action packed horror movie with jump scares and lots of gore, there are lots of atmospheric, moody scenes, but they still up the anxiety The cinematography, and recreation of Victorian England is immaculate. And the use of the more archaic English vocabulary adds to the authenticity. It does get a bit overwrought at times but never fails to stay in the moment and never losses sight of the story. Yes it does stray and cow tow to modern cinemas needs The ending, although not he original, is very effective and actually quite beautiful.

reviews.author: mickeythechamp
reviews.body:
Going for a remake of an older movie like this is bold. It´s an iconic piece of cinema that definitely have the age to be retold, but the daring question of should it is always relevant. Personally I think Eggers did a good job. The familiarity with the story sadly affected my impact on the story and it was hard to turn off, but overall I am very impressed with what we were given here and this is no doubt an incredible display of talent and horror.

We follow the Hutter family who are all haunted by the evil count Orlok

The acting here is phenomenal. While some actors feel a bit read here for the most part we are given stand out performances in a horror movie. Willem Dafoe, Ralph Ineson, Aaeon Taylor-Johnson, Lily-Rose Depp. All phenomenal performances that make you stick in this world. But man, Bill Skarsgård as Count Orlok is absolutely fantastic. His voice an presence makes this movie. From the accent to the raspy breathing to of course the overall look sells this character as this insane force of nature that is just pure evil. The makeup sells the look of Orlok totally, showing him as more than just a plain person but more of a huge presence that seems larger than the average person in the movie. He is more of a force than a character and that is what makes him as scary and unnerving as he is.

Because this movie has a few classic horror scares but to me it´s more of an unnerving movie. There are so many scenes that are just freaky and tense more than they are scary and that works for me. Too many times have I watched a horror movie that fails to deliver on its most basic part, but here I get that and also unnerving imagery that sticks with me. From the possessions, to the blood and gore to implications and reactions, it all becomes this larger than man story that is just truly scary.

The cinematography is as always a work of art when it comes to Eggers movies. There are so many incredibly beautiful frames all elevated by amazing lighting that makes the scenes just the right amount of light and dark. Eggers knows exactly where he wants the camera to make beautiful and terrifying imagery and this movie looks phenomenal from start to finish. The carriage ride scene is a work of art, one of the only scenes in a while that truly moved me. A just beautifully shot scene that works.

A part of Eggers I can´t feel here is his more intimate nature with characters. I connect Eggers with these intimate small scale movies where you really get to get under the skin of the characters, but here it seems like there is a lot of characters and story beets to keep up with and that is also felt here. I´m not saying Eggers was over his head, but the movie seems like a less personal one of his.

Another problem that is more personal to me is that I have watched this story many times already. It is the classic Dracula story and that affected my enjoyment since northing could really surprise me. That is of course not the movies fault, it´s still a solid story worth telling again, but there are so many incarnations of the story already it is cemented into my mind to the point that it becomes a bit redundant to tell it to me again. I enjoyed this movie immensely still, but this may have hurt my overall enjoyment.

I feel like the essence of the original story is kept true while still making some really good decisions such as having Ellen Hutter take more centre stage. Telling the female story here that leads to an ending I find very hauntingly beautiful is great. And having the female protagonist being more of a prophecy forfiller than just a plane heroine, makes so many changes to her and Orloks character in the best way possible. It becomes a more sweet ending to me than anything.

One thing I wasn't a bit fan of is the editing. There is a lot to keep track of I get it, but some of the tonal whiplashes I got by going from horror to just plain talk took me out of it sometimes. This is a complex story with many characters, but making some easier transitions maybe with sound or music would maybe be appreciated. Speaking of the score is great!

Nosferatu is great! It´s such a great movie on so many levels, presenting an old classic and making it work in modern time. The story is incredibly told, performed to perfection by great actors and the cinematography is to die for. Overall I had a blast with this movie and it is decently worth a watch if you have never delved into the Dracula mythos.

reviews.author: masonfisk
reviews.body: The current du jour remake now playing in theaters from writer/director Robert Eggers (The Witch/The Northman). Following the original silent film's plot beat by beat (which took Bram Stoker's Dracula plot verbatim causing original director F. W. Murnau to change the names of the characters) as Count Orlock, Bill Skarsgard, makes his way to England to set up shop in a manse he just bought, w/the help of realtor Nicholas Hoult, where he intends to reconnect w/his reincarnated woman, Lily Rose-Depp, while also wrecking havoc on the populace. Knowing what the plot entails (especially if you watched Francis Ford Coppola's Dracula back in 1992) could sap your enjoyment of the presentation here but if you're going in cold, there is much mirthless fun to be had since Eggers, tackling a passion project of his, directs the material within an inch of its life (after life?).

reviews.author: celticbhoy-62766
reviews.body: Just because of my penchant for everything dark and gothic,I was sure that I would like the film. And, yes, the pictures are great. Unfortunately, the film never really gets going and the characters remain pretty bland throughout the film. Apart from Knock. Maybe I'm comparing too much with Murnau and Herzog, but it seems to me that it is assumed the plot is already known and everything can be classified accordingly. If you don't know any of the earlier versions, the film will probably be a bit confusing. Actually, the story is told too choppy, the pictures deserve a more epic narrative to be considered a classic in the future.

reviews.author: michvanbeek
reviews.body:
Nosferatu is actually the first film adaptation of Bram Stoker's Dracula and dates back to 1922. To avoid problems regarding the rights of the Dracula story, the makers simply changed the names of the characters in the film. Now, 102 years later, a remake of this now legendary story is coming, and it is all directed by Robert Eggers. Eggers also made a big impression in 2019 with the film The Lighthouse in terms of cinematography, and with The VVitch from 2015, he also proved that he can handle the horror genre well. Bill Skarsgård was cast for the role of Orlock, who also made a very good impression as Pennywise the Dancing Clown as a horror figure in It Chapter 1 and 2. Add to that the names of Nicholas Hoult and Lily-Rose Depp, and you have quite a cast on your hands. The first images were already promising, and finally the time has come, and we can give our own opinion about this very special remake.

As said, the film is cinematographically excellent. The grey and especially gloomy atmosphere in the film, with some scenes bordering on black and white, comes into its own perfectly. Maybe Eggers should have just chosen to release the film in black and white, just like he did with The Lighthouse. This film in particular lends itself perfectly to that, and anyone who sees the film will probably come to the same conclusion. The story has been expanded and adapted here and there, but otherwise follows the story closely from the now centuries-old original. Anyone who is waiting for an extremely scary horror film with abundant blood and many exciting moments in the film should lower their expectations a bit. Nosferatu takes its time to get under the skin of the viewer and can sometimes feel a bit long-winded.

It is precisely the slowness that makes the film come into its own and ultimately achieve its goal. Especially the first part of the film, when Thomas travels to Transylvania and meets Orlock, is an atmospheric intention that ensures that you will still get an uneasy feeling about what will happen next. Still, there are some things here and there that will make you scratch your head. The denouement is certainly one of those things that the director should have paid a little more attention to, because in the end it is a bit stupid how it all ends. For the rest, there are some minor flaws here and there in the film, but otherwise not really things that really need to be put through the wringer. The fact that a film like this is being released so big and fills the cinemas is perhaps the most special thing, because Nosferatu is a film that is not really mainstream and may have a smaller loving audience than the visitor numbers suggest.

Nosferatu is a slow film that slowly but surely manages to get under the skin of the viewer. Don't expect an average horror film with lots of jump scares or where the blood flows continuously; no, Nosferatu is more than that. Here and there there are some flaws in the film, and the final denouement is a bit dull, and the director should have tried a bit harder on that. For the rest, the film, with its gray-gray setting, is almost a colorless spectacle, and perhaps Eggers should have chosen to release the film in black and white, like The Lighthouse, to convey the atmosphere even more to the viewer. The fact that the film was released in cinemas on such a large scale is, of course, a nice bonus, but Nosferatu feels more like a film that normally manages to be shown in arthouse cinemas on a smaller scale. For those who are really expecting a mainstream, smooth horror film, it is advisable to adjust your expectations and perhaps choose a different horror film, because Nosferatu is not what you normally get to see.

reviews.author: howard-polk
reviews.body: First of all the depiction of the vampire in the movie had great potential to be a new very scary classic vampire but unfortunately fell way short. The movie's cinematic qualities were excellent but the story line was dull and for a slow dull script the movie was way too long, not one truly scary scene from start to finish. I always feel ripped off when I go to an actual movie theater, which is rarely to see a movie I really think will be better in the theaters and it is not. This is one movie if you must see to wait until it's streaming and watch at home, turn the lights off to maybe make it a little more thrilling.

reviews.author: MaggieQ-public
reviews.body:
Revisionist mediocrity.

Robert Eggers' Nosferatu (2024) is another exercise in revisionist, millennial indulgence, cloaked in a veneer of artistic mediocrity. It will pander primarily to Gen Z viewers who, arguably, haven't been exposed to much greater works across (any) genre.

. And already some have dared call this a "masterpiece." Huh? Much of this seems driven by social media "influencers"-motivated by clicks, likes, and the greedy promise of brand endorsements.

. This points to a larger cultural problem: the internet, social media, and the influencer economy have diluted art, criticism, and cinema. Quick consumption and endless online echo chambers create a climate where mediocrity isn't just tolerated-it is celebrated.

Eggers' Nosferatu struggles to justify its existence. Rehashing familiar ground, the film offers neither fresh perspectives nor meaningful innovation. The performances are competent, but fail to elevate. Lily-Rose Depp gives an eager effort, but her range is questionable. More disappointing is the underutilization of Willem Dafoe, whose immense talent is wasted in his role.

Visually, again, the film is hyped up for greatness. Really? A 19th-century German setting (check), cobblestone streets (check), traditional period costumes (check), and "day-for-night" cinematography (check) is fine but nothing groundbreaking.

. This isn't about competition about craft, but auteurs like Coppola's Bram Stoker's Dracula (1992) remains a towering visually, combining opulent gothic imagery with operatic intensity. Herzog's "Nosferatu the Vampyre (1979)" is more of the eerie, stark beauty. And Carl Dreyer's Vampyr (1932) is more dreamlike in visuals.

. Nosferatu (2024) is an unnecessary, revisionist retelling wrapped in mediocrity. It reflects an increasingly movie model shaped by nostalgia and reboots, serving as a reminder of how movies-(not art)-can falter when innovation takes a back seat to reverence.

reviews.author: hastingsmauff
reviews.body:
Spoilers ahead but I'll give a short review before. Should you see it, yes. But make sure you are ready to sit through 2 hours of nothing interrupted by some really interesting scenes.

Visually it's a stunning movie, the lighting and atmosphere are some of the best I've ever seen. The acting was great for such an old plot. But the only problem was the fact that it is an old plot. It is extremely difficult to make such an old trope scary or entertaining. He likes blood, wants to take this guys wife, and makes people tweak. It could have been 45 minutes shorter without sacrificing any value. But most importantly it was boring for too much of it. Unless someone was going crazy under the influence of Nosferatu or they are confronting him, there is really nothing entertaining for us to watch.

reviews.author: rainbowglitchxbenec
reviews.body: A fangtastic adaptation of the 1920s film; it shows the true horror into a new light, the way that flames are relied on for lighting during the night to the ship that looks so far away but also so close. The visual effects of gore and blood make it worth seeing the film. I saw this film at least twice and I want to see it again sometime soon. The cast was impeccable and you could tell that they were having fun and were molded for the roles. I found it hilarious when Willem Dafoe said in an interview that it's a Christmas film... unfortunately there was no SpongeBob in the film, someone was getting their pretty patties eaten, if you can get past Nastyfreaktou then this film is good for you.

reviews.author: xophaser
reviews.body:
I like this genre so I went to the movie to get the goth vampire out of my system. Actually i saw the trailer and thought it had bloodborne vibe so I had to go Acting is good, I am not into overacting, just settle and if they can convey the mood and story-line. I never seen the original so I won't compare to it. I say it looks more classic horror is when I watched like the old Dracula and Frankenstein, this fits in but more modern. Had the ring and other horror movie vibe. Not the silly beetlejuice style of fun. Nothing super original in the story. Probably a 7/10 but I give it an extra point for the bloodborne vibe. Love that game.

Nosferatu I thought was represented well. The main character was too. The visual is overall artsy, some scenes looked great. A few scenes looks like AI cgi you see on YouTube. This might be my 2nd favorite behind the fearless vampire killers.

reviews.author: jcherrie-43435
reviews.body:
This film was definitely not what I expected it to be, but it did not disappoint either. It's well made and beautiful from start to finish. And, like every Eggers movie, the time period is realized beautifully, from the bustling streets of Wisburg to the old Transylvanian inn and Orlok's castle. There is some good and well-placed scares in the film, but for the most part the film relies on tension and foreboding.

Count Orlok's appearance and behavior may not appeal to everyone: he's far from Max Schreck's uncanny alien-like ghoul from the original film. He is very much an undead Transylvanian nobleman, from the mustache to the costume and his savage, masculine demeanor and voice, unlike Max Schreck's frailness or Klaus Kinsky's sniveling self-pity.

Overall I really enjoyed the film. The runtime, just slightly over 2 hours, did not feel bloated to me. I understand that some others feel differently, but for me most of the film went by quickly and I don't think there was anything here that needed to be cut. The ending is very visceral and intense, I even felt a little bit sorry for Count Orlok. Willem Dafoe's character brings good levity to the second half of the film and of course Lily-Rose and Nicholas Holt are great.

Overall, a very worthy adaption of Nosferatu and a great horror film. I will definitely be rewatching this one.

reviews.author: stevencsmovies
reviews.body: There have been many, many versions of the vampire known as Dracula over the decades, some with another name, Nosferatu. There is now a remake of the classic 1922 silent gothic horror film of the same name, NOSFERATU. It's 1838 in Germany. Thomas (Nicolas Hoult), a real estate clerk, is presented an opportunity for promotion by his boss Herr Knock (Simon McBurney). He must go sell a house to the reclusive Count Orlok (Bill Skarsgård) in Transylvania, leaving behind new wife Ellen (Lily-Rose Depp) and her friends Anna (Emma Corrin) and Friedrich (Aaron Taylor-Johnson). I thought this movie is fantastic. Writer and director Robert Eggers has now made four feature films: THE WITCH, THE LIGHTHOUSE, THE NORTHMAN, and now NOSFERATU. All of these are bangers. It seems like he enjoys telling us dark, twisted stories from the past, this one the darkest of all. Not only the subject matter, but it's physically dark as well. Eggers is so adept here, using shadows to strike fear and a looming sense of dread into his characters. I believe this is my favourite vampire movies. It doesn't hold back; the cinematography and visuals are masterfully done. The acting talent from everybody is Oscar-worthy, especially Bill with his transformative makeup and accented raspy voice, and Lily-Rose with the various aspects of what her character has to go through. Shoutout to Willem Dafoe for being in pretty much everything these days, and always kicking ass, acting-wise. The concept of vampires has always been sexual in nature, and it's no different here. I liked how religion, science, and superstition bounce off each other here. Even though this is a fantasy, it feels authentic. It does feel a little long at over two hours though. Overall, NOSFERATU is a dark, faithful remake that elevates the vampire subgenre to new heights, and I can't wait to see what Eggers does next!

reviews.author: liamirvine-77159
reviews.body:
Skaarsgard again shows he is one of the best horror performers of his generation.

Depp plays her part with grace and elegance while Emma Corrin is underused.

Ineson (the Directors favourite), Johnson and Dafoe make up a terrific trio but for me, the start is Nicholas Hoult. He carries the film from the moment he leaves Wisborg to the end. He's an absolute star and holds every scene together. I was so impressed with his performance that it has made me want to go back and watch it again.

The makeup is brilliant but the direction, sets, cinematography and music just blend into one of the best vampire movies if seen in such a long time.

Dare I say that it's almost on par with Gary Oldman's Dracula? Yeah I'll say it. It's better.

reviews.author: Pjtaylor-96-138044
reviews.body: 'Nosferatu (2024)' is Robert Eggers' take on F. W. Murnau's classic of German expressionism, 'Nosferatu: A Symphony Of Horror (1922)'. Releasing just over one hundred years after its influential inspiration, the picture aims to update its 'Dracula'-adjacent story with one foot in the present and the other in the past. It straddles the line between modern horror blockbuster and classic horror throwback almost perfectly, emerging as an altogether new beast that feels fresher because it isn't afraid to seem old fashioned. Its biggest success is its palpable atmosphere. It oozes Gothic style, harkening to its expressionistic roots by playing with shadow and light and framing and focus, and it completely immerses you in its heightened period setting. The cinematography is incredibly dark yet readable, desaturated yet never dull; the sound design is unsettling, gnawing away at your bones with its growling timbre and angry intent. There's a genuine sense of evil that lurks over the entire affair, a nightmarish energy that emanates from the very idea of its antagonist. The eponymous vampire casts a truly dark shadow over the entire film. He occupies the limbo between monster and man, life and death; his presence is metaphysical, as potent in the ether as in the flesh. He isn't on screen all that often, at least not fully, and there's a sense that his wickedness cannot be contained within the frame, as if it's too much even for the camera to bear. His physical form is rendered with fantastic practical effects, all gross and diseased and dead. In the original, Max Schreck portrayed Count Orlock as unnatural and animalistic, leaning far away from the enigmatic charm and dangerous allure later brought to Dracula by Bela Lugosi and Christopher Lee. Bill Skarsgård takes a similar route, totally disappearing into his role as a disgusting and bestial presence who's legitimately imposing both in body and spirit. He towers over his costars, clearly capable of cleaving them asunder if he so desires, but he does most of his damage by worming his way into their minds and spreading his horror as if it's the plague. His raspy voice, clearly inspired somewhat by Lugosi, has a way of getting under your skin, and it's easy to see why the other characters soon crumble in utter terror after spending mere moments near him. I never would have guessed he'd have a moustache, but it kind of works here. The film is, at least on occasion, fairly scary, and it's also truly horrific at others. For example, its stark final image is sure to stay with you long after the credits have rolled. A lot of it could have been silly, but the sincerity of the filmmaking and the conviction of the performances (which are fantastic across the board) prevent it from ever being so. The story deals with themes of forbidden desire, the source of true evil (internal vs external) and the need to acknowledge something before you're able to fight it. It's also rather horny in its own macabre way, dealing with fairly disturbing sexual elements that play with the role of women in 19th-Century society (briefly examining things like 'female hysteria' etc.) and inspire thought surrounding what is truly immoral in a world in which real evil categorically exists. A lot of these elements aren't explored as deeply as they could be, even if the screenplay is sometimes rather heavy-handed with them, but they add texture and context to the rest of the narrative and are welcome additions. The plotting and pacing is generally a little strained, occasionally feeling ever-so-slightly inefficient (the flick could've been trimmed up slightly). However, the picture is always compelling and it gets by solely on vibes when needed. If it wasn't as aesthetically pleasing, it perhaps wouldn't be as potent as it is. Thankfully, we don't have to worry about that. This is a really well-made movie that's immersive, unsettling, and incredibly atmospheric. It's creepy, well-performed, and confidently crafted in every technical area. It stays with you for a while after it's over. It's really good.

reviews.author: Renarchy426
reviews.body:
... And I willingly watch Tubi original found footage films.

I love the original Nosferatu and I can see in the, to be fair, very beautiful cinematography, efforts to recreate/reference the German expressionism embodied by the original. But ohhh my gosh this thing just goes on forever.

reviews.author: alexmaister-38146

It's a movie that you need to see at the cinema, otherwise you lose the half of it(even more).
