reviews.author: jokishac
reviews.body:
I really appreciated the intense visuals and strong horror elements of the movie, which align with my personal tastes. However, I found myself losing focus at times, as the plot became somewhat confusing. The overall tone of the film was very dark, and I felt it could have benefited from a few lighter moments to break the tension. That said, the acting was excellent, and I loved the cast, scenography, and costumes. While I'm iglad I watched it, I don't think I would revisit it again.

P. S. Bill is completely unrecognizable, so don't waste time waiting for him to appear like I did-haha!

Cheers.

reviews.author: harpenfluit
reviews.body:
Watching Nosferatu, directed by Robert Eggers, is akin to immersing oneself in a cinematic thesis on narrative and visual storytelling. Eggers' signature style-meticulous, authentic, and profoundly atmospheric-shines through, and as expected, the film elicits polarized reactions. Some will detest its deliberate pace and artistic choices, while others, like myself, will be captivated by its brilliance. I fall into the latter group, deeply appreciating Eggers' commitment to perfectionism and his ability to craft a world that feels not only authentic but also resonates on a subconscious level.

I experienced this cinematic masterpiece in an art-house theater, a venue that seemed tailor-made for such a film. The environment added to the immersion and reinforced the film's unique aesthetic.

The cinematography is exceptional, a masterful interplay of light and deep shadow. The balance is impeccable, capturing the eerie essence of Nosferatu's world. The blocking enhances the world and naration, crafting tableaux that feel almost painterly in their composition. The color grading complements the film's tone, imbuing each frame with a haunting palette that lingers in the mind. The production design is stunning, with an obsessive attention to detail that enriches the authenticity of the period setting. The sound design is another standout, perfectly marrying the visuals to create an atmospheric soundscape that heightens the film's ethereal and ominous mood.

Performances across the board are strong, with Lily-Rose Depp delivering a transcendent portrayal that eclipses all others. Nicholas Hoult and Bill Skarsgård also give standout performances, their characters brought to life with nuance and intensity. However, a few supporting performances felt overly theatrical, almost as though the actors were performing for a stage rather than the screen. While this may have been an intentional stylistic choice, it occasionally disrupted the immersive experience.

The narrative itself is straightforward, yet in this case, the story serves as a framework rather than the primary focus. Eggers places emphasis on mood, atmosphere, and thematic depth, and in that regard, the film excels. The narration feels poetic, and the ending is exquisitely crafted, leaving a lingering emotional resonance.

Should you watch Nosferatu? Absolutely. It's a cinematic experience unlike the formulaic blockbusters we've grown accustomed to. Eggers' vision invites viewers to step out of their comfort zone and into a richly textured world of artistry and imagination. For those willing to embrace its idiosyncrasies, Nosferatu offers a hauntingly beautiful journey that stays with you long after the credits roll.

reviews.author: gontarek
reviews.body:
I have talked to 4 people about this movie. Every single one of us thinks the movies looks good. The problem is it's not the right time of year for a film like this. We think at the box office it could have done better if release was in June-July or just before Halloween. It doesn't fit the season unless it revolves around Christmas. Most people want to see blockbuster Christmas flux. I think it was poorly managed on distribution. FYI did not see film.

The film studios need to know what the people are interested in at different parts of the year. People want to see films with their kids. They would more likely go and see red one or another film over this one. It's poorly managed in distribution to the customer.

reviews.author: pedro-48552
reviews.body:
Werner Herzog's Nosferatu (1979) features Klaus Kinski delivering a remarkable performance as the vampire, deeply infatuated with Isabelle Adjani's portrayal of the enchanting Mina Harker. The film's script masterfully guides us through a haunting love story, providing clear insights into the characters' relationships. This depth fosters a strong connection with the characters and the narrative, evoking emotions of fear and sadness as the story unfolds, culminating in the vampire's demise.

In contrast, Robert Eggers' recent adaptation of Nosferatu for me lacks of cohesion, appearing more as a series of visually stunning cinematographic pieces rather than a unified film. The attempt to create a frightening vampire is perceived as falling short. Eggers and the producers seem to have aimed for a multimedia project, emphasizing beautiful imagery that translates into a collection of souvenirs marketed on social media.

reviews.author: ZeddaZogenau
reviews.body:
The story of Nosferatu is known worldwide. The silent film by Friedrich Wilhelm MURNAU has been a classic of film history since it was made in 1922. Everyone has seen a picture of Max SCHRECK as Count Orlok. Werner HERZOG (OSCAR 2009: nomination for ENCOUNTERS AT THE END OF THE WORLD) dared to make a remake in 1979, for which he had thousands of rats brought to the Dutch city of Delft. Klaus KINSKI (GERMAN FILM AWARD 1979 for NOSFERATU - PHANTOM OF THE NIGHT) was allowed to suffer a little as Count Orlok from his inability to love before he was allowed to bite Isabelle ADJANI's snow-white breast. Does a remake by Robert EGGERS really need to be made, and in English at that? Absolutely, even if EGGERS is unable to breathe anything new into the well-known story! Because the story is already strong enough and fits frighteningly well into today's times.

We are in the fictional town of Wisborg in 1838. It is not for nothing that one thinks of the Hanseatic city of Wismar, which at the time belonged to the Duchy of Mecklenburg. It is very nice how the set and the scenery show how tightly built cities in German-speaking countries were before the destruction of the Second World War. The newly married Thomas Hutter (Nicholas HOULT) is given the task of traveling to a Count Orlok (Bill SKARSGARD) in Transylvania to sell him a dilapidated castle ruin in the cozy town of Wisborg. What Thomas does not know, but his spiritually inclined wife Ellen (Lily-Rose DEPP) has long suspected, is that he is bringing absolute evil to his beloved hometown.

The way it is all implemented is absolutely worth seeing. Seldom has the birth of horror stories from the spirit of the Biedermeier era been so well understood as in this remarkable film. And aren't we living in a time similar to the Biedermeier era today, in which we are beginning to suspect that absolute evil is at the door? Or rather, as Ellen asks the vampire expert (Willem DAFOE) in the film: "Does the evil come from within or from beyond?" Of course, evil has long since become native to the Biedermeier town of Wisborg. And the deadly bill is paid primarily by rich ignoramuses like Friedrich (Aaron TAYLOR-JOHNSON), Thomas' best friend.

A truly remarkable film that once again elevates a very German story to a parable that can be understood worldwide. Very impressive!

reviews.author: RebelPanda
reviews.body: I expected a predictable remake, but what I got was a stunning, gothic, and gory experience that took me on the same gradual descent into madness that When Evil Lurks delivered so effectively last year. Lily-Rose Depp's performance in the lead role was absolutely chilling-she should be in every British psychological horror film. Her portrayal was incredibly unsettling, especially during the disturbing possession scenes. The acting across the board was phenomenal, with each performance adding to the growing tension. The music was booming and powerful, amplifying the horror at every turn. The editing, with its sudden cuts and changes in location, created a pervasive sense of unease that kept me on edge throughout. Kudos to the filmmakers for taking risks, breaking away from the conventional, and delivering something fresh and exciting, rather than sticking to a by-the-numbers remake.

reviews.author: Perseus_Monroe
reviews.body:
Set in the 1830s, Nosferatu tells the tale of Thomas Hutter, an estate agent traveling to Transylvania for a fateful encounter with Count Orlok. While away his bride Ellen, is left under the care of their friends plagued by horrific visions and an increasing sense of dread.

The story is solid. Its beautiful but not groundbreaking. It doesn't reinvent the wheel, which is perfectly fine, not every film needs to bring something completely new to the table. I haven't seen the original Nosferatu, Ive watched Dracula like films, and the storyline here feels familiar. I'm not usually drawn to Dracula-type stories but I found it engaging enough. It's not something I'd rush to rewatch but i appreciated the execution.

At times, the film felt a bit too long. Certain scenes could have been trimmed without losing anything important. Nothing wrong with a solid hour-and-a-half runtime for a film like this.

Visually, the movie is stunning, with beautiful scenes and a gothic atmosphere that's perfect for the story. But here's the issue, some parts were just way too dark. I get the choice to keep Count Orlok hidden in shadows early on, that worked well. But in other scenes, the lighting was so dim that I could barely make out important details.

I really liked how Count Orlok was designed! It felt accurate to the time period, especially with his mustache. His body was creepy its like a gross, decaying zombie and when they finally showed his full body at the end, it was disgusting in the best way.

Everyone acted so well. No complaints there. But there was one issue, when Bill Skarsgård (who played Orlok) spoke, it was hard to understand him sometimes. I had to rely on what the other characters were saying to figure out what was going on, especially in the castle scene. Subtitles would've helped a lot. Not saying I couldn't understand him at all, but in some moments, it was a struggle.

Lily-Rose Depp stole the show as Ellen. Her performance was phenomenal. She nailed the character so well that I honestly don't think the movie would've been the same without her.

Overall, Nosferatu (2025) was a solid movie. It's dark, creepy, and has beautiful visuals with some incredible acting. The story didn't blow me away, but it was still enjoyable. If you're into gothic horror, you'll probably love it!

reviews.author: Blu-rayPit
reviews.body: Let's say that as the first film of the year it couldn't have gone better. Dark atmospheres and anxiety that rises more and more with each scene. A color film which however appears to be in black and white most of the time, this leads the viewer to feel fear even for scenes of simple dialogue by candlelight. The soundtrack brings the heart rate to very high levels especially in the scenes with Nosferatu. One thing to note is the first 30/40 minutes of the film where you are afraid of what will come but you never see it clearly, it is the protagonist's expressions that lead you to become increasingly afraid; until the silhouette of Nosferatu clearly stands out in all its sliminess and horror and we understand that things are going to get very serious for the main characters. Excellent scenography, especially when the plague arrives in the city, which goes from being full of life to turning into empty streets with some rotting corpses and rats reigning supreme. Definitely not a film for the faint of heart but if you can get past the most gruesome scenes you have a very enjoyable film that will keep you in suspense until the end.

reviews.author: alienhanni
reviews.body:
Just around a year ago I saw Nosferatu from Werner Herzog with Klaus Kinski. In that movie all main characters started as flawed but normal people, who just happen to be in that situation. Even Nosferatu was portrayed as a poor soul, but of course creepy. Like that character development was possible, and you could understand everyone's decisions.

In this movie however Lily Rose Depp's character is completely insane right from the start, in a way at times I had to laugh. The same for Nosferatu. If you don't know, his intentions were never really clear.

Also the professor (Dafoe) wasn't well written. Somehow he always knew what was happening or about to happen with little to no evidence.

That being said, the atmosphere and the cinematography are stunning. The movie just had way more potential. Since Eggers loves the original movie and also Werner Herzogs, I really wonder why he didn't grasp the essence of the characters.

Nonetheless a movie worth seeing.

reviews.author: Heidiverstunts
reviews.body:
I thought it was a beautiful ode to the original Nosferatu. The acting performances were superb. The visuals were muted, which worked to add the same eerie quality as the original.

However, I couldn't wait for it to be over.

The film moved at a Glacial pace & I personally found that difficult. I'm torn between great acting performances and the speed of the film. 20 mins in and I was already like, hurry up! They easily could've shaved off 20 minutes and still had the same effect.

I don't know what I was expecting, but that wasn't it. Which sucks, because I really think there were great acting performances in the film. It just could not keep my attention.

Both Skarsgård and Depp should be nominated for awards for their performances.

reviews.author: rgalx
reviews.body: As someone who saw the film. I'll give you my honest opinion, it was pretty good. Sure yeah, the story could've been better but that is besides the point. The film delivered what it was supposed to deliver, a good story about a vampire who lusts have a woman named Ellen and will do absolutely anything to get to her. The cinematography, production, costume, make-up, and music are a part of the film that keeps you watching. The performances alone are worth noting as well. Lily Rose Depp absolutely kills it as the lead actress, the only critique for acting is that Aaron Taylor-Johnson overdoes his acting in most of the scenes he is in and that pulls me out of it. The film isn't much of a horror but more of a drama, which works. The length of the film is basic to usual movie length, I didn't find the film to be boring or a slow pace because I was brought into the world of Nosferatu. Other reviews say that Count Orlok's looks is much different than the original, and while that is true, it is more accurate to the portrayal in Bram Stoker's novel. Overall, the film is well done and full of great technicalities and performances. If you're a fan of drama/horror you'll enjoy this film. Though, I would watch one of Robert Egger's films before viewing this masterfully done film.

reviews.author: soeurchampignon
reviews.body:
I wasn't completely enamored with the film on opening night, so I did some light reading on the Dracula story and booked another ticket. I'm so glad I did! A second viewing made it easier to enjoy the movie without trying to "figure it out" at the same time.

It's hard to say much without spoiling the movie. But it is sexy, disturbing, magical, and gorgeous.

As an Eggers fan, this has been my most anticipated movie of the year. Other fans shouldn't be disappointed. And I do believe a general audience will enjoy this film, too. It's more accessible than The Lighthouse, and better executed than The Northman.

The cinematography is stunning, each frame is like a portrait. The performances are good, even great sometimes. The story was great, and the design was brilliant. The pacing is good, though it stalls a bit after the midway point. It is effective at transporting us into another time and place.

I did wish that some of the scenes didn't feel so rushed. It was such a beautiful and captivating movie, and it could've taken its time to linger even more than it did. The shots that do linger (you'll know them when you see them) are delicious, and in those shots I immediately recognized the style that draws me to back to Eggers time and time again.

reviews.author: AlexRWagner
reviews.body:
Robert Eggers' Nosferatu (2024) is an intoxicating, seductive fever dream-a horror film that doesn't just haunt but arouses, thrilling in its power to unnerve while weaving an undercurrent of raw, unbridled lust. Eggers creates a world where gothic romance and carnal desire collide, offering a daring reimagining of the vampire mythos that feels more intimate, visceral, and dangerous than any adaptation before it.

Shot on lush 35mm, Nosferatu pulses with a tactile sensuality that digital could never hope to replicate. The grain, the flicker of the projector, the imperfections-this is a film you feel as much as you watch. Every frame seems drenched in longing, like a forbidden secret whispering directly to you. The cinematography, drenched in shadows and candlelit decadence, is the year's finest, and it's impossible not to succumb to the spell cast by its chiaroscuro artistry.

Lily-Rose Depp's performance as Ellen is a revelation. She exudes an ethereal, almost dangerous fragility that becomes the emotional and erotic core of the film. Her chemistry with Bill Skarsgård's Count Orlok is electric-a dance of power, submission, and hunger. Skarsgård, transforming himself into something otherworldly, plays Orlok as a creature driven equally by torment and desire. The result is less a villain and more a metaphorical embodiment of temptation, his every movement slow, deliberate, and impossibly magnetic. Together, they share scenes that are charged with a sensuality so thick you can almost taste it.

The film redefines the eroticism of the vampire myth. While it leaves much to the imagination, Nosferatu revels in suggestion and implication-its forbidden touches, glances that linger too long, and moments of near ecstasy where desire and death blur into one. Eggers balances this eroticism with a restraint that makes every revealing moment-yes, even the brief glimpse of flesh-feel both shocking and poetic. It's sexier than any explicit film could hope to be because it knows the real power lies in what is hidden, in what is craved but cannot be fully attained.

The score is hypnotic-a wailing, otherworldly dirge that echoes the film's themes of longing and despair. Paired with the production design and costumes, which immerse you fully in a plague-ridden, gothic world of decay and decadence, Nosferatu becomes a fully sensory experience. It's not just a movie-it's an invitation to lose yourself in a dark, kinky fantasy where the lines between pain and pleasure, love and obsession, predator and prey are deliciously blurred.

This is not just a horror film. It's a masterpiece of erotic storytelling that dares to explore the taboo, that invites you to feel not just fear but also forbidden passion. With Eggers at the helm, Nosferatu is elevated to the heights of cinematic art-an X-rated fantasy in spirit, if not in rating, that makes you complicit in its desires. You don't just watch Nosferatu. You surrender to it.

reviews.author: berndgeiling
reviews.body:
Robert Eggert's Nosferatu is no modern reinterpretation for our time, it's an almost too faithful hommage to it's predecessors, especially to the expressionist german silent film from 1922.

It is a visual feast, set design, lighting and camerawork are nothing else than brilliant.

The first act is overwhelming and very promising. Then it slowly falls apart and starts lacking tension, especially in the last act, which could have been much shorter.

Nosferatu is being shown late and you never see a lot of him, until the very final sequence, when you see Nosferatu in full sunlight. Mark: the fewer you see of him the better it is.

Less would have been more.

The acting cast delivers solid performances, but nothing extraordinary. Sometimes woody, sometimes overacting, sometimes ridiculous, I don't name anyone in particular.

Anyway: the main and most interesting aspect of Eggers remake lays in its style, and Eggers taste for style is unbeatable here.

reviews.author: sereirotanachong
reviews.body:
I really don't understand the split of amongst viewers. I thought this movie was a visual spectacle. The lighting and darkness of the film was great. Beautiful shots throughout the movie along with Masterful camera work. Love that atmosphere of the movie, it's makes you feel uneasy throughout and a bit terrified especially the encounter with Count Orlok in his castle. You could feel the characters fear of the situation.

Lily Rose Depp was outstanding. Her performance is worthy of an Oscar. Bills Skarsgard's was awesome, definitely a different look from the 1920's Count Orlok but a awesome take. He looks a bit more like an undead Vlad the Impaler here. I would definitely watch this again maybe in IMAX. Go in with a free mind and just enjoy the movie. No need to compare to other Dracula's.

reviews.author: MB-reviewer185
reviews.body:
This is a remake of the old movie Nosferatu (1922) which was based on the novel Dracula by author Bram Stoker, I have not read the book, but I have seen the old 1922 movie and thought it was fine for something long ago, so having a remake especially one by director Robert Eggers was going to be interesting to see; I will just start by saying that I liked this remake and thought it visually great to watch, but I can't see myself watching it that often. The remake Nosferatu (2024) was a visually pleasing and dark film that had excellent performances, beautiful cinematography, cool practical effects, disturbing and unsettling moments, great directing and writing, and a creepy antagonist; there are a couple intense moments I guess you could say that might turn people off while watching the film, and though it was a little hard to watch, it still had something to do with the plot, along with the two hour and twelve minutes runtime making this not the most rewatchable.

All the performances in this film are excellent, like Nicholas Hoult as Thomas Hutter who goes to Count Orlok's castle because of a real estate deal for him to buy a house in town, he gave an exceptional performance, and you can feel the growing sense of fear when he is at the castle; the best performance would be from Lily-Rose Depp as the wife Ellen Hutter, because throughout the whole film she has to play insane, infatuated, normal person, and loving wife all at once and she does an excellent job, especially when she has to do insane things or weird love scenes because she is giving it her all despite how intense they are. Aaron Taylor-Johnson and Emma Corrin as Friedrich and Anna Harding who are friends with Thomas and Ellen also give great performances, with them trying to help with certain things that occur to Ellen Hutter but get effected in the process leading to dark and disturbing moments in the film later. Lastly, in terms of other characters, Willem Dafoe as Prof. Albin Eberhart von Franz gives a satisfactory performance; despite having a weird voice, he still gave a believable performance as this person who has some knowledge on Count Orlok and warns people about him rising again many years later, which leads to a big moment by the third act.

Actor Bill Skarsgård as Count Orlok was great as in when you see him in full view near the end you cannot recognize him at all which was amazing to see, but also the whole film he is in the dark shadows or is shown in dark silhouettes which led to some cool looking camera shots and eerie scenes; the voice of him was intimidating and all throughout the film he was giving off a dark, gothic, and creepy feeling which made the film not necessarily scary but at least creepy and disturbing to watch. I will start by saying that the cinematography of this film is excellent, with it having great wide shots of the scenery including the main town, Orlok's castle, or shots of the landscape while Thomas is travelling, along with snowy shots of the town or landscape that were pretty in that dark gothic sense; the film was not scary to me but I thought it was creepy and disturbing to watch, especially since there are quite a few intense scenes that could be hard to watch depending on the type of audience member who can handle it. Lastly, I will just add that this did have similarities to the original 1922 film with it copying small scenes but also focusing and expanding on ideas from the original that were only hinted at in a subtle way, like the pain of a Plague in the town.

The remake Nosferatu (2024) was a visually pleasing and dark film that had excellent performances, beautiful cinematography, cool practical effects, disturbing and unsettling moments, great directing and writing, and a creepy antagonist; there are a couple intense moments I guess you could say that might turn people off while watching the film, and though it was a bit hard to watch, it still had something to do with the plot by doing something dark that fits the theme, along with the two hour and twelve minutes runtime making this not the most rewatchable film. It might not be as rewatchable as could have been, but I still like it for the new take on the story with the beautiful cinematography and great performances; not something I will instantly go back to, but if you can handle what occurs in this, then I will recommend giving this at least one watch because of the effort and dark visuals put into it.

reviews.author: lagrie
reviews.body:
Robert Eggers just proved once again why he's one of the best in the game. Nosferatu (2024) isn't just a remake; it's a dark, chilling masterpiece that honors the original Eine Symphonie des Grauens while carving out its own space in horror history.

Let's start with the visuals, holy hell, the cinematography! Eggers' signature style shines, with every frame looking like it was pulled from a twisted, Gothic oil painting. The lighting, shadows, and camera work create this creeping sense of unease that never lets up. The set design and costumes? Absolutely insane. Every crooked building, crumbling wall, and threadbare cloak feels so real you can almost smell the damp wood and candle wax.

And then there's the acting. Bill Skarsgård as Count Orlok is beyond brilliant. He's terrifying but in this hypnotic, can't look away kind of way. He doesn't just play Orlok. He is Orlok, a perfect mix of grotesque and tragic. Every movement, every look he gives, feels so deliberate and inhuman.

Lily Rose Depp, though, wow. Her performance is completely unsettling, but in the best way possible. She has this eerie, otherworldly vibe that perfectly fits the story. It's hard to pin down if you're drawn to her or scared of her, and that's exactly what makes her so memorable. She adds this haunting energy that lingers long after the credits roll.

Eggers also nailed the balance between paying homage to the original and making it his own. The nods to Eine Symphonie des Grauens are spot-on, but he breathes new life into the story, making it feel fresh and alive while still deeply respectful of its roots.

This isn't just a horror movie, it's an experience. It's dark, moody, and so atmospheric that you'll feel like you've stepped into a Gothic fever dream. It exceeded all my expectations, and then some.

A MUST see for fans of Eggers, the original film, and anyone who loves great cinema.

reviews.author: DanTheMan2150AD
reviews.body: Nosferatu is simultaneously an exciting, repulsive and beautifully chilling cinematic nightmare, a visual feast for the beasts of the night. However, as much as this film looks the part, immaculately framed in all its expressionist trappings, the material often veered too heavily into unintentional hilarity for my liking, even with its cavalcade parade of understated Brits populating the cast. Much of the dialogue has a flowery late Victorian melodramatic feel that often results in odd-line delivery; the make-up effects on Orlok left me giggling, especially with the moustache and asthmatic breathing, he wasn't a threatening presence whenever those elements took up the frame. The additional sex and nudity feel like he's playing catch up to the dominating performances of the Dracula roles before him. There's a good reason they kept his goofy ass out the marketing. Skarsgård did nothing for me as Orlok sadly. Eggers' direction is fantastic, but the cheap jump scares detracted from the oppressive atmosphere he attempted to craft with the pacing and the runtime coming off as overly self-indulgent and excessive. There's a multitude of sequences you could cut down or trim out entirely to get a much tighter focus. That all being said, most of the male cast was fantastic and Dafoe pretty much steals the film out from under everyone; the kicker for me was that my girlfriend pointed out that Lily-Rose Depp sounded like she was on the brink of an orgasm every time she spoke. There's not a whole lot you can do with Nosferatu that doesn't retread the already tried and tested story, as much as I admire Eggers' attempt, it falls short and doesn't really deliver on the iconography of this count, instead falling into a weird middle ground that doesn't know if it wants to be Dracula or the Vampyre, cheating itself and cheating its leading actor, by distancing us from the Orlok we know and love. Despite its creative approaches, this Nosferatu left my thirst for the darkness thoroughly unquenched, less a symphony of horror and more a cacophony of nightmares. Herzog's version still comes out on top for me.

reviews.author: Squirrel_the_Grip_1
reviews.body: One of the best horror movies I've seen as of late. A superb retelling of the 1922 Nosferatu, Robert Eggers completely knocked this out of the ballpark! The a superb performance from Lily-Rose Depp, Nicholas Holt, and Bill Skarsgard as Count Orlock made this movie look and feel dark and foreboding. The cinematography from Jarin Blaschke absolutely makes it feel like an old vampire movie by making the dark feel like a character in itself! The amazing visuals of 1800's Germany and Transylvania really make the period piece feel the way it should have been back in 1922 when the original was made. I highly recommend this film!

reviews.author: drewconsumes
reviews.body:
I love a beautiful, slow, haunting horror film. I appreciate low light photography. The play of light and darkness where the only color discernable is a barely detectible shade of blue. There are numerous scenes that live on the day after... the scene where Hutter is picked up by the carriage is a classic.

This film is visually striking and the performances, script and setting are worthy of many re-watches. I put it up their with The Shining, Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and the more recent Long Legs.

I'm stunned that some people didn't like it. I was giddy through-out and I want to go back and watch it again.

Bravo!

reviews.author: UniqueParticle
reviews.body: Robert Eggers is so talented no matter what most think all his projects have complex dialogue, exceptional acting and top notch cinematography! I don't know how Bill Skarsgard does his dark characters he's unrecognizable as the Count in every aspect. I understand any mixed critics there's some slowness but Nosferatu is well worth it at least the bulk of it. Aaron Taylor Johnson and Nicolas Hoult have stayed busy with Kraven for Aaron, the other one was in The Order that was excellent! Nosferatu is the most horror experience by the director since The Witch that starred Ralph Inneson that co starred in this so that was satisfying. Highly recommend to anyone no matter what!

reviews.author: lee-cooke2
reviews.body:
Sadly, some of the Marvel generation in attendance at the cinema left half-way through, surely expecting this to be a mindless, jump-scare movie, wrapped up in some new cinematic "universe".

Luckily, this film offers much more. The cinematography, style, costumes, locations and overall feel of the visuals were outstanding. A typical for Robert Eggers, to fully immerse you in the world of the story.

Solid performances from the likes of Willem Dafoe (as expected), Nicolas Holt & Aaron Taylor-Johnson, but the stand-outs were certainly Bill Skarsgård's unsettling take of Count Orlok and the scene-stealing Lily-Rose Depp, who did a fantastic job as Ellen Hutter. Surely a nod or two for her during awards season.

Is this Eggers' magnum opus? Well, that remains to be seen. But for now, a fine job and a very entertaining watch.

reviews.author: jfalslev
reviews.body:
The cinematography is absolutely breathtaking. The stark contrasts between light and shadow, the unsettling use of distorted angles, and the overall monochromatic aesthetic create a truly unforgettable visual experience. The possession scenes are particularly disturbing, showcasing the film's ability to tap into primal fears and evoke genuine unease.

"Nosferatu" is a film that lingers in the mind long after the credits roll. It's a slow-burn that masterfully builds dread and suspense, culminating in moments of genuine terror. While the film may not be for the faint of heart, its artistry and enduring power make it a must-see for any serious film enthusiast.

reviews.author: SPZMaxinema
reviews.body: Johnny Depp's daughter (Lily-Rose) acted very well in the movie with her more intense scenes and overall, it looked very good. One particular scene where Thomas is approaching the castle at nighttime looked like an actual painting and left me kind of in awe. This movie also reminded me of the classic horror movie, the Exorcist, in quite a few scenes as well! While some plot points were a bit confusing and unclear as well as the time-jumps between scenes and events, this is still an undeniably quality horror movie on many levels. The other actors did very well too and the radically creepy, dark, gruesome, and menacing vibe throughout the whole movie helped keep me invested! Horror movie-goers may very likely be pleased!

reviews.author: lucalothschutz
reviews.body: "Nosferatu 2025" is a masterful reinterpretation of the classic horror film that captivates both long-time fans and new viewers alike. The director has managed to preserve the dark atmosphere and eerie charm of the original while employing modern cinematic techniques to create an even more intense and claustrophobic mood. The standout performances and meticulously crafted sets immerse the audience in the sinister world of Count Orlok. The psychological horror elements are skillfully used, ensuring the film lingers in the mind long after the credits roll. Overall, "Nosferatu 2025" is an outstanding example of how a remake can be both respectful of the original and innovative. 10 out of 10.

reviews.author: TheReviewerBoyar
reviews.body:
Good preface to say I haven't seen its source material whatsoever.

I think technically it's great! Sound design was awesome and it's overall effective in that regard.

However, the story like my recently reviewed squid game kinda suffers here.

For example, main character talks about being a child but we never see that. Or, for ending, someone being near a coffin and sitting it ablaze but then somehow ending up with the characters at the same time even though he was behind them by maybe 10-30 minutes... the movie jumps logic once or twice.

Overall, it's a serviceable film that doesn't push any boundaries or teach you anything.

reviews.author: tresm87
reviews.body: I don't know how this director keeps rising in the ranks . To me he has to be the most overrated aside from maybe Peele. Ever since his debut with the witch, I've been baffled by this as he makes some of the most boring and dull films that are somewhat carried by his keen eye for period piece visuals. I will give him that. He knows how to set movies in a very anachronistic and detailed way to fit the timeframe in which they are belonging to. Aside from that, I cannot say that this film excels the way the critics and the hype is claiming it to. I gave it a shot just because of the much larger budget they gave him , thinking Maybe it would have more visceral intense actual horror as well as Skarrsgard . Once again, nothing comes out of this more than a bunch of hilarious accents and a couple really well shot scenes. I don't know how people keep hailing This guy as the greatest horror Director of our generation. If anything, I'd say he's more of a drama director at this point.

reviews.author: Quinoa1984
reviews.body:
Is this a romantic Gothic melodrama, or is it a Demonic Possession story? Or a story of a less than great husband's redemption? Why not a little of all three? My first impression is that Eggers's Nosferatu, a shmorgasbord of spectacle and details that is far more about its surface than its bleeding-out heart, and at the same time I wish it was more focused on an emotional focal point than what this is, which is... often staggeringly impressive as a visual feast for the dark-hearted of this all.

This is Nosferatu but, let's not mince words, it is also Dracula, and when it comes to a terrifying and mortifying and soul-sucking combination of horror and romance, it's hard to top Coppola and Eggers ultimately does not. I was enraptured in the scale and scope of Eggers' direction and there are great scenes and moments throughout, and Hoult, Depp, Skarsgard and especially Dafoe really bring some depth to their characters and how heightened they are while still feeling real to Eggers's aesthetic concerns (if that makes sense).

But the problem and it isn't a small one is there needed to be more time, perhaps in cutaway style between when Thomas is at Orlock's castle, to see Orlock in Ellen's cracked-up visions and possessed states. I think uniformly the performances in this are all strong while at the same time something is missing with the pathos, and this is despite that you can feel a bond with Hoult and Depp and that Dafoe is a formidable Professor Eberhart (err Not-Helsing)? Maybe there is also a little too much time with the ATJ Harding family who we don't really care about anyway but gets significant time anyway.

I like the focus on plague and pestilence, which is congruent with Murnau and Herzog (though never quite so haunting and bizarre in its simple depictions as in the latter), and yet there isn't any sense of what much of the community does about it (Murnau showed how much the populace, and this was in recently the Spanish flu swept the world, would fight back against Knock-nay-Renfield). That's the thing that's frustrating about this Nosferatu; there are some of the most visually arresting moments in any horror film this decade, and I really dug everything in the first half when Hoult is approaching (those townspeople speak to this director's love of folklore) and then at that Castle.

Scary? Sure. Am I actually shook by what I have seen after it ends though, or feel the awful pain of a woman who knows what she has to do to stop this Agent of Plague that's haunted her since she was young? Not so much. I heard a clip of an interview with Eggers that he watched of all things Mel Brooks's Dracula Dead and Loving It of what sorts of Vampire movie tropes are most laughable and what to not so much avoid but what to emphasize while adding a level of eroticism. That's noble and a great goal and if it is too long and less than masterful, it's good to have inspired filmmakers reaching for their visions with as much resources as possible. 7.5/10.

reviews.author: moviesfilmsreviewsinc
reviews.body: Robert Eggers, an American director, has a unique talent for creating immersive cinematic worlds. His films, such as The Lighthouse (2019) and The Witch (2015), are deeply rooted in 17th-century folkloric rituals and terror. Nosferatu, a remake of Murnau's 1922 German expressionist silent film, is an atmospheric and richly realized work that leaves a lasting impression on the audience. Eggers's world-building goes beyond detailed backdrops and embraces period-specific cadences and peculiarities of language. The screenplay is filled with gorgeously ornate curses and florid turns of phrase, as crucial to character development as the choices of costumes. These full-blooded and fleshed-out worlds require performances to match. Lily-Rose Depp's performance as troubled newlywed Ellen Hutter is particularly noteworthy. In a shimmering, erotically charged prologue, Ellen unwittingly summons an ancient evil, Count Orlok, who invades her dreams. Ellen's marriage to Thomas Hutter brings temporary respite from the feverish nightmares and fits that possessed her. Their life together in 1838 is impoverished but blissfully happy. However, Thomas is sent by his prospective employer Herr Knock to Transylvania to present the deeds of a ruined mansion to a "very old and eccentric" client. Ellen lives with her friend Anna Harding and her brusque and businesslike husband Friedrich, struggling with an underwritten role that requires him to repeat lines of dialogue in a tone of blustering incredulity. Ellen Hutter, a young woman suffering from night terrors and convulsions, is treated by her hosts as they prepare for an approaching horror. Dr. Wilhelm Sievers, a local psychiatric specialist, advises her to be shackled to the bed and tighten her corset to calm her womb. As Ellen's symptoms intensify, Sievers calls on the expertise of his disgraced former professor, Albin Eberhart von Franz (Willem Dafoe), who has been rejected by the scientific world due to his fascination with the occult and personal hygiene. Robert Eggers' gothic drama Nosferatu balances themes of feral abandon and wild urges against a tightly controlled buildup of unspeakable dread. The film's arresting drama of photography is the picture's most distinctive element, with scene transitions and vivid hues. The filmmaking style in this remake of F. W. Murnau's 1922 silent original invokes the sensation of falling in a dream, causing nightmarish propulsions through its plot. The deeply enrapturing result is one of the finest, most viscerally exciting works of horror this year. The filmmaking style in this remake of a classic involves retreading old ground, with the familiar broad strokes of its setup. Newlyweds Thomas and Ellen Hutter live in 19th-century Wisborg, Germany, and are soon separated when Thomas is sent by his boss, Herr Knock (Simon McBurney), to the Transylvanian castle of the mysterious Count Orlok (Bill Skarsgård). Anyone who's seen a version of Nosferatu or any Dracula movie knows the tale all too well. However, Eggers' remake makes a key change to the material that alters the story's point of view and who it is actually about, making this interpretation something new and untemplated. Orlok, a vampire in the film Nosferatu, is both human and bony and corpse-like. His design resembles previous versions from a distance, but up close, he stands out as a unique take. Eggers' version of Orlok is a mustachioed 15th-century conqueror with regal fur robes, giving him a sense of width and stature. However, this appearance serves to serve a surprisingly thoughtful and complicated story. Orlok is both powerful and paternalistic, revolting and seductive, and a thorny physical embodiment of Ellen's repression. Ellen's story is a tale of shame and desire, with a bone-deep contradiction that Depp performs with burgeoning rage and considered physicality. The blurred lines between Ellen's sexual awakening and the violent and macabre in Nosfaratu's animalistic prologue create discomforting nuance. Orlok's presence in the distance functions as a twisted personification of arousal, making Ellen's story one of suppressed feminine sexuality in need of liberation. The ambiguous nature of her first sexual encounter at a young age also introduces the possibility of her having been forced or coerced, making Nosferatu equally a tale of sexual desire and assault. Ellen's emotional afflictions in adulthood take on dueling meanings, making her story a tale of sexual desire and assault. In the original film, Dr. Sievers provides answers on defeating Orlok, a creature he treats as a pathogen. Murnau's film was a response to the Spanish Flu pandemic, and Eggers' film focuses more on the COVID crisis. Instead of retreading Murnau's sickness metaphor, Eggers has Sievers turn to Von Franz, a character deeply immersed in historical detail and the occult. Von Franz is deeply immersed in religious symbols, some tied to pagan religions and others to mainstream Christianity. In Nosferatu, both pagan and Christian characters have control over various characters, which Von Franz seeks to break through ritual or convincing people to let go of their preconceptions. Dafoe's matter-of-fact approach to the strange and supernatural adds an amusing layer to the story, subtly acknowledging that these ideas are familiar to modern audiences. He ensures the story gets quickly to its point, even when it slows down for the occasional expositional chat. Nosferatu is not languid or uninteresting, even in its most dour moments. It's the polar opposite of Herzog's travelogue version, where physical spaces and locations were all-important. Eggers' remake feels entirely metaphysical, with an enveloping, assaultive sound mix that compliments its aggressive images. It is a sensory experience that forces us to wrestle with our control over our own physical and emotional responses. In conclusion, Eggers' Nosferatu is a metaphysical and artistically accomplished work, with an enveloping sound mix that complements its aggressive images.

reviews.author: Horrordelights
reviews.body:
Eggers's imagining of this classic tale fills the narrative with dread, tension and timelessness. Eggers is a poet with the camera, weaving every scene with intricate detail and stunning imagery. It is as if I watched a historical tale unfold in front of me, overcast by mythos. Eggers wraps you into his story, immersing the viewer into his fantastical world.

The purity of the grey colour scheme brings the focus solely on the story, grounding the viewer to the action in front of them.

Skarsgård's enigmatic Orlok is the stand-out, actor completely unrecognizable under all those prosthetics. His voice is a character in itself, showcasing Skarsgård's utmost dedication to the craft.

The scene in which Thomas Hutter arrives on the grounds of the castle evokes the sublime magnificence of a Friedrich painting. The landscape envelops him, alive with the looming shadow of doom. Every moment, every word, is carefully thought out.

reviews.author: tink-22503
reviews.body:
The vision of Eggers is so profound and meticulous that each frame in this movie is a perfect picture in itself. The atmosphere, coldness, darkness all add to the feeling of wanting to shiver in my seat and almost expecting snow in the theater simply by watching.

It's a stunning, enthralling fairytale that sweeps you off your feet, acting was superb especially by Skarsgard and Depp.

I can honestly say that this film made a larger impact on me than the Keanu/Ryder one and eventhough that's a beautiful product this one just echoed in my mind for days after I watched it and even came to haunt me in a scary dream. I watch a lot of scary movies and that hasn't happened in years so even there the score is great ;-) Go see this one. Just. Do. It.

reviews.author: zacharycarr-34309
reviews.body:
Robert Eggers does it again. Not only does Nosferatu put a spin on a classic film but it beautifully combines the lore of the original with the classic tale of Dracula by Bram Stoker.

The simplest place to start is the score. Beautifully done and impactful in the moments required.

Now on to cinematography and visuals. In classic Eggers style the camera panning was used masterfully, as well as shadows to really emphasize tone. But what really stands out is the use of colors in this film. Black and white is used to contrast not just the tone but also to differentiate the moments in plot. Truly a masterful use of colors, or lack there of.

Acting and directing go hand in hand to make the movie unnerving to a level that is true to Eggers style. Disturbing without pushing it to the point of driving people away. You want to look away but you just can't. Bill Skarsgard's portrayal was truly masterful and as always he makes you completely forget about past performances. Lily Depp made you both uncomfortable and sympathetic for her plight. Aaron Taylor-Johnson and Willem DaFoe do a wonderful job at portraying individuals who, as many of us would, look for any reason to believe it is something other than the truth presented by the main characters. All of these roles brilliantly tied together by Eggers directing.

Lastly we have to talk about tone and plot. Horribly deranged and disturbing as all Eggers films are, with lots of beautiful artistry. It makes you sick and in awe all the same. It was sexual and innocent, violent yet reserved.

reviews.author: thomasellery
reviews.body:
I'm not a major vampire fanatic, I've seen the usual big Hollywood Draculas, the odd Hammer Horror and had a quick rewatch of Winona and Keanu give it a go in the 90's, before watching this, so my expectations were artsy gothic, with big spooky nods to the 20's version.

It delivers on the historical goth aesthetics big time. The sets and landscapes are one of the films strong points. Stylised evil is constantly creeping across the screen and every single prop seems to be symbolic. Think oversaturated vampire story paraphernalia but done well.

I really enjoyed the first 1/3 of this film, the cinematography was gorgeous. The camera is slowly zooming and panning like nobody's business and for this section the sudden cuts to waking up worked.

Our titlle's star's introduction was fantastic, keeping him mainly in the shadows, as he teleports around the table. All the credit goes to Nicholas here though, it's Thomas's terrified reactions that really tell us what's going and he genuinely looks like he's gonna pee his pants.

Once his bloodthirsty contract comes out we get Bill doing what Bill does best, marking himself firmly as horror's darker Johnny Depp. Personally I liked the vampiric look here, more demonic than dark prince and heart suckling creeps me out way more than neck biting.

On the flip side, think more ye olde Exorcist for our dark maiden back home. Nothing we haven't seen before here, but it pulls it off without being campy.

Then the style remains, the talented cast stay talented (again Nicholas is great) and William Dafoe is enigmatic throughout, but the story seems to both drag and get choppy at the same time.

It's like they keep the love triangle element and film work slow, but quickly race through getting everyone together, offing a few of them and getting to sunrise. It would have worked better if the terror took the lead for a while here and let the love story take it back for the end.

Ultimately this is a tragic romance though, (that's a little horny), not a horror and we do get some good dollops of the spookies and a little bit of good gore.

Overall, I'd watch this again, I'll probably buy it when it's reduced on streaming, but I enjoyed more for its style and Georgian macabre aesthetic than the story. The kind of thing I'd double bill with The Others or Woman in Black for a spooky stormy night in, without actually bringing scared.

Definitely a winter movie as well - really matched the January chills outside the cinema (not sure why it's set at Christmas but barely mentions or shows it though - guess I can add it to my alternative Xmas movie list though).

reviews.author: jdizzolena
reviews.body: Director Robert Eggers' film "Nosferatu" blends elements of horror and romance to tell the story of a toxic love triangle involving Ellen (played by Lily-Rose Depp), her husband Thomas (portrayed by Nicholas Hoult), and a vampire named Count Orlok (played by Bill Skarsgård). Count Orlok becomes obsessed with Ellen and, driven by jealousy, devises a plan to be with her, which leads to dark and deadly consequences, which ultimately ends with a bang. This film was beautifully shot by cinematographer Jarin Blaschke, known for his work on other Robert Eggers films, and shout out to the art department and costume designers for successfully creating a chilling, immersive setting reminiscent of Transylvania. You almost feel like you're going to walk out of the theater with the flu, which actually might just be the plague. The performances by Lily-Rose Depp, Nicholas Hoult, Bill Skarsgård, and the ultra talented Willem Dafoe are top-tier. Overall, it is definitely a strong entry in the horror genre, I give it a 8 out of 10 or 4 out of 5 stars.

reviews.author: colingear
reviews.body: I'll give credit where it belongs, the cinematography and setting was masterful. But the rest of the movie was a pretentious snooze fest. The assemble, and cinematography couldn't save this movie. Many main cast members were over acting, especially Lily-Rose Depp and Aaron Taylor Johnson. When Lily was having a moment near the end of the movie, her performance nearly made this horror movie a comedy. The scene with her eyes rolled back, and her slack jaw wide open as her tongue hangs out like a Dog lingered a few seconds too long. This movie was made just so pretentious people, can hangout and look a mess on screen. The movie lacked diversity, it was like it was filmed in the in the 50's-00's in that regard. As well, the musical score was amazing. Don't see how this movie is getting the praise it's getting, guess people love pretentious snooze fests.

reviews.author: sivadparks-89786
reviews.body:
Having never seen any of the Dracula/Nosferatu movies or read the book, the movie was compelling from the first scene. It did an excellent job at portraying the pure evil of Count Orlok, especially when Thomas first encounters him. It is easily one of the most effective horror scenes I've even seen.

Having now listened to the first 4 chapters of the book and watched the 1922 movie, I've grown in appreciation for how the 2024 film faithfully conveys the Nosferatu story and captures the eerie religious tones of the book (which aren't really present in the 1922 movie). There is a lot of passion and care given to the source material.

Where this movie goes wrong is twofold. First, because the introduction of Orlok is so effective, the movie fails to keep the momentum going and can feel repetitive and slogging. Lots of horror movies seem to hit this problem since the horror is less effective the more you know.

The second problem is that the movie has quasi religious themes but I'm not really sure that the movie actually has anything to say. I heard that Eggars prides himself on making films that both conservative Christians and Satanists like, a sentiment I commend, but here it feels so non-commital to the point of being vacuous.

In The Witch and Northman, the religious elements could be explained away as visions and not true reality, but Nosferatu seems to affirm that Orlok is in fact a supernatural evil. Which would seem to demand religious practice to defeat Orlok.

What's most confusing is the sexual repression theme. The sexual horror is incredibly effective visually and is more repulsive than arousing. But it again feels neutral to the point of saying nothing. You would expect this movie to be set in a deeply religious society where women are treated like property. But instead, Thomas' hometown is quite secular and there's no hint that there are pervasive norms about sexuality. The movie almost seems to have a religious affirmation of the power of marriage which only makes the thematic story more confusing and muddled.

As a horror movie, Nosferatu is extremely effective at the beginning and compelling enough for the rest of the film. It leaves the audience with a lot to think on. But thematically, it feels noncommittal despite having interesting ideas at play.

reviews.author: MrDHWong
reviews.body:
"Nosferatu" is a remake of the 1922 gothic horror film of the same name, which itself is heavily based on Bram Stoker's "Dracula". Written and directed by Robert Eggers ("The Witch", "The Lighthouse", "The Northman") and starring Bill Skarsgård, Lily-Rose Depp, Nicholas Hoult, Aaron Taylor-Johnson, and Willem Dafoe, it is a frighteningly effective experience that earns its scares through atmosphere and visuals rather than outright violence.

In 1838, Ellen Hutter (Lily-Rose Depp) resides with her estate agent husband Thomas (Nicholas Hoult) in the German town of Wisborg. In an effort to attain financial stability for the both of them, Thomas agrees to sell a local old stately home to the mysterious and reclusive Count Orlok (Bill Skarsgård). Leaving Ellen in the care of his close friend Friedrich Harding (Aaron Taylor-Johnson), Thomas travels to Orlok's castle in Transylvania, where upon arriving is shunned and jeered by the local populace. After finally making it to the castle in the Carpathian Mountains, Thomas is impatiently welcomed by Orlok in a hostile manner, where he insists on completing his purchase of the home immediately. While her husband is away, Ellen frequently experiences terrifying nightmares of Death himself as well as bouts of sleepwalking and seizures, which Professor Albin Eberhart Von Franz (Willem Dafoe) later deduces is being caused by Nosferatu, a demonic vampire capable of enacting unspeakable evil in its wake.

Predating Universal Studios' 1931 classic "Dracula" by nine years, F. W. Murnau's silent film "Nosferatu" is widely accepted as being the very first vampire movie ever made. Originally conceived as a result of Murnau's inability to acquire the rights to adapt Bram Stoker's novel "Dracula", "Nosferatu" has since taken on a life of its own, essentially setting the template for modern horror films as we know it (according to film historian Kim Newman). Even more than one hundred years later, Murnau's landmark feature still packs a punch for those craving their fix of gothic vampiric horror thanks to its highly influential visual style and frightening imagery. In 2024, filmmaker Robert Eggers has now created his own version of "Nosferatu", which in many ways is as equally impactful and horrifying as its original counterpart.

Beginning appropriately at night, the film opens on a young lady named Ellen yearning and praying for peace among her melancholic loneliness. Soon enough, Ellen's desperate pleas are quickly answered, albeit, not by something angelic but rather a terrifying entity that suddenly attacks her out of the darkness. Collapsing to the ground convulsing and flailing about, Ellen soon awakens from this ordeal, revealing to us that this whole thing was actually a nightmare she was having from her bed. However, it soon becomes clear that what Ellen experienced was far from a simple bad dream, setting the stage for sinister events to play out many years later.

Flashing forward to the winter of 1838, Ellen is now married to real estate broker Thomas Hutter, who is determined for the couple to stay financially stable through ensuing difficult times. At the behest of his boss Herr Knock (Simon McBurney), Thomas accepts a job selling an old decrepit state home to the eccentric Count Orlok, who is currently located far away in a castle in Transylvania. Sensing something amiss about this whole situation, Ellen begs her husband to stay at home but Thomas ignores her and sets off on his own. From this point forward, the film shows things play out from two key perspectives; Ellen's nightmarish visions of Death incarnate and Thomas dealing with the fearsome wrath of Count Orlok. To that effect, the film interweaves these characters' fates near flawlessly, making their love for each other an important driving force for how the film builds towards its clever conclusion.

As he previously showed us with his first two films, Robert Eggers is one of the best horror filmmakers working today, and his take on "Nosferatu" gives him every opportunity to demonstrate his talents within the genre. His superb atmospheric cinematography is bound to leave a lasting impression on both seasoned horror audiences and newcomers alike. For instance, one scene that filled me with awe was when Thomas arrives at the foot of Count Orlok's castle, which contains a long road surrounded by tall trees. While there, Thomas looks ahead towards the darkness where he suddenly and fearfully notices a horse-drawn carriage heading closer and closer towards him that is supposed to transport him up to the castle. What makes this moment work so well is the way it sets an ominous tone for what's to come once Thomas finally meets with the notorious Count, as though he is actually venturing right into the very essence of evil itself. There are also many other beautifully shot moments throughout the movie, which would make me go so far as to call this one of the best looking horror films I have ever seen.

Additionally, Eggers also uses minimal lighting and shadows to invoke as much fear in the viewer as possible, even coming close to mimicking the original 1922 film in certain places. As a way to keep Count Orlok looking as intimidating as possible, Eggers chooses to have him remain in the dark at almost all times, only showing parts of his body whenever he needs to demonstrate the extent of his evil powers, whether it's by haunting Ellen in her dreams or by manipulating others to do his bidding. One of the most effective ways this is achieved is whenever we see Orlok's long fingers with sharp nails casting a literal shadow over people, places, and objects, showing the strong demonic influence he can have right at his very fingertips. This gives the viewer a sense of paranoia by showing them that nowhere is safe from this evil vampiric creature and that he could appear at any given time to claim yet another victim.

The film's cast members all fit the appropriate mould of a horror film, but of course it is Bill Skarsgård who stands out the most as Count Orlok. Already well established at playing an evil, demonic entity, Skarsgård's onscreen presence is certainly nothing to underestimate. As mentioned above, the film will have you believe that Orlok is capable of appearing out of the darkness without warning to terrorise his victims, and Skarsgård encapsulates the very notion of fear itself in that regard. Like Max Schreck before him, I'm sure Skarsgård's performance will continue to frighten viewers for many years to come.

Everyone else is used well too, with Lily-Rose Depp being quite an efficient female victim for someone like Orlok to target. From her pained, fearful expressions to her longing for peace, Depp plays into Ellen's damaged psyche so well that you can instantly empathise with her whenever she is under attack. Likewise, Nicholas Hoult is suitably likeable as Thomas, who only wants what is best for himself and his wife. Seeing a relatively ordinary man like him go up against an embodiment of pure evil gives you the feeling that he is the true underdog in this fight, someone who is easy for the audience to side with. As much as I would like to elaborate on both Aaron Taylor-Johnson and Willem Dafoe, it is difficult to do so without revealing what happens to them at the climax so all I will say is that they are each a necessary contribution to the overall story.

Succeeding as both a remake and as its own self-contained story, Robert Eggers's "Nosferatu" is a highly satisfying horror film that utilises every classic method of scaring its audience without ever resorting to cheap cliches. Its gorgeously dark visuals complimented by its foreboding atmosphere will ensure that it stands the test of time, much like the original 1922 classic before it. For fans of gothic horror or anything to do with vampires for that matter, this film is a must see, especially in theatres up on the big screen. This is one remake worthy to stand shoulder to shoulder with its predecessor, and considering the important legacy behind it, that is saying quite a lot.

I rate it a solid 9/10.

reviews.author: maggie-17492
reviews.body: This remake is, as far as remakes go, wonderful. A staple to gothic horror genre. The visual experience of watching this movie is superb, it is visually stunning and the music builds that experience even more, and creates that kind of dark atmosphere which just pulls you in. Lilly Rose - Depp has outdone herself in this movie, and the rest of the cast is also amazing. The costumes are really good also. If you are thinking of going to watch this movie in theatres, I did and I am really glad I did. It wasn't groundbreaking in the sense that it brought anything new thematically, but it is an interesting experience nonetheless.

reviews.author: englishcomm
reviews.body:
So my wife thinks this is about male Patriarchy, something we argue about all the time. Inasmuch don't be bad girls and have sexual desire - the rule of church and repression, females bodies are for children and only and men have fun outside of marriage.

Personally I just went eeeek and wonder if there are to many feminist books out there, but funny to debate - I always rate films on if I fall asleep or not - and I didn't with this film.

It would be wrong to compare this to traditional Dracula films it has its own charm. And as a sub note I would say the main female in the heroine.

Right on the cusp of being 15 rated not because of sex but the overall gory factor.

reviews.author: rod-61954
reviews.body:
Having watched both the Murnau and Herzog films, Eggers further develops the plot making it deeper, more gripping and interesting as is appropriate for 2024. Putting a lot of focus on Ellen making her the driving force of the plot adds another layer to the well known story, while the basic structure of the plot is kept and references to both Murnau and Herzog can be recognised. Even so, they tried putting a spin on Orlok, making him their own character, both visually as well as personality wise. I don't particularly like that they did that by making him have a moustache and being more authoritarian. Sometimes being more polite but more insane is scarier. At the same time they keep Orlok in the dark and don't show him clearly compared to previous adaptations which is an interesting choice but confusing - it's almost giving a message of them not being certain about the changes they made to the character.

The horror aspects were done well and according to modern standards really scaring me at some points. I personally enjoyed Herzog's emotional breaks, whereas Eggers tried to keep tension high for most of the movie. Aesthetically it's a bit too clean for me, even though one could argue that it adds to the eeriness.

All in all a nice watch and good story development, but still prefer the other films.

reviews.author: asmithee23
reviews.body: Robert Eggers' films have never thrilled me but this had such good reviews, I thought it was was worth seeing in the theater. While it was more interesting than his other movies, it still has moments that are like watching paint dry. The acting is fine, the costumes amazing and enough can't be said about how fully committed Lily-Rose Depp is to her performance. She carries this film. I know the lack of color is to help set the mood but when Depp's Helen wears a vibrant blue dress, it stands out in an odd way. Everything is exceedingly drab. In my unqualified opinion, this is one to wait for streaming.

reviews.author: Elvis-Del-Valle
reviews.body: Making a remake of a cult gem like Nosferatu is a topic of discussion. The truth is that the choice of Robert Eggers as director was the right one because he knew the original film and because if the project had been in the hands of another director, the final result might not have been as pleasant. When Werner Herzog made his version of Nosferatu, he copied several obvious things from Murnau's film, but he also gave it his own touch and some new ideas so that Nosferatu (1979) was an acceptable remake of Murnau's classic. With Robert Eggers' version it is the same, but taken to a higher level. Here Eggers does not copy 100% of the original film, but tells the same story with his own touch and changes that give this version a more developed plot and a deeper insight into it. As is characteristic of the director's style, this film offers a rather dark vision and a pace full of tension. Like The Witch and The Lighthouse, Eggers' direction makes this film feel like a nightmare. There are times when Count Orlock's influence affects the characters mentally to the point that they feel like they are trapped in a nightmare from which they cannot wake up. There are times when it seems that reality is distorted and creates a sense of tension in the environment. Thomas Hutter is already entering into a nightmare and it is not until he meets Count Orlok that he becomes quite suspicious. In Murnau's film, Thomas was skeptical until he discovered what Orlok really was. In Herzog's version, he was already suspicious of the count when he met him and in this film that happens too, but with more intensity. The control that Orlok has over Ellen is quite disturbing and is manifested as something similar to a demonic possession. The romanticism that the film offers about Ellen and Orlok seems to be partly based on what Coppola did with Dracula, but the relationship between them in this film is much darker. Bill Skarsgard's Count Orlok is much darker and more sinister than his original counterpart. He spends most of his time in the shadows and that makes him look much more mysterious and creepy. The vampire created by Murnau was based more on the Strigoi who were much more gruesome vampires than a common human vampire. At that time, they gave him a more rodent-like appearance because of his link to the bubonic plague. Count Orlok in this film follows the same parameter, but with a much more grotesque and emaciated design. Here Orlok is a more cadaverous vampire and feels like a real undead who has been wasting away for centuries. They were also able to give a brief explanation of how Orlok became an undead. The makeup is excellent and they were able to give a macabre version of the Nosferatu vampire in his full splendor. The mustache was taken from Bram Stoker's novel, since in that book the description of Dracula includes a mustache and it is a detail that has been used very rarely. Here it managed to fit together with the clothing that shows the age of the creature. Robert Eggers managed to add more character development, surpassing what Murnau and Herzog had done. The only difference would be Orlok, who in Herzog's version is more human and melancholic. Just as Herzog has offered new memorable moments to feel like an original film, Robert Eggers does the same. There are very good shots with wonderful photography, great costumes, good production design and the correct use of light and shadow. There are scenes that are a bit reminiscent of Tim Burton's style. The film becomes a gothic work with disturbing scenes, it is quite poetic and terrifying. Robert Eggers knew how to renew this beloved classic and make a film that lives up to the original. Like its predecessors, this film is destined to be a classic. Nosferatu (2024) is a beautiful artistic film, a gothic tale that revives the art of vampirism in cinema and a worthy successor to Murnau's work. Irrefutable proof that Nosferatu managed to continue to endure over time, despite 100 years having passed. My final rating for this movie is a 10/10.

reviews.author: shandocalrissian
reviews.body:
A must see on the big screen.

Dark, atmospheric, and tense.

It's not easy bringing to screen one of the most filmed stories of the last 100 years but Eggers delivers an enjoyable period script, that is well directed and acted throughout the movie.

Eggers ability to create tension and stress in a scene is actually the biggest downside to the film as it is used throughout the movie, regardless of the scene, script or scenario, but it is also hard not enjoy this too. And not reliant on shock factor gore is also a plus in this film.

Lighting, photography, editing, costumes, sets, effects, score are all perfect.

I want to call this modern Hammer; What the guys in the sixties and seventies would do now in this decade.

Nuff Said.

reviews.author: SpyroDungeon
reviews.body:
A magnificent film story offers a valuable story.

You fall in love with a person to the point of addiction and they attract your attention, but would you sacrifice the masses for this love? Personally, will your love stay close to you, will you hold on here, will you leave your love to die when it is given to you?

Should we remain under naturalism and science and distrust occultism, even if it costs our lives?

Nosferatu is a movie that deals with these issues and it also has a good actor. Count Orlok, played by Bill Skarsgård, was very nice and suited the vampire role, but the atmosphere we expected in the movie was passed quickly and some scenes were passed quickly. The movie is good and watchable, but these are also very problematic. The castle scenes were really good. There was a scene in the movie that I liked very much, William Dafoe had it cast again, it was really successful. I think Thomas Hutter is also average. I found the bloody scenes quite interesting, the movie was very detailed and the ship scene was also interesting.

So if there is a cinema in your country, definitely go.

reviews.author: realrelateinc
reviews.body: Nosferatu was undoubtedly the most unique film I saw in 2024. The film's theme and visuals were hauntingly dark, gory, and deeply unsettling, with an eerie atmosphere that lingered long after the credits rolled. The acting was nothing short of exceptional, and the cinematography was out of this world-every shot felt meticulously crafted, drawing you into its grim, nightmarish world. However, despite the impressive technical elements, the story itself was disappointingly weak, lacking the depth and cohesion that could have made it truly memorable. The pacing was also painfully slow, dragging at times, which made it harder to stay fully engaged. While critics will likely praise its artistry and boldness, I believe it will struggle to connect with mainstream moviegoers who may find it too slow and abstract for their tastes.

reviews.author: porshaconnoly
reviews.body: Nosferatu (2024) is a hauntingly beautiful reimagining of the classic tale with stunning visuals and a deeply atmospheric tone that lingers long after the credits roll. The performances are mesmerizing, especially the chilling portrayal of the titular vampire, which balances menace and melancholy perfectly. The cinematography and score elevate the film to an unforgettable experience, making it a standout in modern horror. That being said, the movie isn't without its flaws. The pacing in the middle section feels sluggish at times, as certain scenes linger longer than necessary and detract slightly from the tension. Additionally, while the movie pays homage to the original, some of the creative liberties taken with the story might feel a bit jarring for purists. A few of the supporting characters are underdeveloped which leaves their motivations and arcs feeling a little thin compared to the richly layered leads. Despite these minor shortcomings, Nosferatu (2024) is a bold and gripping adaptation that respects its roots while carving its own unique identity. It's a must watch for fans of gothic horror.

reviews.author: Camerenth
reviews.body:
Nosferatu (2024) is a breathtaking reimagining of the classic gothic horror tale, cementing its place as an essential addition to the genre. The film's set and costume design are nothing short of stunning, crafting a richly atmospheric world that feels both meticulously historical and nightmarishly otherworldly. Every frame is steeped in eerie beauty, drawing viewers into a story where dread seeps from the very walls.

From start to finish, the film is an unrelenting experience-bleak, intense, and deeply unsettling. Eggers masterfully builds tension with a slow burn that crescendos into moments of pure horror, reminding us of his unparalleled ability to blend artistry with terror.

At the heart of it all is Bill Skarsgård's towering portrayal of Count Orlok. His performance is grand and ominous, embodying a predator whose presence alone is enough to send chills down your spine. Skarsgård transforms Orlok into a figure of both menace and tragedy, commanding attention with every movement and lingering gaze.

Nosferatu is a dark and mesmerizing triumph, a film that honors its silent-era predecessor while forging a bold, modern identity. It's a must-watch for horror fans and anyone who appreciates gothic cinema at its finest.

reviews.author: s-prosser10
reviews.body:
Now before I start, I'm fully aware the original 1922 film was an unauthorised adaptation of Bram Stoker's Dracula hence the glaring similarities in the story. But if Dracula IS the story you want then ignore this and go watch Coppola's 1992 Dracula movie. This film cannot hold a candle to that.

The cinematography is really good and creates a wonderful atmosphere. But I can't replay say much more than that. Even the acting from some usually reliable names such as Willem Dafoe and Aaron Taylor-Johnson isn't really up to scratch... and as for Lily-Rose Depp, let's just say having a famous father must be doing her favours. There were times where it felt like she was literally reading from an autocue, and struggling to do it at that.

Max Shreck as Count Orlok has an iconic look, and that mark is missed by a country mile here. We are given a really poor CGI version and it cheapens the film beyond belief.

I was really looking forward to seeing this movie, maybe my expectations were too high but I certainly left the cinema feeling flat and disappointed.

reviews.author: psgorio
reviews.body: If there's any such thing as a perfect monster horror movie for me it would be present in Robert Egger's 2024 remake of the silent film of the same name. Not only was this rendition masterfully told but it was done so in a way that it was prominently shaped by its atmospheric rich and lush 1800's gothic setting that was absolutely breathtakingly captured. The acting was also very intentionally dramatically and deeply personified by the terrors that plague them. Willem Dafoe continues to be a national treasure for being both eerie and entertaining on screen all at once. And speaking of plagues, this movie not only made me want to run out of the theater and fire up the Bloodborne video game but also A Plague Tale: Innocence game as well. Even the score was so bone chilling yet subtle at times it couldn't help but get under your very skin. Some scenes were disturbing too and I give the director props for showing some images of violence that would be considered too morbid for cinema. And the very look of Count Orlok was different from the original but not so much in a way I minded nor took away from his overall menacing presence and nature but rather remained haunting throughout all of his scenes down to the last drop. Overall, while it is mostly an artsy piece at heart, it is still my favorite thing to come out of classic monster horror in the past two decades. Well done Mr. Eggers. Good form. Good show.

reviews.author: ignisnoctu
reviews.body:
