This is one of the movies I'd recommend anybody in their 20's to watch, it's one of the best movies in 2024 and that has been made in a very long time.

reviews.author: astridsutan
reviews.body:
The movie The Substance is deeply personal to me. It explores the fear of aging and the fear of being forgotten. This film resonates with those who struggle with body dysmorphia, the pressures of mass media, and society's current beauty standards. Demi Moore and Margaret Qualley both delivered outstanding performances. Coralie Fargeat, known for her exceptional work since Revenge, does not disappoint.

I'm giving it a 10/10!

reviews.author: Doctor_Enigmatic
reviews.body:
The slog thru production cards is getting ridiculous. Seriously, we had to see Mobi or whoever multiple times before the movie even started. It's kind of amazing I ended up having such a positive mindset when this is how the movie started. It's not as bad as Late Night with the Devil, that was overwhelming self...umm...pleasing. Most of those idiots didn't do anything real anyway and most definitely won't care about them anymore after seeing so many. It's a horrible trend that really needs to be neutered. I miss old IFC films. It had a quick little animation and some catchy music, the after dark for the horror films was like a direct switch to my brain that let my body know we were about to see an amazing horror film. Less is more.

Take ones part serum from Reanimator, take one part Call On Me music video, take one part Sloth origin story (which I totally didn't see coming), sprinkle in a wicked witch from Disney, and add a handful of nudity and what do you have? A movie that is full of sounds to make you uncomfortable. Ooof. Seeing people rate it a 6 reminds me of every time I look at reviews to get an idea of how the movie was received. It's clear people haven't seen enough movies, they really just don't understand quality cinema.

I watch the Terrifier series for a fun time, I am not one to shy away from graphic. I will watch most anything, hence why I have thousands of movies owned and even more watched. I also watch MST3K and RiffTrax, so I know bad films. This movie was so far from average or bad. Any movie that can really reach out and make you squirm or just FEEL, is doing something right. Too much is sanitized, made for everyone, pleasing nobody style movies, are released anymore. It's exhausting when most new releases are just remakes or reboots done in an incredibly inferior way. I am a child of the 80's, I know low budget and I have seen what low budget can do with heart. This is NOT a low budget affair. This is...art. Pretentious as it can sound, it really is.

I always remember hearing "youth is wasted on the young" "enjoy it while you can, you grow up too fast" etc... We never listen because we can't know. We don't really have a frame of reference to what they could mean. We do go about our lives trying to enjoy them and as we get older time moves so much faster. Before you know it you have more behind you than you got in front of you.

This movie really tackles the existentialism that is life and our time here. I heard it was body horror, I heard it compared to Society, and I can see that. It is moist. Watching it for the first time I remember watching When Evil Lurks the first time. I had a real bad existential trip watching that, a little too many magical little friends were taken prior and waaaaaaaaay too many horror movies put me in a bad frame of mind, but I still remember the feeling of how something can just make you feel... dirty. It is one of those times you get a funny feeling, and I don't mean like climbing the rope in gym class funny.

It isn't graphic for the sake of it, at least not really. The stuff you see, the sounds you hear, all engineered to have maximum effect. I was already... feeling it two seconds into the movie and there are so many sound effects for a needle to be poking an egg. I guess it is a good litmus test to see how exactly the rest of the movie will make you feel. If you already feel the moistness that early, you are going to be feeling it heavy later. I loved it. I love a movie that makes you feel. Too many movies come out and you can watch it and take nothing away. It is just forgetful because there isn't heart or meaning behind it, making it just another soulless cash grab. Which is fitting seeing as how this movie shows the greed side of things.

I think I can say it now that I'm deeper in and it won't make me sound skeevy; GD Demi is wow. It feels like I've been seeing her movies since I was a child. Granted there were maybe more seen whilst I was a teenager... Could be why I always was curious what she was doing next. I still feel sad about how her and Bruno divorced. Anyway, holy moly she is gorgeous. It's also amazing how at the beginning she looks like she hasn't aged much since the movies of the 90's. I was in shock. I know she has always looked good, but even still, in this, she was truly a captivating beauty. But as the shots changes and mere minutes go by and you start to see more and more the effects of time. You can catch a wrinkle here or there, things were done to highlight age. It is amazing and incredibly subtle. Of course her acting is really powerful. It added so much weight to the movie and made it feel so real.

That is the movie really. A very real look at time and age, and the unfair double standards when you want to be famous and a woman. Dennis Quiad, to me, has always had this kind of... meh, quality about him. I haven't really ever thought he was that special. At least his brother was memorable for good reasons before it was clear how crazy he is. In this film tho, you can't help but feel like you need a shower every time you see Dennis. I feel the most squeamish part for me, was watching him eat lunch. I was trying to eat a coney dog and I lost my damn appetite. Once again, the sound effects were so on point. It is shot to really showcase that not only is he a sleazy guy, he's just overly gross. The super zoom of his nasty yellow teeth as he's smoking, or feeling like you're standing in front of him and he is taking a wee between your legs, I legit am about to go take a shower. Just all kinds of off putting, but I love the director for doing it. I really couldn't help but feel "off" the entire film.

I expected things to go a little longer than they did before the citing incident that always kicks off movies like this. Apparently this movie didn't want to waste time showing a gradual change. Nope. Things started to get less than good real fast. I swear, she couldn't even follow the rules a week! You can really feel the struggle between the two halves. Things of course crank to 11 as you near the climax. I don't get how people can hate the ending. I guess the tone shifts slightly, but really it shouldn't be a surprise that it was going that way when you see how the story is built and flowing. It goes from less existential battle, to this rather, monster movie finale. I for one LOVE the ending. I was laughing, much as I do when I see doing what Art does. It goes hard and gets super moist. There are a couple of great homage moments at the climax, between musical score choices and cinematography choices. Just absolutely fantastic.

First I have to say, we spent so much time going down these long hallways, I felt like a 757 could have landed in the space we traveled. There was like, miles of long corridor shots. Of course one of those corridors has The Shinning style color scheme and carpet. There are definitely real homages in this film. I loved the carpet and will always think about The Overlook when I see something like that; and I feel the director had to know that we would make that jump. I feel like that was the "Chekov's gun" moment. Chekov's carpet, as it were. There was going to be blood. You can't have that carpet and not have a Gallagher style squirt-fest. It did not disappoint, and I even love how near the end of the credits it talked about the people that got hosed down by fake blood. So awesome. Just like the final seconds of the film leading up to the last shot. I couldn't help but laugh because of the absurdity of it, and just how good it was. It was exactly the ending I expected, even if I didn't know how to put the pieces together early on.

When they say it is worth the praise, I whole heartedly agree. I feel like this movie made me way more uncomfortable than Art did weeks ago. I'm still sad about that movie feeling neutered compared to the others. This movie did not disappoint. Tho, I am now going to be stuck with the "Call on Me" music video playing in my head for a while. I also feel like that has to be on purpose, not that many would know the video anymore. I always loved the song and it took me some time before I finally saw it. Of course you can't help but laugh at the absolute absurdity of the music video, so I feel it all comes around together perfectly. It also showcases the rather predatory practices used to oggle women. Overly sexualized is the way they refer to it anymore I guess. I wouldn't say that, I think it was very tongue and cheek and another time when people weren't exactly looking to be offended all the time, but I also don't feel the need to be a creep leering at ladies, like you see men act in this film. I can't understand how dudes can be that clueless and push that hard, and yet I know that had to be pretty tame compared to what so many go thru so often. Lol, I end up feeling super second hand embarrassed seeing such idiotic, clueless behavior. Ew for creepy dudes.

Also, I feel like I have to point out, man the young version has such horrible taste in guys. All the dudes in this movie were chuds, man. Serious oof factor. It is an interesting effect now that I think about the moments in the film when you see the crusty dudes droolling all over themselves leering at women. The camera putting you in her point of view, I think, was a super powerful tool. It is not a good feeling to be looking at stuff like that. There was no chance I had any same sex feelings in me, this movie made it even more radicalized. Going to be waking up in cold sweats feeling those crusty old white guys leering. I really need that shower now.

reviews.author: salmatiti7
reviews.body: Du fond du coeur, merci! Lately, I had a bout of doubt regarding my appearance and my body image. I had a long discussion with those closest to me, one of them was my mother who is in her mid sixties and she was telling me if she had a time machine to go back to her younger self, she would have loved every imperfection and lived her life perfectly: happily and without self doubt! I didn't really believe her (seeing as she is my mother and all right) but then later that day, I met some friends and I was curious about the new Cannes sensation without any prior knowledge, so in we go to lift my spirits. I like to let my movies surprise me. So imagine when I was faced with the epitome of horror: my own insecurities and fears thrown at me! And it was... GLORIOUS! The most liberating feeling ever! I think that every woman should watch this movie (maybe a curated version for young girls? ) it's an essential manifest in the era of image! So during the movie, when I understood the plot, I started laughing and crying at the same time, because it was rebuting every little nagging negative thought that still lingered regarding my body! So not only did I call my mother immediately after to tell her she was right, but I also typed out this lengthy comment in my notes to remember and tell Ms Fargeat that she is absolutely right and that she indeed changed someone's perspective today about themselves! And this , for me, is Art, and this is why we watch movies and read stories, not always to escape, but to face our fears head on and conquer them! So here is to an essential movie.

reviews.author: AtiqohSukaHorror
reviews.body:
"The Substance" seems to be a compelling concept that could dive deep into themes of self-identity, perception, and the blurred line between reality and illusion. To make the film truly impactful, I would suggest focusing on strong character development, especially the protagonist's internal struggles as they navigate a world full of distorted truths and shifting realities. The film should also maintain a mysterious tone, with plot twists that challenge the audience's perception without becoming overly confusing.

Visually, it could benefit from a distinctive style-perhaps using surreal imagery or visual effects to represent the protagonist's unraveling understanding of reality. A gripping soundtrack, with subtle, atmospheric music, would elevate the mood and keep the audience engaged.

However, the film must ensure it doesn't overcomplicate the story. A balance between intellectual depth and accessibility is key to maintaining the audience's interest. The concept is intriguing, but it's essential that the narrative is presented in a way that feels cohesive and satisfying.

Rating: 7.5/10. With a strong script and careful execution, "The Substance" has the potential to be a standout film. It just needs to avoid becoming too abstract or convoluted, ensuring that the emotional core is never lost in the complexity of its themes.

reviews.author: martimusross
reviews.body:
The Substance

This was a top quality horror and one not to be missed by aficionados of the genre. The movie presented a reassuring arch like structure, from "shiny star" to "damaged icon". A simple story of an aging actress trying to preserve her place in the world, that required continuing public adulation and acknowledgment to define her existence. Of course it is rooted in Hollywood, and remains a Hollywood story, however this detail does not limit the scope of the movie.

Demi Moore played Elizabeth Sparkle, it was a mesmerising performance, a deeply physical role with little dialogue from start to finish, she pursued relentlessly her goal of preserving her place in the world. I had forgotten how good Demi Moore could be given the right role, shame on me! Without doubt this was an Oscar winning performance, let us see how that works out in the little acknowledged horror genre!

Everything was sacrificed for the central story, but alas there was one central plot flaw, if you could become a better and more beautiful you by splitting in two, and becoming a new you and the old you, what was the benefit for the old you. If you had a shared consciousness then perhaps yes, but here the central plot revolved around resenting the other half of you to your eventual destruction. But perhaps it's better not to dwell on such minutiae.

There were, of course some reflections and derivations from other places, Dorian Grey, Limitless, Poor Things, and Space Odyssey. But on the whole this was brand new serving up of ideas and this is why the movie was so hard hitting.

In terms of themes, many were sacrificed in creating such a powerful story, they were present but only in a broad brush way and never resolved. These was the societal pressure on beauty and a premium of the fresh and new. The corruption of media in pandering rather than shaping societal views on aging. The supplemental pressure to provide even more extreme medical outcomes in the pursuit of perfection. A brief examination on who it is in society demanding such perfection. And that we (the matrix) feed our own demons (the other self) as we are one.

But as I say like Poor Things last year, the central story came before any thematic development so we should not dwell to much on theme.

Many comments on here dwell on a feminist perspective. It is clear Coralie Fargeat wrote the screenplay on feminist themes, but to presume her intent is limited to this reductive trope in a post feminist age in the west is absurd. It is not impossible to conceive of a man in the lead role with the same pressures. Agreed, on the surface the movie presented trite and casual misandry of a stereotypical nature. All men were either presented as entitled, superior, vain, idiotic and simplistic. However this I feel was more of a foil on which to attach the action. In reality Elizabeth's exercise show was made for and watched by largely women who judged her. Then in the closing sequences it was clear women denounced her as a monster all the shouting was done by women, and her most damning criticism is by her other self at multiple points in the movie, if she finds herself disgusting what must of the rest of the world think of her.

I would add that the male media execs reflect society not create society, they pander to demands for the fresh, new, young and vital from a largely female audience. It is to easy to see it entirely the fault of men and through a feminist prism. Women do not come off well in this movie either

Another comment I have read is the movie itself panders to the male gaze, the simple answer is yes it does, and it was meant to pander both to the male and female gaze as the pursuit of body beautiful in integral to the story. Was it gratuitous, yes it was, as it intentionally rammed home the point it was trying the make. Great art requires us to squirm and this movie did it in spades. Such an accusation in this context is the greatest of compliments.

I could not miss highlighting Harvey, the "monster" producer played by Dennis Quaid. He was pervasively evil, relentlessly obscene and the personification of the relentless consumption of youth and talent, the destruction of all things good and pure. This was another Oscar winning performance not unlike Mark Rufalo in Poor Things.

It was a tour de force in cinematography, set design, prosthetics, score and CGI. It was faultless. It was great how, what must've been a bizarre script and idea could be transformed and realised into a finished movie of such style and panache.

Overall I'm going to give this a very firm 9 out of 10, there are many that will not see this movie as it clearly not for anyone with a weak disposition. I on the other hand loved every moment.

reviews.author: baneg4
reviews.body: Honestly, after giving it more thought, I still can't understand why people call this movie a masterpiece. Sure, the audio effects are well-executed and constantly create a sense of pressure, but the rest of it is just an empty shell. It feels like the whole world is moving in the wrong direction, blindly following the media and everything presented to them, as if it must be the truth or worth their time. This film, in particular, tries to push some ideology that is far from normal, yet people swallow it without a second thought. I regret wasting two hours of my life on this. I truly wonder what has happened to people's minds, and how they can celebrate something like this as art. What's considered "normal" today is far from what it should be, and it's sad that we've reached a point where something empty and meaningless is placed on a pedestal.

reviews.author: okcknet
reviews.body:
"The Substance" once again demonstrates how powerful cinema can be as a tool for social critique. As an exceptional example of its genre, the film holds up a harsh mirror to our modern world, delivering a striking and thought-provoking message. Its narrative not only compels viewers to reflect deeply but also sheds light on real-world parallels.

I hope those who resemble the characters or scenarios depicted in this film find the courage to pause and ask themselves, "What are we doing? Where have we come to?" With its impactful storytelling and powerful message, this is a must-watch for anyone who appreciates films of this genre.

reviews.author: ogzhndmnl
reviews.body:
"The Substance" is an in-your-face visual feast with impressive scope on female self-image and societal pressures. Elisabeth Sparkle is a sensational past aerobic queen who finally breaks when a setback in her career makes her reassess things. Desperate to regain the lost youth and beauty, she clings to a mysterious substance promising to change her appearance.

With brash confidence, Director Coralie Fargeat tells an unflinching narrative about body image, aging, and what people would do to try and achieve unattainable beauty standards. The film is visually jolting: surrealist imagery, a bold color palette, and an easy-breezy aesthetic match up with cruelty and violence.

Margaret Qualley gives a powerhouse performance that shows the anguish of Elisabeth both inside and outside, with raw intensity in this character's transformation. It is a sympathetic yet disturbing portrait showing the devastation wrought by social expectations.

While "The Substance" is a witheringly critical look at standards of beauty, it is not squeamish about them either. Some viewers may find the graphic imagery and disturbing themes challenging to watch. To those who are prepared to confront these uncomfortable truths, "The Substance" offers an unforgettable experience on-screen that beats much of what has gone on before.

Overall, "The Substance" is a visually beautiful and intellectually stimulating movie that really tests the bounds of social norms and the 'dark' side of the beauty industry. Though not for all tastes, its bold storytelling and powerhouse performances make it required viewing for those looking for an unconventional yet unforgettable cinematic experience.

reviews.author: mbell-56214
reviews.body: This film certainly won't be to everybody's taste but I really enjoyed it. The last 10 minutes did feel like they didn't know when to stop, but overall it was very entertaining. Just be ready for a very sexualised film and a very gory film especially towards the end. It's a dark horror/comedy and a satire on beauty and how age is perceived in TV. Great acting from all involved and very retro stylised imagery. I suspect this will be one of the most unique film experiences of the year. Would I watch it again? Probably not, but it is definitely worth a watch and worthy of praise. Hats off to all involved in this.

reviews.author: mikeosfpz
reviews.body:
So to be honest, I was kinda hyped for this movie but I wasn't sure that it was going to be good or not because I have seen some news that people left the theaters and I was like okay it's something really strong and disturbing.

I am generally into that stuff but I wasn't sure about that one, so I would say that it really hit me deep and I think that that's the goal of the movie.

To think about the ways that we behave to ourselves and that we create that inner split of who we want to be and who we are.

The bigger the distance between those two people the more pain, disturbance and generally a feeling of emptiness occurs.

The movie is actually talking about this split, talking about how not acceptance of ourselves, of all of our pieces leads to pain and discomfort.

You have to love yourself.

You have to love yourself if you want to feel whole, no matter the external circumstances which obviously are going to affect you, you are a human being after all, but not the same way as if you are not there for you.

You must be there for you and this is the biggest lesson I learned from this movie.

That I must be there for me. It's a must not because someone else tells me that it's a must but because I know it is a must.

I know how it feels to not be there for you, I know how awful it is, I know how much effort it needs to be someone else to compensate for the things that you do not accept yourself.

For me this movie is a must guys and girls.

One of the best movies if not the best movie I watched in 2024.

PS. It's very very graphic, so if you are sensitive on the things you consume, I wouldn't suggest you watching it. You are probably not going to enjoy it.

reviews.author: timmyhollywood
reviews.body:
There are 1200 reviews for The Substance. Cheers if you've come across this one. I watched this movie 4 days ago and am still thinking about it. And I think that's the point.

It's over the top. But it has to be. We're drowning in entertainment, in "content" and you've got to stand out from the crowd.

Of course, there's more than one way to stand out. Ultra violence and gross-out body horror are just one. (Or two, I guess.) But these are deliberate choices.

Filmmaking is a very deliberate process. Ray Liotta was cast in this film in 2022, though he passed in May of that year. That means it was written before 2022. Movies take years to make. Aside from a few avante garde, naturalist filmmakers like Cassavetes, you don't make stuff up on the spot. Every choice in The Substance is for a reason. But I'd wager it's more than to just stand out or get attention.

I enjoyed Margaret Qualley's copiously filmed perfect body because I was meant to. Even though the movie is making a point about the objectification of female bodies in Hollywood, that's not all its doing. First of all, that point is being made with a sledgehammer. And that's not because writer-director Coralie Fargeat thinks we won't get it. She using the medium of film to affect us. Because when she starts turning on the gore, when she start juxtaposing squashed turkey bits with shots of Margaret's body, she's doing something with body horror film I don't think has ever been done. She's conditioning us with it. She's associating these disturbing images with these salacious ones to go to work on our subconscious.

Film is a visual medium. (Never has sound been made use of so well as in The Substance, though.) When David Cronenberg uses body horror or unpleasant images, it feels like we're being taken into a dark dream. The Substance is dreamlike in its allegory and hyperrealism, but the body horror is a tool for us to make an internal connection. Not an intellectual one ("oh yes, objectifying women is bad!") but a visceral one.

Film is a visual medium and men are visual creatures. We're aroused by what we see. This has systematized an objectification of women in the visual medium of cinema for decades. Fargeat uses that same medium to crash into the male psyche so that we may never forget. Because while all this conditioning is going on through the body horror, the narrative of Elizabeth pulses like a vein. So desperate is she to remain ideal and relevant, she's willing to share her very existence with a younger quasi-version of herself. She's willing to get old and decrepit before her time and beyond any normal limits in order to feel the vicarious thrill of the false accolades bearing down on "Sue" for her perfect rump and smile. Elizabeth becomes absolutely hideous -- words cant describe -- and in the middle of it all, her recognizable face peering out, trapped, screaming, a nightmare she can't wake up from. She douses the audience in blood for their complicity. She vomits a breast onto the stage. As if Fargeat is saying, You will never look at a boob the same way again.

No, ma'am, I won't. I will never look at anything the same way again.

reviews.author: MrDHWong
reviews.body:
"The Substance" is a body horror film written and directed by Coralie Fargeat. Starring Demi Moore and Margaret Qualley, it is a superbly dark satire on society's view of beauty standards and the endless desire for outward perfection.

In Los Angeles, the once famous but now washed-up actress Elisabeth Sparkle (Demi Moore) is informed on her 50th birthday that her long-running aerobics TV show has been cancelled due to her advancing age. Devastated, Elisabeth finds great difficulty in processing this bleak news, causing her to become involved in a serious car accident while driving home. As Elisabeth recuperates in hospital, a young male nurse bequeaths with her a small USB flash drive with the words "The Substance" written on top. Later, Elisabeth plugs the flash drive into her computer where she finds it contains an advertisement for a black market serum promising a more beautiful and perfect version of the user. After some initial reluctance, Elisabeth decides to take The Substance which causes a much younger and prettier version of herself to emerge from a hole in her back. The younger self calls herself "Sue" (Margaret Qualley) and is immediately hired to replace Elisabeth in a new aerobics programme tailored specifically to modern viewers. However, the rules of The Substance explicitly state that Elisabeth must transfer her consciousness between herself and Sue every seven days without exception, otherwise dangerous side effects will occur for both bodies.

It is an unfortunate certainty in our professional lives that the older we get, the greater the risk we run of being discarded in favour of younger, more attractive alternatives. This applies to few other professions more than in the world of Hollywood, where one's age and physical appearance is usually the deciding factor as to whether or not somebody soars to stardom or sinks without a trace. Regardless, no matter how much effort someone puts into preserving their youth and vigour, the cruel ravages of time will always catch up at some point to claim yet another unfortunate victim. In the 2024 film "The Substance", we are shown a brutal and often scathing social commentary on the way the general public continues to value superficiality over intellectualism, especially within the cutthroat entertainment industry.

As the film begins, we see the installation of Elisabeth Sparkle's star on Hollywood's Walk of Fame from a top-down perspective. Though her place in Hollywood history is initially met with rave responses, as time marches on, it becomes clear that Elisabeth's star presence is fading away both literally and figuratively. Despite her best days in the spotlight being well and truly behind her, Elisabeth at least has her aerobics programme to keep her somewhat relevant in the public eye, that is, until she is suddenly fired because of her old age. To rub salt in the wound, this redundancy occurs on Elisabeth's 50th birthday, which leaves her with little to no options for her future prospects.

Soon enough, Elisabeth learns of "The Substance", a mysterious illegal drug that can allegedly create a better, younger version of herself. Desperate and against her better judgement, Elisabeth decides to take The Substance and build a new life for herself inside the body of the young and beautiful "Sue", whose alluring good looks and moxie are everything that she no longer once had at her disposal. As to be expected, Sue's popularity skyrockets, leading to many new opportunities to do things she could not while as Elisabeth, but all of this immediate success naturally comes at a deadly price. Although it's quite obvious that things will eventually go horribly wrong for both Elisabeth and Sue, part of what makes the film so great to watch is anticipating exactly how bad events are going to play out.

Since there is a strict rule regarding Elisabeth and Sue only being able to masquerade as each other for just seven days at a time, there are several moments where the film cleverly shows the paradoxical relationship between the two while they are living in their respective bodies. For instance, when Sue is seen taking the world by storm as the new face of aerobics fitness, Elisabeth meanwhile goes about her daily business revelling in her insecurities as an older woman. Here, the film shows extreme close-ups on Elisabeth's worried face to emphasise her prominent wrinkles, which is in stark contrast to Sue's clear skin and radiant smile. On the other hand, we also see how Sue must ration her fun carefully, knowing that if she enjoys herself too much she could lose track of time and suddenly revert back to Elisabeth without realising it. Throughout the film, I couldn't help but feel invested in witnessing the growing animosity between this single consciousness sharing two conflicting personalities, which leads to an explosively entertaining finale.

Perhaps the best way to describe this film's distinct style is to take the visual cues of Stanley Kubrick, add in a nice helping of gory body horror from David Cronenberg, season it with a healthy dosage of surreal imagery from David Lynch and then sprinkle in a dash of John Carpenter's unsettling mood of paranoia. In any other case, this strange amalgamation of directorial styles shouldn't work this harmoniously, but somehow Coralie Fargeat managed to find a way. I was absolutely fascinated watching how Fargeat weaved everything in her film together so creatively without ever giving the impression she's arbitrarily stealing from these filmmakers that she clearly considers her biggest influences. Of course, I would have to say that the film feels most like something Cronenberg would make due to its graphic blood and gore practical effects, which particularly brings to mind his movie "The Fly". With that in mind, if the grisly sight of someone literally forcing their way out of another person's skin like how a butterfly emerges from a cocoon sounds shocking to you, then this film might not be your cup of tea.

For what can be described as possibly her greatest performance, Demi Moore brilliantly embodies the role of Elisabeth, whose yearning to stay relevant in the wake of growing old strikes the perfect balance between sympathetic and sinister. Watching how Elisabeth becomes increasingly obsessed with reliving her glory days as a young, beautiful icon of the screens is quite tragic the more you think about it. Moore's take on the character of Elisabeth allows the audience to understand why it is so important she seeks out this desire to adopt the alter-ego of Sue, who is everything she can no longer be at her current age. Ironically, in an effort to confirm the unfairness in society preferring more youthful, fresh-faced people in the limelight, Elisabeth soon discovers she prefers her own younger counterpart over her old true self.

Working flawlessly in sync with her co-star, Margaret Qualley stands out just as much in the role of Sue, whose peppy, enthusiastic attitude is undeniably infectious to watch. It is clear that Sue thrives on all of the attention she receives from her admirers, whether its the leering eyes of the sleazy male TV executives to the modern young generation who idolise her for having a perfect athletic figure and perpetually positive attitude. I was impressed with how Qualley was able to maintain a certain level of dignity as Sue, not playing her as an air-headed bimbo but instead as a confident young woman with a hidden insecure side that shows through as a result of Elisabeth's longing to reignite her waning popularity. Without giving away spoilers, the film's final act makes great use of both Elisabeth's and Sue's contrasting dynamic, culminating in a rather appropriately poetic climax.

Standing leagues above virtually every other film of its genre, "The Substance" just might be one of the most disturbing yet thought-provoking satires about human vanity to grace movie screens in the longest time. Though its gross-out imagery will likely prove off-putting to many viewers, I encourage those with a strong stomach to stick with it, as you are likely to find plenty to appreciate in the otherwise clever way the film handles its important subject matter. No matter how hard we try, there's no escaping the inevitability of growing old as this is simply a dark byproduct of being human. However, if there's one thing this film can teach us, it's that human egoism can be even darker.

I rate it a solid 9/10.

reviews.author: arungeorge13
reviews.body:
First thought: The Substance, without even trying, makes modern-day food blogging look like an incredibly disgusting career, if you understand what I mean. The close-up shots offer a uniquely harrowing perspective, sometimes. The abundance of butt shots is a Coralie Fargeat signature, I believe?

Further thoughts: This is a deeply disconcerting film. It has body-horror frames that make you want to look away, and not just because they're "gory". Coralie conceptualizes every form of body horror one can imagine, using splendid prosthetics to gross out even the toughest of viewers. Also, the film manages to be tremendously entertaining while at it.

Both Demi Moore and Margaret Qualley offer performances worth diving deeper into - the former, for her nuanced take on loneliness and being a has-been; the latter for her sultry take as a selfish, attention-loving, Gen Z(?) model. Big shoutout to Moore & Qualley for the prosthetics-heavy scenes - both handled them like true body-horror-victims (David Cronenberg would be proud!). Qualley is busy playing "bad gal" in ways only she can, making viewers' jaws drop. Her prosthetic-heavy bits almost remind you of the mutated abominations from The Thing (yikes!).

Some scenes also reminded me of Shankar's "I" (2015), for cosmetic reasons. The ugly side of showbiz is explored in greater satirical detail, with characters like that of Dennis Quaid's only serving to drive that point home. Aiding the storytelling big time is Raffertie's score, which underlines the personas' growing hatred of each other. Pierre-Olivier Persin (make-up effects designer & supervisor), take a bow!

A late twist even adds a spectacularly blood-soaked set piece, reminding us why Fargeat's very much an action director (I wasn't a fan of Revenge though - maybe, I should rewatch it?). But, good lord, can anything prepare us for what awaits us during the climax? Nope. This, my LB geeks, is a SPECIAL film.

P. S. The relevance of that first shot - just wow!

reviews.author: Steven_Likes_Movies
reviews.body:
Cool movie that goes completely off the rails. The skill and creativity of the cinematography, editing, music, and sound design are amazing. Really captivating. Camera angles and movements are bold and grab your attention from the get-go. The close ups are wild. The lighting and colors of things are equally technically impressive. The shots trailing the yellow coat on the run are hilarious. The rather long movie moves quickly largely because it is so sonically and visually tantalizing. It's really in your face. The story itself unfolds briskly. It all makes sense, is intriguing, and clear to follow. The acting too holds your attention convincingly.

The film gets increasingly gruesome, particularly about halfway through. I had to look away and past my hand a few times. I did laugh though when the special effects went into Cronenberg territory. The final act is a film of it's own. The story and associated special effects go from uncomfortably realistic to outer space. The film on a whole goes from bizarre to absurd to ridiculous and I don't know why. It would have been nice to have the story resolve in a more intelligent way, punctuating the main premise and the tone of the beginning and middle of the film with some poignancy, even subtlety, or even just letting it all sit as a question, but alas acute violence and over-the-top gore was the filmmaker's exclamation point. Questionable, the decision to take technical brilliance into rather comical cliché, but good movie to see anyway, all things considered.

reviews.author: anon-15964
reviews.body:
This movie reminds of the best parts of Poor Things and Annihilation.

The central theme of the movie is how far are we willing to go in sacrificing the long term for the short term. A concept that applies equally to movie stars, drug addicts, and frankly everyone in everyday life.

This theme is perfectly portrayed through a lightly surrealistic story of an established actress living through a younger version of herself 7 days every other week. Although there are no sinister motives to this setup, the younger version quickly starts sacrificing her older self for the here and now.

This is a concept we all relate to. Another drink on a fun night, passing the hangover to a different version of yourself tomorrow.

This movie was close to a 10/10, but ultimately goes way off the rails in an uninteresting way in the last 20 minutes. Thematically, the story had already concluded, but to finish the movie we have to suffer through an oddly placed scene of derivative body horror that looks like a 70's version of concepts stolen from annihilation.

So dropped it from a 10/10 to an 8/10. If you stop watching when you see a tooth in a sink, you have seen the best of it.

reviews.author: troy-boulton
reviews.body:
Gratuitous and craftily, unapologetically derivative, Coralie Fargeat's brilliant social comedy channels Cronenberg and a good dose of Carpenter and even early Peter Jackson, with nods to Kubrick and Oscar Wilde thrown in for good measure. Quite the melange, but it never feels forced - except for when Fargeat skilfully intends it to be. A film like this can't avoid ironic levels of hypocrisy, and this director knows how and when to lay it on thick.

But don't mistake "The Substance" for a simplistic feminist boot to the groin of the Youth Industrial Complex, or only a commentary on Hollywood and its shallow beauty standards. It is a piece that is as conceptually nuanced as it is graphically unrestrained. It speaks out not only against the cult of youth, but eviscerates our very relationships with ourselves as we age in a culture that worships cosmetic and physical perfection.

Blaring 80s semiotics in a homage to Kubic's visual style, the film manages to capture our moment in times's obsession with liminality and nostalgia for the late 20th century aesthetic, and shape it into a commentary about a culture that is consuming itself. As wryly amusing as it is equal parts visually striking and disgusting, this isn't one to miss, nor to underestimate.

reviews.author: smythersrc
reviews.body:
"The Substance" delivers a cinematic experience that feels straight out of the mind-bending world of "Black Mirror"-a high compliment for fans of thought-provoking sci-fi. With its unsettling and intense atmosphere, the film explores themes that push the boundaries of reality, pulling viewers into a vivid, sensory-driven journey. It's as visually mesmerizing as it is psychologically intriguing, blending suspense with a surreal tone that lingers long after the credits roll.

However, be warned: this film isn't for the faint-hearted. Its immersive style and heavy focus on sensory details can be intense, sometimes bordering on overwhelming. For those who are easily unsettled by sensory overload, it might be worth approaching this one with caution. Yet for those who can embrace the experience, "The Substance" is a bold, thrilling dive into a darkly imaginative narrative that keeps you guessing and thinking. This is a film that doesn't just ask to be watched-it demands to be experienced.

reviews.author: maxkjaerremy
reviews.body:

reviews.author: apg123
reviews.body: Strong movie, strong topic, strong dialogs, strong characters. Well executed. A movie to think about for days and days, and to tell your friends about. I give it a 10 out of 10 because I think that's how movies should be. HOWEVER, I was not prepared for a horror splatter movie in the old style, like Bad Taste, Braindead or Meet The Feebles. This actually quite spoiled my evening, and my sleep that night, since I was looking forward to a psychological, mid-life crisis themed movie, as I'm 50 myself. I was expecting something like Smashed, or maybe even Silver Linings. I was expecting some drama, some shouting, some crying, and some insight into the nature of life and human existence - but sure not this level of extreme blood, splatter and gore. So be warned!

reviews.author: brockfal
reviews.body:
This 'body horror' drama/comedy starts impressively and imaginatively. In modern LA, a self consciously ageing movie star gets fired but by chance discovers a 'substance' that could restore her younger self. Ok, so what a clever idea, one with infinite possibilities for humour and insight. Unfortunately, after the first 30 minutes or so the film becomes more and more crass and less and less clever. Demi Moore is indeed excellent in the lead role and Dennis Quade gives his all as a particularly obnoxious TV executive, but I got less and less interested as the film went on, giving up completely in the last 20 minutes, when it really does go off the tracks.

The film won the best screenplay at Cannes, and although the concept might be inspired and clever, I couldn't help thinking that so much more could been achieved here.

reviews.author: Movie_Rating_n_Ranking
reviews.body:
For me, there is no such thing as a perfect film, so I have never given a film a 10/10. That said, when the credits for The Substance were rolling, I seriously considered it. But no. It's a solid 9. Let's see why.

When a feature film is brave enough to show itself conceptually, full of analogies, metaphors, satire and exaggerated representations, but without losing its way in its harsh, acidic and sharp criticism, there is no other option than to give it the respect it deserves, because it's a film that shows respect for the viewer's intelligence.

The Substance is that and much more, because if that weren't enough, it allows itself to pay homage to great classics of past cinema with obvious references. And again, if that weren't enough, it adds to the mix a subgenre that impacts, amazes and stays in the public eye for a long time, such as Body Horror.

There are so many things to highlight here, that I will run out of characters. Photography and direction, top notch. Symmetrical shots that play with perspectives, geometry and the perception of space. Vibrant colours that combine with impeccable illumination. Choice of daring lenses that transform simple shots into a spectacle. The visual effects and prosthetic make-up are all on point.

The sound is a show apart. The sound editing is raw, impertinent, impeccably disturbing, adding a great element to the tense and grotesque atmosphere.

The performances are excellent. Demi Moore shows her credentials and leaves us speechless. Margaret Qualley and Dennis Quaid are spectacular.

If we get into the plot, it's a mix of many things. Unfortunately, it's my main obstacle to keep this film from getting a perfect score. There are situations that could have been closer to reality so that the conviction is not lost. There are situations that could have been shorter or more defining, especially in the last act. In any case, they are tiny details that do not take you out of the plot.

To conclude, this movie blew my mind. Few movies take my breath away and this is one of the few from 2024 that did it.

Side note: Don't watch it with any food or snack.

reviews.author: karmendrasingh22
reviews.body:
The Substance delivers a compelling cinematic experience, showcasing masterful editing and a tightly woven script that keeps viewers engaged throughout its runtime. The film's stunning visuals and inventive camera work elevate the narrative, immersing the audience in the haunting world of Elisabeth Sparkle (Demi Moore) as she grapples with age and identity. Demi Moore and Margaret Qualley deliver outstanding performances, capturing the emotional turmoil of their characters with depth and authenticity. This combination of strong acting, sharp writing, and impressive production values makes The Substance a must-see for fans of innovative horror and social commentary.

Beyond its surface narrative of lust for youth, The Substance explores profound societal themes that resonate across generations. At its core, the film critiques the relentless expectations placed on each generation by the preceding one, revealing how these pressures distort emotional landscapes and standards of quality living. The story illustrates a cycle where society's insatiable craving for success drives individuals to the brink of inhumanity, resulting in a chaotic mental and psychological toll that affects generation after generation.

This relentless pursuit of an ideal life fosters a toxic environment, creating rifts filled with both positive and negative emotions between individuals. The film poignantly captures this chaos, showcasing how the characters' interactions reflect their struggles against societal norms and personal desires. Through its haunting visuals and compelling performances, The Substance invites viewers to reflect on the cost of societal pressures, revealing that the quest for perfection often leads to self-destruction and despair.

Ultimately, The Substance serves as a powerful commentary on the destructive nature of societal expectations, illustrating that the price of chasing unattainable ideals can be devastating for both individuals and society as a whole.

The Substance presents a compelling narrative that transcends its superficial focus on beauty standards, delving into the profound psychological ramifications of generational expectations. While the film features the obsession with youth as a subplot, its core message critiques the relentless pressure exerted by previous generations on the next to fulfill unachieved desires or to exceed them in ways that often lead to emotional detachment and psychological turmoil.

At the heart of the story is Elisabeth Sparkle (Demi Moore), a once-celebrated actress who embodies the struggles faced by many individuals caught in the web of societal and familial expectations. The film poignantly illustrates how these pressures manifest not only in personal aspirations but also in the broader context of societal norms that encourage individuals to seek validation through material success and external approval. This relentless pursuit creates a cycle where each generation feels compelled to achieve more than their predecessors, often at the expense of their mental health and emotional well-being.

As Elisabeth grapples with her identity and self-worth, she becomes a vessel through which the film explores the damaging effects of this generational pressure. The narrative suggests that what is often framed as "sacrifice" or "motivation" from one generation can, in reality, lead to profound psychological damage for the next. The expectation to excel or to relive past glories creates an environment where individuals feel they must constantly prove their worth, leading to feelings of inadequacy and despair when they inevitably fall short.

Moreover, this cycle of expectation extends beyond familial relationships; it permeates social structures, affecting peers, colleagues, and even students. The film highlights how such pressures can lead to emotional detachment, where individuals become disconnected not only from their own feelings but also from those of their loved ones. This detachment fosters an environment where mental health issues can flourish, resulting in tragic consequences when individuals reach a breaking point.

When these individuals collapse under the weight of their burdens, it is not just their immediate family that suffers; the ripple effects extend throughout society. The film effectively portrays this horror, illustrating how communities bear witness to the psychological trauma inflicted by unattainable expectations. The aftermath of such collapses serves as a stark reminder of the collective responsibility we share in fostering environments that prioritize mental well-being over superficial achievements.

In conclusion, The Substance is a powerful exploration of how generational expectations can warp individual identities and lead to devastating consequences. By framing beauty standards as a subplot within this larger narrative, the film invites viewers to reflect on the societal structures that perpetuate these cycles of pressure and trauma. It challenges us to reconsider our definitions of success and fulfillment, urging a shift towards understanding and compassion for those navigating the complexities of modern life. Ultimately, The Substance serves as a poignant reminder that while aspirations can inspire us, they must not come at the cost of our humanity.

reviews.author: MamadNobari97
reviews.body:
This film is already a classic for me and I pretty much loved everything in this. But I doubt anyone who hates gore and isn't a fan of body horror gonna like this one, because it goes hard on the body horror in the third act and I don't even think The Thing or any Cronenberg films can even compete with the body horror of this film.

So even though I pretty much hinted at what you're gonna be in for when going into this film, especially with my title, I don't want to spoil anything from this film and even allude to what the plot might be about. Because this movie is one of those you just have to hit play without any prior knowledge whatsoever.

Do not even read the synopsis on here. Do not watch the trailer. Even my review is a spoiler, but at the very least you're gonna know beforehand that if you're a fan of body horror you're gonna love it, and if not, you might not like it. But definitely go into this movie blind because it's a wild ride and better to be experienced blind.

The movie itself isn't that deep or even subtle at all. Every aspect of the film screams in a very obvious manner what the film is about. The dialogue isn't subtle, the editing, the camerawork, and the direction are certainly not subtle in conveying what they want to say either. So why is this movie that lays its message bare from the beginning and doesn't even try to be subtle about so highly rated by people, and also gets a 9/10 from me? Because it's so well-made and enjoyable to watch. I'm a sucker for body horror, so obviously I loved this film especially the utterly goofy ending of it.

What makes this film so great firstly is its impeccable and unique camerawork and editing. Although the editing might seem way too hyperactive and ADHD-inducing, and you might think it's gonna get really annoying real fast if they keep it up for the entire 2:30 hours of the film, but thankfully they pump the breaks on the paranoid schizo editing and camerawork for most of the second act so it doesn't get annoying and overdone.

I also loved all the practical effects and makeup in this films and I kept saying "This looks so good, how did they do that?" while watching the film. It's just refershing watching such a well-crafted art of makeup and body suits in a modern movie that doesn't use cheap CGI for it.

I don't know where this Coralie Fargeat lady came from, but it feels like she came out of nowhere and just dropped one of the most well-directed and well-made films of the year and the past couple of years out of the blue. She only has one other movie called Revenge in her filmography which I haven't but will definitely watch. So I am actually surprised how well-written and well-directed someone's only second film can be. I will certainly follow this director from now on and watch everything she's gonna make in the future, she has a lot of talent. Hopefully, the quality only gets better.

And the acting is also really good, especially Dennis Quaid who pretty much steals the show here. Demi Moore is also great in this and she gets gradually more material to work with throughout the film and she gets better and better.

The film starts with a similar concept to a Black Mirror episode and turns into the most Cronenberg thing you'll ever see. I don't think I've even seen a Cronenberg film that leans this much into the body horror aspect before, they have much more restraint honestly. I was actually thinking how much restraint this film has with the gore and body horror at first, but the end went full gross-out body horror.

Anyway, I can't really say much else without spoiling, do yourself a favor and don't read synopsis or watch trailers before going into this. Even if you're not a fan of body horror, you will definitely still enjoy the great direction, cinematography, and editing it has to offer. It's a must watch.

reviews.author: chand-suhas
reviews.body:
Elisabeth Sparkle (Demi Moore) had a successful career, making the transition from the big screen to the small screen as aerobics show tv host. As she turns 50, she overhears her producer talking about replacing her with an younger host. She gets distracted at the fact her age has caught up with her fame and ends up at the hospital after being in an car accident. The male nurse attending her, offers her a black market serum named The Substance which can turn her into a perfect, younger looking self. Elisabeth goes through with it, creating Sue (Margaret Qualley) her younger self. All she has to do is transfer her consciousness every 7 days into Sue's body without fail. What happens when the two start getting jealous of each other and break the one rule, forms rest of the story.

I will come to the body horror part later as I got mighty impressed by the story itself. A fading Hollywood star wanting to hold onto her younger beauty due to the beauty standards levied on her by the entertainment industry. The struggle she has with her true identity, outside her celebrity status was well established early on. It's a brutal world out there and not everyone is cut out for the competition yet the one who do make it, just want to last longer at any cost. This is what pushes Elisabeth to pay the price, just to feel wanted. The performances by Demi Moore and Margaret Qualley were spot on, especially during the latter growing her own consciousness. The story entirely revolves around the two and the director ensures she never loses focus on any other sub plots. This further gets aided by the body horror and that elevates the film perfectly, prepping for that climax. Those last few minutes at the new year's party to the walk of fame shot, was completely worth watching this.

reviews.author: ObsessiveCinemaDisorder
reviews.body:
I winced, cringed, and laughed nervously throughout The Substance, the arthouse body horror film from French director Coralie Fargeat. Even covering my eyes at its most cringing toe-curling moments of dread and disgust, I loved every moment of it.

Elisabeth Sparkle, a fading film-now-turned-aerobics TV star, is fired by her producer, Harvey, due to old age. Desperate to stay in the spotlight, Elisabeth injects an underground illegal substance that creates a copy of her younger self...

The film's opening shot, which I will not spoil, is the perfect visual exposition, showing how the Substance functions. Immediately, I nervously giggled, dreading all the horror that was about to unfold. What an opening...

To follow the adage "good artists copy, great artists steal," The Substance is Ocean's Eleven, pulling the perfect heist in glorious style, simultaneously stealing from Stanley Kubrick, David Cronenberg, and Requiem for a Dream.

I wonder how different the film would have been if it used an original style. The lack of an original style is perhaps the reason that it won Best Screenplay instead of the Palme d'Or at the 2024 Cannes Film Festival. But no, that's not Coralie Fargeat's primary concern.

These combined visual styles act as a shorthand, punctuating the moment with established cinematic language efficiently, rip-roaring through its long list agenda of shock and awe.

Writer-director Coralie Fargeat destroys the male gaze, delivering endless gratuitous fast-cut pounding close-ups of the female body until it's nauseating. There's no subtlety to speak here. Supertext is subtext.

The film brilliantly dramatizes the surmounting pressure women (I'd argue everybody) go through as beauty standards become increasingly unreachable from make-up, diet, cosmetic surgery, and now AI filters... It's increasingly difficult to accept one's looks as they are.

Demi Moore, Margaret Qualley, and Dennis Quaid deliver great performances, each equally physical and daring, and are committed to taking things up to eleven. If the awards trends blow in its direction-and the Golden Globes indicate so, I suspect Moore and Quaid will receive award nominations.

reviews.author: NathanVzz
reviews.body:
*The Substance* takes a premise that, while not entirely new, is masterfully revitalized through Coralie Fargeat's sharp direction. By reimagining the familiar pursuit of perfection, the film critiques modern societal pressures surrounding beauty and aging with a fresh, contemporary lens. The narrative feels both timely and unsettling, drawing viewers into a chilling exploration of how far individuals will go for acceptance. The film's sharp social commentary is provocative without losing relevance, making it an essential reflection on today's obsession with appearance.

Demi Moore and Margaret Qualley deliver standout performances, balancing the film's emotional weight. Moore brings gravitas and nuance to her role, effortlessly portraying a woman on the edge of societal and personal collapse. Qualley complements this with a raw, visceral energy, creating a powerful dynamic between the two characters. While Moore's commanding presence slightly overshadows, both actresses elevate the film with their chemistry, making it hard to choose a clear standout. Moore's performance, in particular, is Oscar-worthy, with a depth that leaves a lasting impact.

Visually, *The Substance* excels with its blend of practical effects and striking visuals. The body horror elements are crafted with precision, immersing the audience in a world that is both grotesque and captivating. Fargeat's direction keeps the tension taut from start to near finish, with a strong narrative drive that holds attention. However, the film's extended runtime dilutes its climactic impact. The ending, while effective, lacks the explosive twist it seems to build toward. Nevertheless, *The Substance* revitalizes a familiar concept, delivering a relevant and bold critique. As a horror, it terrifies; as a drama, it shocks-an outstanding film of 2024. I could easily see Demi Moore at the Oscars.

reviews.author: ahmed-alnahhass
reviews.body:
Well first, it is not a horror movie.

But,

Its amazing in terms of visuals. The cinematography, colors, and every shot are beautifully crafted, creating a world that feels both eerie and elegant. The film's visuals alone make it worth watching, drawing you right into Elisabeth's story.

The movie is split into two main parts. The first half feels almost like a long commercial, where every sound and detail counts, setting up the allure of beauty and perfection. This builds up the tension as Elisabeth dives deeper into her journey to regain her youth.

In the second half, we see the real horror unfold. Elisabeth's new, artificial self begins to take over her original self, which is a smart way to show how chasing youth with chemicals can destroy the real person inside. The more youth she gains, the more harm it does to her, revealing the painful cost of these "enhancements."

One downside, though, is the overuse of nudity and some lengthy shots focused on body parts. While this was likely meant to highlight themes of beauty and objectification, it sometimes felt unnecessary and took away from the story.

Overall, The Substance is a unique film that uses body horror to explore society's obsession with youth and beauty. It's haunting, thought-provoking, and visually stunning, leaving a lasting impression.

reviews.author: icaropc17
reviews.body:

I thought about walking out of the theater multiple times, and the only reason I stayed was because my friends were with me.

The premise is completely cliché. Cloning yourself? I've seen this same concept play out a million times.

The editing is also terrible, with excessive close-ups and awkward cuts. It seems like it's trying hard to be edgy and modern, but it only makes things worse.

Do yourself a favor and skip this one.

reviews.author: HuziFilmGuru
reviews.body:
Okay, let's talk about The Substance. This body horror film is an absolute trip and one of the best horror movies of 2024, hands down. Seriously, if you're looking for a flick that's both surreal and intense, look no further. It dives deep into the themes of gratitude and self-acceptance in a way that hits hard and stays with you.

Demi Moore is back and better than ever-she absolutely kills it in this role. Her performance brings a weight to the film that you just can't ignore. And can we please talk about Margaret Qualley? She's becoming a force to be reckoned with, proving she deserves all the praise and more. Watching her in this movie, you can't help but feel like she's just on the brink of becoming a huge star.

What I loved most about The Substance is how it reminds us to appreciate what we have, even when things get dark and twisted. The body horror elements are intense and unsettling, but they serve a purpose: to remind us that our bodies are beautiful as they are. In a world that often tells us we need to change, this film boldly flips that narrative.

If you're in the mood for a horror movie that not only scares you but also makes you reflect on your own self-image and gratitude, this is it. Don't sleep on The Substance. It's a wild ride that will leave you thinking long after the credits roll. So grateful for movies like this that push boundaries and challenge our perspectives. Definitely one to catch in theaters!

reviews.author: vagpapakonstantinou
reviews.body: This is one of the few times in my life when I walked out of a movie theater and I felt shock, awe, dismay, shock, excitement, tension and anxiety. If the purpose of the film was to show through the body horror genre the cry against the exploitation industry of women and the extremes to which they can go to, even the alienation from their own self that leads to disfigurement, it succeeded completely! The performances of the two leading actresses were FANTASTIC, exciting, serving perfectly the script and the competition between them until their final fall. I feel great respect for Demi Moore being reintroduced to the general public and watching her you can only be proud of her not only for her choice to be in this film, but how she served it. Margaret Qualley I have to say is a shining star; not because she is beautiful and glamorous, but because she fully enters into her role, knowing that she is aware at one point that it is a one-way street.

reviews.author: vinaymenon-70095
reviews.body:
The Substance is a movie that is relentless in shashing your face into the message of it. Every set piece somehow feels worse than the last set piece. If you're not into body horror, avoid this movie at all costs, because it revels in its body horror and sticks your nose in it.

The best way I can describe this movie without spoilers is that it's a Black Mirror episode that's on steroids and is actively punching you in the face.

The camera work and music and even subtitles are good embellishments for the film.

Watch the movie with that state of mind, don't worry about the logistics and logic of the film, and I'm sure you'll definitely enjoy it.
